Branch memory

Each premise below was written three times by the same model. Story A is written scene by scene with nothing else to go on. For B and C, the model proposes several next moves, one is picked at random, and the rest are kept as unused directions that can colour later scenes. In B those directions fade over the scenes; in C they never fade.

Story 1: fantasyStory 2: weird westernStory 3: comedy of mannersStory 4: science fictionStory 5: cozy detectiveStory 6: literary mysteryStory 7: psychological thrillerStory 8: quiet horrorStory 9: family dramaStory 10: historical fiction

fantasy

In a walled city where bakers swear an oath never to refuse a loaf, a young apprentice is ordered by the governor to refuse one woman.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Isel was raking coals when the governor's steward came into the bakery, and the steward did not wipe his boots. The master baker, Orrin Dace, kept his hands in the dough.

"Baker's oath," the steward said, and nodded at the lintel, where the words had been cut into the stone a hundred years ago and blackened by smoke: *No hand turned from this oven.*

"I know what's over my own door," Orrin said.

The steward unrolled a strip of paper with the governor's red seal dripping from its corner. "A woman named Wenna Hale lives on Tallow Stair. Gray coat, left hand missing two fingers. She will come for bread. She is not to be sold any. Not a heel, not a crumb."

Orrin pressed the dough flat with his knuckles. "The oath—"

"The governor knows the oath. He says the apprentice will carry it out." The steward looked at Isel for the first time. She was fourteen, with flour to her elbows and a peel in her fists as long as she was tall. "Your master's name is on the guild roll. Yours isn't yet."

Isel looked at Orrin. He kept his eyes on the dough.

"She comes at second bell," the steward said. "Usually."

He left the paper on the bench. When the door shut, the draft lifted one corner of it, and Isel set a loaf pan on top to hold it down.

Scene 2

Orrin finished the dough, shaped it into four rounds, and set them under a cloth before he spoke.

"Rye," he said. "Half a loaf, every third day. She pays in coppers and counts them twice on the counter."

"Who is she?"

"A woman who buys rye." He wiped his hands down his apron, slowly, one finger at a time. "Her husband laid stone for the east gate. Fell from the scaffold, I heard. Years back."

"What did she do to the governor?"

"The paper doesn't say, does it."

Isel lifted the loaf pan and read the strip again. The steward's handwriting leaned hard to the right, as if the words were being pushed through a door. *Not a heel, not a crumb.* She put the pan back.

Orrin went to the rack and began turning the morning loaves, though they didn't need it. "My hands are on the guild roll," he said. "They'll take the shop, and the oven with it. Forty years that oven's been lit. It's never once gone cold."

"Then I should say no to her."

"I didn't tell you to do anything." He rapped a crust with his knuckle, listened, and moved to the next. "I'm going down for flour."

The cellar door shut behind him. Overhead, the tower struck first bell.

Scene 3

Isel moved the rye to the back of the rack and then moved it forward again. Whichever way it sat, she could smell it.

The bell had not yet struck when the door opened. The woman wore a gray coat buttoned to the throat. Her left hand, on the latch, had a thumb, a forefinger, and a smooth place where the rest should be.

"Orrin's down in the cellar," Isel said.

"I don't need Orrin. Half a rye."

"We're out."

Wenna Hale looked at the rack. Four rounds sat there, crusts split and pale with flour, and steam still curled off the nearest. She looked at them for as long as it takes to say a short prayer. Then she looked at Isel, and her face did not change at all.

"All right," she said.

She unknotted a cloth from her sleeve and tipped the coppers onto the counter. She pushed them into a row with her good hand and counted them, lips moving. She swept them back and counted again.

"Six," she said. "It was five last spring."

"I know."

"Then you know what half a rye costs."

Isel's hands were wet inside the peel's worn grip. Beneath her feet, a sack dragged across the cellar floor, and stopped.

Wenna set the six coppers in a line on the counter and folded her arms.

Scene 4

"Steam's still coming off them," Wenna said. "Out of what, then?"

Isel's mouth opened. Nothing in it was ready.

Wenna's eyes went past her to the bench, to the loaf pan and the strip of paper under it, and the red wax gone hard at its corner. She did not reach for it. She only looked, the way she had looked at the rack.

"He sent one to the chandler, too," she said. "Wouldn't sell me tallow. I've been burning rushes since the thaw." She tucked her ruined hand into her sleeve. "I don't mind the telling no. I mind being told it's *out*."

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be sorry. Be plain."

The tower began to strike second bell. Isel counted without meaning to. At the first stroke the cellar went silent, and at the second she heard the creak of the bottom stair, where Orrin put his weight when he was listening.

Wenna did not turn toward the sound. She slid one copper an inch nearer to Isel and left her finger on it.

"Half a rye," she said. "Whenever you've decided what you are."

Isel's palm lay flat against the nearest loaf. It was still hot enough to hurt.

Scene 5

Isel took the long knife from its hook. The rye was hot enough that the crust crackled under the blade, and when it parted, steam rolled up into her face. She cut straight through the middle and laid the halves on the board, crumb up.

Wenna Hale did not move her finger from the copper.

"Wrap it," Isel said to no one. She tore a square of linen from the roll, and her hands shook so badly that the first fold slid open. She folded it again, tighter, and tucked the corners under.

The cellar door scraped. Orrin stood at the top of the stairs with a sack of flour on his shoulder, white to the eyebrows. He looked at the half loaf in the linen, at the other half on the board, at the coppers in their row. He said nothing. He walked to the bin, tipped the sack in, and the flour went down in a long soft roar that filled the room with dust.

Isel pushed the bundle across the counter. Wenna lifted it and held it against her coat with her good arm.

"Still hot," she said.

"It'll stay that way until Tallow Stair."

Wenna took her finger off the copper. She left all six on the counter. At the door she stopped, hand on the latch, and looked back at the strip of paper.

Then she went out, and the bell over the door rang twice.

Scene 6

Flour dust was still settling over the bin when Orrin set the empty sack down. It hung in the light from the front window and dropped onto the counter, onto the six coppers, onto Isel's wrists.

"Put the knife back," he said.

She hung it on its hook. The blade was clean, but she had to look at it twice to be sure.

Orrin gathered the coppers into his palm and weighed them there. He didn't carry them to the till. He went to the slate by the oven, took the chalk from its string, and under the morning's tally he wrote *3½ rye*. The chalk squeaked on the last stroke.

"The steward counts loaves," he said. "Not what's said over them."

"You heard me tell her we were out."

"I heard." He tipped the coppers into a chipped crock on the high shelf, between the yeast pot and a jar of caraway. "Four rounds went under that cloth this morning. I'm not going to chalk three."

Isel opened the firebox. The coals had burned down to a red crust. "Do I go to the guild?"

"Feed the oven."

She split oak against the chopping block until her arms stopped trembling. When she straightened, a boy in the governor's green was walking past the window. He slowed at the glass, looked in, and kept walking. A moment later he passed back the other way.

Scene 7

The steward came back before the tower struck third bell, and this time he wiped his boots on the mat, once each, deliberately, so that Isel noticed.

He did not look at the paper under the loaf pan. He went to the slate by the oven and read it with his hands clasped behind him.

"Three and a half rye."

"Yes," Orrin said. He was shaping again, and his thumbs did not slow.

"The boy at your window saw a woman in a gray coat leave with something wrapped in linen." The steward turned. "Apprentice."

Isel set down the split oak. Her palms were gritty with bark. *Be plain.*

"She asked for half a rye. I told her we were out. She saw the rack and knew I'd lied. Then I cut her a half and wrapped it and she took it." Her voice stayed level, which surprised her. "She left six coppers. They're in the crock on the high shelf."

The steward looked at the crock, then at the lintel, then at her flour-whitened arms.

"The governor receives petitioners at the hall tomorrow, at first bell," he said. "You'll come. Not your master."

He lifted the loaf pan, took the strip of paper, and folded it in thirds along its old creases. The red wax cracked as it bent.

"Bring the crock," he said.

Scene 8

Isel carried the crock in both arms with a linen cloth tied over the mouth, and the coppers shifted at every step up the hall's stone stairs. The steward walked ahead of her and did not look back.

Petitioners sat along the benches: a man with a goat's rope looped around his wrist, two sisters arguing in whispers. None of them looked at her crock. The governor sat at a long table with a ledger open before him. He was older than she had pictured, thick through the shoulders, with a stonemason's scarred knuckles gone soft with years of pens.

"Set it down," he said.

She set it on the table and untied the cloth. He tipped the coppers into his palm and spread them across the page with one finger. He counted them, lips still, and counted again.

"Six."

"Yes, my lord."

"Half a rye was five last spring."

"Yes."

He pushed five coppers back toward the crock, one at a time, until they clicked against the rim. The sixth he kept under his thumb. Outside, the tower began first bell, and the man with the goat rope shifted on his bench.

"Your master's name stays on the roll," the governor said. He did not look up from the ledger. "Go and feed your oven."

Isel gathered the coppers into the crock, tied the cloth, and carried it down the stairs.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The governor's man had come at dusk, stood in the bakery doorway with his gloves on, and said it plainly: from tomorrow's first bell, no loaf to the widow Maret. Not sold, not given, not dropped in the street where she might find it. Then he left. Wren's master said nothing and went on scraping the trough.

She woke in the dark to a smell that did not belong to the hour. Bread, hot, close. She sat up. On the windowsill, a loaf rested on a square of cloth, and when she touched it the heat went straight into her palm. Someone had pressed letters into the crust with a thumb or a bone stamp: MARET.

Wren held it a long moment. Nobody ordered a loaf to be named for the person who couldn't have it. Maret had been told, or had guessed, and had baked her own refusal and delivered it first.

Flour lay along the sill in a pale smear, and below the window it began again: a dusting on the cobbles, a handprint on the rain barrel, a white scuff on the first step of the lane. Wren pulled her boots on without lacing them.

The trail wandered. It crossed the sleeping market, passed the dry fountain, and ran along the wall where the night watch sat with their backs to the city. At the foot of the east stairs it thickened, and Maret was sitting on the bottom step, floured to the elbows, waiting.

Wren realizes Maret already knows what is coming, and follows the trail of flour-dust through the sleeping city to find her.

Wren leaves carrying it, knowing she has just been made part of something larger than a single refusal.

Scene 2

Wren stopped two steps above her and held the loaf out in both hands, the way you hold something you're returning to a stranger.

"I can't take it," she said. "You know I can't. The order starts at first bell."

Maret looked at the bread and did not lift her hands from her lap. Flour had settled into the creases of her knuckles. "It isn't first bell."

"Then it's nearly."

"Then it's nearly mine, and not yet yours to refuse." Maret tilted her head. "A refusal needs someone to receive it. I'm not receiving it. Put it down if you like. It'll still be a loaf you tried to give back."

Wren crouched and set it on the step between them. Maret slid her feet aside so it wouldn't touch her. The crust ticked as it cooled. MARET, pressed deep, the M slightly crooked.

"Take it," Wren said.

"No."

"I'm told not to give it."

"Then don't give it."

Along the wall a watchman coughed and spat, and neither of them turned. The sky over the east stairs had gone the grey of old dough. Wren's toes were cold through the unlaced boots. She counted the steps above her, twenty-two to the gate, and thought of her master's hands scraping the trough without a word.

The dawn bell rang from the Guildhall tower, flat and unhurried. Nine strokes. Wren listened to all of them.

She looked at the loaf again. The letters weren't her master's crust or her oven's. The scoring was wrong. The flour was wrong, coarse and grey.

"You baked this," she said.

"In my own oven," said Maret. "Yes."

"Then the order doesn't say anything about it."

Maret smiled, and finally reached down.

Scene 3

Maret picked up the loaf and broke it over her knee. The crust cracked with a sound like a dry twig, and steam rose from the torn middle. The letters split down the center of the A. She held out the larger half.

"Take it."

"I told you, I can't."

"You can't give. Listen to what you swore." Maret kept her hand out, steady, though flour sifted from her sleeve. "A baker never refuses a loaf. Never gives a loaf by the governor's leave or without it. Nobody wrote a line about receiving. Whoever drew up that oath was hungry at some point."

Wren looked at the half-loaf. The crumb was grey and dense, gleaming where the knife of the break had pulled it. Her stomach turned over once, loudly, and Maret raised her eyebrows.

Wren took it. The heat went into both palms. She sat down on the step, two above Maret, and tore off a piece. It tasted of smoke and something mineral, like a stone held in the mouth, and under that a sweetness she couldn't place. She ate another piece. Crumbs caught in the unlaced collar of her jacket.

Above them, on the wall, a boot scraped.

A watchman stood at the head of the stairs, spear grounded, looking down. He was an older man with a bandaged thumb. His eyes went to Maret, to the crust in Wren's hand, to the flour on her boots. Wren stopped chewing.

He didn't move. The bell had rung, so the order was in force. He rubbed the bandage slowly with his other thumb.

Scene 4

Wren folded what was left of her half into the hem of her jacket and pushed it into her pocket, where it kept its heat against her hip. Maret stood, brushed off her skirt, and climbed. Wren followed, counting. Twenty-two.

At the top the watchman stepped aside. He tilted his spear out of the way like a man making room on a bench, and he looked at the sky instead of at them. His good thumb kept rubbing the bandage. The east gate was a single iron-banded leaf with the bar already lifted and leaning against the stones. Maret leaned on the door, the hinges complained, and they went through.

Outside, there was wheat, or what had been wheat. The stalks stood waist-high and grey. The heads were either missing or gone to black powder that came off on Wren's sleeve when the wind moved. The rows ran downhill to a dry ditch. No birds.

Maret walked the furrow without looking down. At the bottom, behind a fallen fence and a stand of dead thistle, a mill squatted with its sails bound in sacking. Inside were a stone, a hopper, sacks stacked to the rafters, and one cold oven mouth in the back wall. Flour hung in the air and settled on Wren's lashes.

"Light it," Maret said. "Kindling's under the third sack."

"Me?"

Maret held up her hands. The knuckles were swollen, and the grey had worked in under the skin. "I can't hold a peel past this week. The governor's men will come by the road. An hour, maybe less. Bake before they do."

Scene 5

Wren had the kindling out from under the third sack and was fitting it into the oven mouth when Maret said, "Someone's coming down the furrow."

She went to the doorway. The watchman from the stairs was walking between the grey rows with his spear gone. In its place he carried a sack, flat and empty, folded over his forearm. He walked like a man whose knees had opinions. Nobody followed him on the road behind.

He stopped at the mill door and did not come in. Flour lifted off the sill and settled on his boots.

"I left my post," he said, to Wren and not to Maret. "They'll know by now. The governor's men are an hour back, maybe less, and they're slow because they're dressed for it."

"We're closed," Wren said, and heard how foolish it sounded.

"You're not." He unfolded the sack and held it open between both hands, bandaged thumb crooked out of the way. "I've been on the wall since yesterday's second bell. I'd like a loaf."

Wren looked at Maret. Maret was looking at the cold oven.

"The order's for her," Wren said. "Not you."

"No. Not me." He nodded slowly. "So I'm the first one you can't turn off. I swore your oath at twelve, in my father's shop, before I ever held a spear. I know how it reads." He lifted the sack an inch higher. "Bake for me first."

Wren struck the flint. The kindling took, and the flame came up pale.

Scene 6

Wren dragged the nearest sack to the trough and slit the stitching with her thumbnail. The flour ran out grey and coarse, and it smelled of the stone in the loaf, mineral and faintly burnt. She added water from the bucket, a fist of salt, and the last of a leavening crock that Maret pointed to without speaking.

The dough was heavy and fought her. She leaned her weight into the heel of her hand, folded, turned, leaned again. By the tenth fold the grey had climbed to her wrists and stayed there when she wiped them on her apron.

The watchman sat on a sack by the door with the empty bag across his knees. He watched her hands. The oven ticked as the stones warmed.

"My father's flour was the color of milk," he said. "What's in this?"

"Wheat," Wren said.

"That's not what I asked."

Maret was at the hopper, one swollen hand flat against the wood. "It's wheat that's sick," she said. "The whole east field. The blight is in every grain, and the stone grinds it in with the rest."

Wren's hands stopped. "And you bake it."

"Baked, it's the only thing I've found that settles it. Eat it hot, eat it all." Maret turned her palms up. "I wasn't quick enough with the first ones."

"Does the governor know?"

"His cook buys from me by the back door. His wife. Two of his children." She looked at the oven. "He knows exactly."

Wren cut the dough in four and began to shape it.

Scene 7

Wren pulled the first loaf with the peel and it came out heavy and dark, the crust crackling as it met the air. She tipped it onto the sack he held open, and he didn't wait. He tore the end off with his good hand, hissed at the heat, and ate standing in the doorway with steam going up past his face.

Halfway through the second mouthful he stopped chewing and looked down.

The bandage on his thumb had a grey stain spreading through the weave, wet at the center. He unwound it with his teeth and fingers. The skin beneath was split along the pad, weeping something the color of dishwater, and the veins ran dark up to the knuckle. He ate another piece. They all watched. The grey drew back from the knuckle first, slowly, like a tide leaving a step, and the split edges went pink.

"I thought it was the spear," he said. "The cold on the grip."

"How many on the wall?" Maret asked.

"Forty-one on the night rolls." He flexed the thumb, then stared at it. "Hobb's hands cracked in autumn. Dannet lost two nails. We eat from the wall kitchen. The flour comes in from the east gate." He looked at the open field through the door, at the grey stalks. "I carried it up myself."

Wren turned to the oven. Three loaves left, still tight and pale in the glow. Her wrists itched under the grey.

She counted them again anyway.

Scene 8

Wren pulled the last three loaves and packed them into the watchman's sack, still too hot to hold without the cloth. "Wall kitchen first," she said. "Then the rolls, every name."

"Captain's Ostrel," he said, nodding down the furrow. Dust had risen on the road, and there was a glint of mail. "His wife's been at Maret's back door since spring." He shouldered the sack and went up the field the long way, through the grey stalks.

Maret had taken the peel and stood with it braced against her hip, saying nothing. Wren left her the oven.

She carried the fourth loaf against her stomach and walked the furrow to the road. Black powder came off the wheat heads onto her sleeves. By the time she reached the ditch the soldiers had stopped, eleven of them in boiled leather, and the man in front had pulled his gloves tight at the wrist.

Wren held the loaf out in both hands.

"A baker never refuses a loaf," she said. Her voice came out thin, so she said it again, louder. "Never gives by the governor's leave or without it."

"Girl," said the captain.

"It's hot. It's the only kind that works."

His eyes went to the grey in her wrists, and stayed there. Behind him a soldier shifted, and mail chinked. The captain pulled off his right glove, finger by finger, and reached.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

The knock came while the ovens were still ticking from their first fire, three taps, evenly spaced. Wren set down the peel and slid the bolt.

A woman stood in the lane with her hands folded in front of her, as if she had arrived at a church. Gray coat, wet hem, no basket. She looked about forty, and she was not shivering, though the cold off the wall was the kind that split lips.

"A loaf, please," she said. "Whatever's cooling."

Wren knew the face from nowhere. She knew the words, though. *No hand that knocks goes empty.* She had said them at twelve with her palm over the oven flame. She took a round from the rack, still too hot to hold comfortably, and wrapped it in cloth.

"You'll burn yourself," Wren said.

"I don't mind." Maret took it against her chest. She glanced once down the lane, to where a lantern hung at the corner by the cooper's, and nodded to it, almost politely. "Thank you, Wren."

Wren had not told her the name.

By the time the shutters were up, Master Oren knew. He stood in the doorway with flour to his elbows while a steward in blue read from a sealed sheet, and the sheet said *refuse*, and the date on it was yesterday's. Oren took the paper when it was offered. He folded it small, and he did not look surprised.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Before the order is even delivered, Wren meets Maret at the bakery's back door in the dark, and Maret asks for a loaf with strange calm, as if she already knows what's coming. Wren gives her the bread out of habit and oath, then learns by morning that the governor's guards saw it, so the order arrives too late to be obeyed.

Scene 2

Oren led her down past the flour bins to the cold cellar, where the ice from the winter pond still sat in sawdust and breath showed white. He did not light the lamp until the door was shut. From behind a rye sack he drew a bundle in oilcloth, and unwrapped it on the cutting block.

The ledger was thick as a brick. He opened it near the middle and turned it toward her.

Black ink for the loaves, line after line: *a carter, a widow, two boys, a priest.* Then, in red, a single word beside certain lines. *Refused.* And beneath each red word, a shorter note in the same cramped hand.

*Tinker's wife. Her street burned by harvest.* *Soldier, unnamed. Granary rotted through in one night.* *Girl with a cough. The baker's own sons, both, before spring.*

Wren read six of them. Her mouth had gone dry.

"They teach you the words," Oren said. "They don't teach you what answers if you break them." He touched the red with one floury knuckle. "Every baker in this city has signed this book at the flame. Most never turn past the first pages."

"The governor knows?"

"The governor's father knew. This isn't the first order, Wren. Only the first in my time."

He turned to the last red entry. The date was forty years old. The hand was steadier than the others, and rounder, and she knew the shape of the *R* because it was the one chalked on every flour sack upstairs.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Master Oren takes Wren down to the cold cellar and shows her the old baker's ledger, in which every refused loaf in the city's history is recorded in red ink, and each entry is followed by a death or a ruin. He tells her that the governor's order is not the first, and that the oath has teeth the apprentices are never taught about.

Scene 3

The drip trail was still there. Maret's hem had left dark beads on the cobbles, thinning toward the cooper's, and Wren followed them with the bakery's flour still on her sleeves.

The lantern at the corner was unlit. Beneath it, a man in blue leaned against the barrel stack, peeling an apple with a short knife. He did not startle.

"You're quick," he said. "Oren's girl."

"Who is she?"

"Maret. Six weeks the governor's had men on her. Her coat's been to every bakery from the east gate to the tanneries." He cut a slice and ate it. "Eleven loaves. She's never once been refused."

Wren looked at the lane, the wet stones, the shut shutters. "Then why am I the one?"

"Because you're new. Her face won't have taught you anything yet." He wiped the blade on his thigh. "Listen. The oath says no *knocking hand* goes empty. So she must not knock. Tonight, before the bell, you go out and meet her at the lane's mouth. Walk her to the east gate. No knock, no refusal. Your oath stays whole."

It was clean. It was so clean she could feel it settling over her like a warm cloth.

"And Oren?"

"Tell him you'll do it at the door, as written. Let him sleep upstairs."

Wren thought of the red ink, and the round *R*. Her mouth tasted of ash.

"Before the bell," the watcher said, and went back to his apple.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Wren follows Maret's trail through the wet lane to the lantern by the cooper's and finds a watcher in blue, who reveals the governor has been tracking Maret for weeks and offers Wren a way to fulfill the order without breaking her oath. The offer is tempting, but it means she must lie to Oren.

Scene 4

Wren stood at the lane's mouth with a round wrapped in cloth under her arm. The bell was still a quarter hour off. The lantern at the cooper's had been lit, and its light lay yellow and shaking on the wet stones.

Maret came from the east, walking the middle of the lane. Her coat was dry this time. She slowed when she saw Wren outside the door, and her eyes went to the cloth.

Wren had practiced the walk to the gate all afternoon. She did not say any of it. She held out the loaf at arm's length, and the heat came through the cloth into her wrist.

"You haven't knocked," Maret said.

"No."

"Then nothing's owed."

"Take it anyway."

Maret did not move. Behind her, a shutter clicked shut. Boots scraped on the cobbles, three pairs, unhurried. The watcher stepped out from the barrel stack with the apple core still in his fist, and two men in blue came behind him with rope.

"That was not the arrangement," he said to Wren. He sounded tired.

"You said no knock, no refusal." Her voice cracked on the last word. "You never said I couldn't give."

He dropped the core. One of the men took Wren's wrists, and the loaf fell and rolled against the curb. Another bound Maret, who held her hands out like a woman being fitted for gloves.

"Twelve," Maret said, low enough that only Wren heard. "Eleven took it because I knocked. You're the first who put it in my hands first."

The rope drew tight. Wren looked at the loaf in the gutter.

Wren waits at the lane's mouth before the bell as instructed, but when Maret arrives she offers her the loaf first, unasked, and breaks the order's logic. The blue-coated watcher steps from the shadows to arrest them both, and Maret quietly reveals she has been testing which baker would choose the oath over the governor.

Scene 5

The cell had one slit window and a bucket. Wren sat with her back to the wall, rope burns weeping under her cuffs. Maret sat across from her with her hands in her lap, as she had stood in the lane.

"The ledger," Maret said. "You read it."

"Some."

"Then you've read me. Every red line is me. The tinker's wife, the soldier, the girl with the cough." She said it the way a person lists what she had for supper. "I don't do it. I'm only what it looks like when the oath is broken and nobody mends it."

"Rhenna," Wren said. The name came out of the round R, out of the chalk on the sacks.

"Oren's Rhenna. Forty years ago I shut my door on a man with a knife in his belt, and I was right to. It didn't matter." Maret turned her wrists over, showing the marks. "I don't starve. I don't die. I walk to every bakery in the city and I knock, and they give, and for one night the walls hold. Eleven times they've held. I'm so tired of being the reason."

Wren's mouth was dry. "What do you want?"

"A loaf, from your hands only. Kneaded with ash from the crock Oren keeps packed in the cellar ice, the ash from the first fire." Maret leaned forward. "Give it to me freely, and I can stop."

"And my oath?"

"Spent. You'd bake it, and it would be the last thing the oath ever bound you to."

Somewhere above them, a bell began to ring.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

In the cell, Maret tells Wren what she is: the Refused, the thing the ledger records, or the first baker, Oren's Rhenna, who broke the oath forty years ago. She offers to end the curse if Wren will bake her one last loaf, from her own hands and ash from the cellar's ice, but it will cost Wren her oath.

Scene 6

Keys rattled in the corridor, too many and too fast, and then the door swung in on Oren. His apron was gone. He had a steward's ring in one fist and a bruise coming up along his jaw. Behind him, down the passage, a man in blue lay with his cheek on the flagstones.

"Not breathing hard enough to be dead," Oren said, to no one. He crouched and worked the rope burns on Wren's wrists with his thumbs, checking them. "Don't bake it."

"Master—"

"Not till you've heard what's in the crock." He did not look at the woman across the cell. "I packed that ash in ice forty years ago. I told myself it was the first fire's. Every baker's told that." His voice scraped. "It's what the oven kept of her. The night she shut her door, and it didn't matter."

Wren turned. Maret had not moved her hands from her lap.

"You said Rhenna's ash is what bakes it," Oren said.

"I said the first fire's."

"Same ash."

"Yes."

Overhead the bell went on, one slow stroke after another. Dust sifted from the ceiling onto the bucket.

"Kneaded in, it ends the curse," Oren said to Wren. "And it ends whatever's left of her. That's the price. She left it off the list."

"Would you have come, if I'd said it?" Maret asked him.

Oren's keys stopped swinging. He did not answer.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Oren breaks into the cell block with the keys he took from the steward's belt. He will not let Wren bake the loaf until she knows its price: the ash is Rhenna's own, and the loaf will end her as well as the curse.

Scene 7

Wren carried the crock up from the ice herself. The lid had been waxed shut forty years, and it came off with a sound like a knuckle cracking. The ash inside was fine and pale, almost white. She worked it into the dough with the heels of her hands, and it turned the flour gray as she folded.

Oren stood at the bench with his ring of stolen keys and watched her shape it. Maret waited in the doorway, out of the light.

"It's for her," Oren said. "Get it in the oven before the wall gives."

"No."

Wren slid the peel under the round and put it in the fire. They waited without talking. The bell above the city kept on, slower now, and somewhere east a shutter banged. When she drew the loaf out, the crust had split along the top, dark as slate.

She set it on the bench in front of him.

"You packed it," she said. "You kept it cold and told everyone it was clean."

Oren looked at the bread a long time. Then he tore the heel off with his bare hands, still steaming, and ate it standing up. He ate all of it. He wiped his fingers on his trousers, as there was no apron.

He walked to the door. Maret stepped aside for him. He went out into the lane, and the lantern at the cooper's guttered once.

The bell stopped mid-stroke.

Maret stood on the dry cobbles and listened to nothing at all.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Wren takes the ash but bakes the loaf for Oren instead, since he is the one who made Rhenna's ash and broke faith with her. He eats it, the curse takes him in her place, and Maret is left standing in a lane that is suddenly silent.

Scene 8

The crock was nearly empty. Wren scraped the bottom with a spoon and got a thimble of ash, pale as flour, and tied it in a rag.

The governor's kitchen was already warm. The cook let her in without a word, because a baker at the door was a baker at the door, and pointed her to the trough. Wren made the household loaf the way Oren had taught her, with the same salt and the same slow fold. The ash went in at the second kneading. The dough turned the color of a pigeon's back.

"It's darker than usual," the cook said.

"It's the rye."

A boy carried the round up on a board. Wren followed as far as the dining hall's doorway and stood against the jamb with flour to her elbows. The governor sat alone at the long table, a thin man in a fur collar, a plate of cold mutton at his elbow. She had never seen him eat. He tore the loaf open, looked at the gray crumb, and put a piece in his mouth.

He chewed twice.

Somewhere below, a door slammed, and then another. A steward ran past Wren shouting about the granary, the roof, the grain gone to black mush overnight. The governor's hand stopped on the table.

"Who knocked?" he said. His voice had gone small. "Nobody knocked."

The candles along the wall went out one by one.

Wren carries the last of the ash to the governor's hall and kneads it into the loaf the household eats at breakfast, as written in the oath. The governor is the one man who never knocked on a baker's door. When he eats it, the wall's wards answer him instead, and he learns what refusal costs the way the tinker's wife did.

weird western

A long-haul trucker crossing a salt desert picks up a radio call from a driver who gives her own name and her own route, one day ahead of her.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

The salt flats ran white to the edge of the world, and Dee Marrow had been staring at them for two hours when the CB woke up.

It had been dead since Wendover. She had her thermos wedged against the seat and her boots off, driving in socks, the Peterbilt humming at sixty-two with a load of drywall sheeting behind her. The speaker coughed, and a woman's voice came through the static, flat and dry as the ground.

"Anybody on this stretch, this is Dee Marrow, westbound on 80, mile marker ninety-one. Got a soft shoulder and a dog on the road. Slowing down."

Dee looked at the mile marker as it went by. Ninety-one.

She picked up the handset. Her thumb left a damp print on the plastic. "Say again your handle?"

"Marrow. Dolores. Hauling gypsum board out of Salt Lake for Reno." A pause, a crackle like paper burning. "Who's this?"

Dee's mouth had gone dry. Her bills of lading were on the dash. Gypsum board. Reno.

"Where's the dog now?" she said.

"Standing in the lane. Brown one. Won't move."

Ahead of her the road was empty, the white shoulders clean and hard. No dog. The sun sat low and orange on the salt, and her shadow-cab stretched a hundred feet to the left.

"Ma'am?" the voice said. "You still there?"

Dee set the handset in her lap and kept both hands on the wheel.

Scene 2

Dee thumbed the handset. "What's today's date?"

"Tuesday. The fourteenth." The woman sounded irritated, the way Dee sounded to herself on the phone with dispatch. "Why?"

Dee looked at the logbook open on the dash, her own block capitals in the top margin. Wednesday, the fifteenth. She'd written it at the Wendover fuel stop, standing at the pump with the ink pen she kept on a string.

"No reason," she said. "Keep your speed down. Soft shoulder, you said. Which side?"

"Right. Passenger side. I'm riding the line."

Dee eased off the throttle. The Peterbilt shuddered down through fifty-five, fifty. The white crust ahead was seamed with old tire scuffs, and a quarter mile on she saw it: a pair of dual-wheel ruts cut into the right shoulder, deep and wet-dark where the salt had broken through to the mud beneath. The edges hadn't crumbled. They had the crisp look of something made hours ago.

Beside the ruts, pressed into the muck, were the prints of a dog. They ran across the lane, four-toed, and stopped at the center line.

She stopped the truck. The engine ticked. On the speaker, someone breathed.

"Dee Marrow," the voice said, quieter now. "Don't you get out."

Scene 3

Dee's hand was already on the door latch. She hadn't felt herself reach for it.

"Why not?" she said into the handset.

"Because I got out." The static rose and fell. "Thought I'd move it off the road. Thought it was hurt."

Dee looked through the windshield. The prints ran out onto the pavement, where a skin of salt lay over the asphalt like frost, and they stopped at the center line. There were no prints on the far side. There were no prints going back.

"It's not there now," she said.

"No. It wouldn't be."

Her thermos had slid across the seat. She caught it against her thigh without looking and sat holding it, still warm through the steel. Out past the hood the flats were turning pink, then a bruised gray at the far edge, and the wind had started to move the loose salt in low sheets across the lane.

"Where are you right now?" Dee asked.

"Mile ninety-one. Where do you think?"

"I'm at ninety-one."

Nothing came back. Then, faintly, a sound that wasn't static: the click of a door latch, the same flat metallic snap as the one under Dee's palm.

She took her hand off it.

"Dee," the voice said. "Look at your mirror."

Scene 4

Dee tilted her head toward the driver's mirror.

The trailer filled most of the glass, its white flank gone pink with the light. Past the rear duals the road ran straight back to the dark. She saw the salt blowing in thin sheets and the yellow line sliding under it.

Then the dog. It sat in the lane twenty feet behind the trailer, brown, ribs showing, head cocked as if she had called it. It was not blowing or blurring in the wind. Its fur lay flat.

A half mile past the dog, small and steady, a pair of amber hazards pulsed on and off.

"I see a truck back there," Dee said. Her voice came out smaller than she meant. "Flashers going."

"Is the door open?"

She squinted. The cab was a dark block against the dusk, and a rectangle of lighter dark stood out from its side. "Yeah."

"Anybody standing by it?"

"No."

"Good," the woman said. She let out a breath that crackled through the speaker. "That's good. I didn't know if I'd be."

The dog stood. It shook itself, and no salt fell from its coat. Then it started up the lane toward her, not hurrying, its nails ticking faintly on the pavement. Dee could hear them through the glass.

She put her bare foot on the clutch.

Scene 5

The Peterbilt dropped into first with a grind she felt in her teeth. Dee let the clutch out slow, and the rig rolled forward, tires crunching through the salt skin.

The dog kept coming. It drew even with the trailer wheels, then the fuel tank, and she lost it under the edge of the passenger window. Its nails ticked on the pavement, steady as a clock.

"Dee," the radio said. "Where's it at?"

"Beside me. Passenger door."

"Don't slow down."

She hadn't been going to. She put the truck through second and third, and the speedometer needle crept up past twenty, thirty. The ticking didn't fall behind. She looked right, and the dog ran at the height of her door handle with its head turned up, one pale eye on her. It wasn't panting. Its mouth was closed.

At forty the ticking stopped. She looked again and the shoulder was empty, the crust unbroken.

In the mirror the amber flashers went out. Behind her there was only the long dark road.

The handset slipped in her damp palm. Out ahead, a green sign rose in her headlights and went by: MILE 92.

"Dee?" the woman said, very close, as if she were sitting in the passenger seat. "Tell me what's on the shoulder."

Scene 6

Dee leaned toward the windshield. Her headlights ran out across the shoulder, white and hard, and a hundred yards on they caught something upright.

"Boots," she said.

"How many?"

"A pair. Standing side by side, like somebody stepped out of them." She eased off the throttle without meaning to. "Laces still tied."

"What color?"

"Brown. Salt up to the ankle." The truck closed the distance, and the boots swelled in the light. The left heel had a strip of silver duct tape wrapped around it, curling at one edge.

Dee's eyes went to the floorboard. Her own boots sat where she'd kicked them off at Wendover, the leather dark with sweat. The left one had a strip of silver duct tape on the heel, curling at one edge.

She looked at the shoulder again. Then back at the floor. Both pairs were there.

"Dee?"

"They're mine," she said. "Or they're yours. They're the same."

"I figured." The woman's voice had gone thin. "I left mine at ninety-two. I don't remember taking them off."

The boots slid past the passenger window. Dee watched them in the mirror until the dark took them. Beside her left foot, on the clutch, her sock was wet through, and the wet was cold.

Scene 7

Dee glanced at the logbook on the dash, because she needed to look at something that would hold still. The top margin read *Tuesday, the 14th* in her own block capitals. The ink had the shine of fresh writing. The pen hung from its string, swinging a little.

She didn't remember changing it. She didn't touch it.

"Dee," the radio said. "I'm walking."

"Walking where?"

"West. Same as I was driving." Gravel shifted under the voice, a dry grinding that had no business in a truck cab. "My feet don't hurt. That's what bothers me. Salt ought to cut them."

"How far have you gone?"

"Past the boots. Past the sign. I can see headlights coming up behind me. They're throwing my shadow out ahead, long as a telephone pole."

Dee looked at her own dash. High beams on. Her shadow-cab, if she'd had one, would have fallen forward.

She came around a slow bend in the road, and the lights found her. A woman on the right shoulder, a hundred yards ahead, small and upright, walking in the white crust with her arms loose at her sides. Gray braid. Canvas jacket, the same tan one hanging behind Dee's seat. Her socks were dark to the ankle.

She didn't turn around.

"Dee," the radio said, from the speaker and from the woman's mouth, a half second apart. "Please don't hit the horn."

Dee's hand was already over the wheel's center.

Scene 8

Dee took her hand off the wheel's center and laid it flat on her thigh.

She let the Peterbilt coast down through twenty, ten, until the engine was grumbling at a walking pace and the headlights lay steady on the woman's back. The braid swung against the canvas jacket. Salt creaked under the dark socks.

Dee leaned across the seat and cranked the passenger window down. Cold came in, smelling of minerals and old rain.

"Dolores," she said.

The woman's head moved a little. "Nobody calls me that but my mother."

"I know."

"I can't stop walking." She said it evenly, the way you'd report a flat tire. "I keep trying."

Dee set the brake and put the truck in neutral, and it rocked once on its springs. She reached over and pulled the door handle, and the door swung out into the lights. Then she sat back against her own seat, both hands where the woman could see them, and did not get out.

The woman turned. Dee saw her own face, sunburned across the nose, a chip gone from one front tooth. The woman looked at the open door, then the step.

She climbed up. The seat took her weight and the springs sighed. She smelled of salt and diesel and sweat. She picked up the thermos from the floor and held it in both hands.

On the dash, the CB hissed, empty.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The CB had been dead static since Wendover, so when it spoke Marisol nearly took her foot off the pedal.

"Marisol Vega. Don't say hello. Listen."

The voice was a woman's, dry as the flats outside. Dusk had turned the salt the color of a bruised peach, and the white line ran ahead of her hood like a thread.

"Tomorrow, mile marker 212, you're going to choose. You won't get to unchoose it."

She thumbed the mic. "Who is this?" Nothing came back but hiss. She tried channel 19, then 9. Hiss, and under it something like wind through a bottle.

Her hands were damp on the wheel. Mile marker 212 was on her paper log, penciled in for tomorrow's afternoon run. She hadn't said it aloud to anyone.

Four miles on, a gap in the reflectors showed a service road, just two ruts of cracked salt crust and no sign. She braked hard and swung onto it. The trailer shuddered over the crust like a plate breaking.

A quarter mile in, her high beams caught a shape ahead. A Peterbilt, white cab, trailer hitched, the same dent over the left fender that hers had. The same Utah plate.

She stopped thirty feet back and left the engine running. The driver's door hung open.

She walked up and laid her palm on the hood. It was warm.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The voice gives Marisol a warning instead of a greeting: tomorrow at mile marker 212 she will make a choice she cannot take back. Spooked, she pulls off onto an unmarked salt-crust service road to avoid the route, and her headlights find a truck identical to hers, abandoned and still warm.

Scene 2

She climbed the step. The rail was warm, too, and the vinyl seat had the same split along the seam that she'd been meaning to tape since March.

The logbook lay on the passenger side, spine cracked open. It was her green Rite in the Rain, the one with the coffee ring on the cover. Her own was in the door pocket of the truck behind her. She knew that without checking, and she checked anyway, a glance back through the windshield at the dark shape of her own cab.

She picked it up. Her handwriting, the slanted sevens, the way she crossed zeros. Tonight's entry: *Wendover, 6:10 p.m. Radio dead.* The next line was the service road. Then a date she hadn't reached yet, and fuel stops and weigh stations in order, a pencil note about a bad tooth. Her hand shook, and the page shook with it.

The last legible line read *212, and I took the* and stopped. A ragged edge of paper ran down the gutter where the rest had been torn out.

The dash radio clicked. Static rose, then settled into the dry voice.

"The engine's still warm," it said. "When it's cold, this cab won't be here. Read fast, Marisol."

She sat down on the seat that was already shaped to her, and turned the page back to the beginning.

Scene 3

She read it the way she'd read a bill of lading, finger under each line.

Tonight was right. Wendover, the dead radio, the service road. Under it, in ink: *Fuel at the Flying J, 7:40 a.m. Coffee, two creams.* She never took two creams. She read it again and tasted them anyway.

Tomorrow's pages ran on. A scale house with a closed lane. A bad tooth, lower left, *ibuprofen, 400 mg, with the cold fries*. A phone call to her sister she didn't remember deciding to make.

Then, in pencil, pressed hard enough to dent the page: *Mile 150. Man on the shoulder, no gas can, no truck. Picked him up. Against every rule I have.* Below it, smaller: *He knew the way I take my coffee.*

Marisol had not stopped for a hitchhiker in eleven years. She put the book down on her knee, and the cab ticked.

It was the sound of an engine cooling, but it came too fast, a tick every second, like a clock being wound forward. The vinyl under her palm had gone from warm to merely room temperature.

She pinched the corner of the hitchhiker page and tore it along the gutter, slowly, so the perforation of the old tear wouldn't take it. The paper sounded loud as a zipper. She folded it twice and shoved it in her breast pocket.

The ticking quickened.

She didn't wait for the cab to go cold. She jumped down from the step with the page in her fist and dug her Zippo out of her jeans, the one she kept for flares and frozen air lines.

The hood was still warm under her hip. She held the page flat against the metal and thumbed the wheel. The flame stood up straight in the dead air.

The corner caught. *Picked him up* curled brown, then black, the pencil gone silver for a second before the paper took it. She turned the page so the fire ran down through *no gas can, no truck* and *He knew the way I take my coffee.* Heat bit her fingertips. She let go and it fell burning to the crust, and she stamped what was left into gray flakes.

Behind her, in the open cab, the radio laughed.

It was not a loud laugh. It was the dry voice, easy and tired, the way you laugh at a kid who has just locked the keys in the car.

Marisol turned toward the highway. Four hundred yards off, the first reflector post caught light from nowhere, white as a struck match, and went dark. The next one flared and died. Then the next, post after post along the interstate, each one burning out a little nearer the service road, an even, unhurried pace.

She looked down at the ash on her boot. The Zippo was still open in her hand, still lit.

Scene 5

She ran back to the cab with the Zippo still burning and climbed the step one-handed. The logbook lay where she'd left it. She snatched it up and flipped to the gutter, thumb jamming into the ragged stub where the pages had been torn.

The stub was blank. Past it, the last page was not.

*212, and I took the*

The ink was wet. She could see it shine in the flame. The letters had been pressed in a little deeper than she remembered, and the sevens no longer slanted. They stood straight up, the way she'd made them in grade school.

Then the line began to move. The *t* in *took* swelled and thinned like a hair in a drain. The entry above it, *Wendover, 6:10 p.m.*, bled brown at the edges and wrote itself again, slower, with *Radio dead* replaced by *Radio dead, then not.* The ink crawled after her eyes. When she looked at a word, it was already different.

Outside, a reflector flared white through the windshield and died. Closer.

After *the*, at the end of the line, the page darkened. A single stroke rose from the paper, a short vertical with a hook at the bottom. It might have been the start of an *r*, or a *b*, or a *d*.

She held the book out over the open door. The Zippo flame leaned toward it, a finger's width away. The stroke kept growing.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Marisol runs back to the open cab, grabs the green logbook, and flips to the torn gutter to read what the ripped pages held. The ink is rewriting itself as she watches, and the last line now ends *212, and I took the* with a new word forming, so she has to decide whether to keep reading or throw the book into the fire.

Scene 6

She dropped the Zippo's lid with her thumb and the flame died. The cab went dark except for the green glow of the radio, and in that light the stroke on the page was still rising.

A pencil lay in the dash tray, sharpened to a bevel with a knife, the way she did it. She took it. Her hand had stopped shaking, and she noticed that the way you notice a noise ending.

She put the point on the stroke and pressed. The ink fought her, soft and warm as a vein. She wrote straight through it, over the hook and the stem, until the graphite shone silver on black.

*I took the pencil.*

Then, underneath, in sevens that slanted: *Nobody's coffee. Nobody's road.*

The ink quit crawling. The *t* in *took* sat still. Above it *Radio dead, then not* dried to a flat brown, and the page smelled like any page.

The radio had been hissing the whole time. She only knew because it stopped. No click, no fade. The silence sat in the cab like a fifth wall.

Through the windshield, light came up white on the salt.

She looked. Every reflector post along the interstate stood lit at once, hundreds of them, a single stitched line of struck matches. They ran east past where Wendover's glow should have been, and west past where the flats ended at the mountains. The line kept going, level and bright, into a dark that had no mountains in it.

Scene 7

She climbed down with the book under her arm and the pencil still in her fist. The salt crackled under her boots. Behind her the white cab sat with its door open and its dome light out, and she didn't look back at it again.

Her own Peterbilt was where she'd left it, engine running, headlights laying two yellow lanes across the ruts. She went up the step and opened the door.

The door pocket held a map, a tire gauge, and a pack of gum with one stick gone. She dug deeper. The green Rite in the Rain wasn't there. Her fingers found paper, and she pulled out a narrow strip with a ragged edge, a few torn fibers still holding a blue ruled line. It was the gutter stub, and it was the right size for the book in her hand.

She checked the seat, the floor, the sleeper, under the bunk where she kept the spare chains. She found her thermos and one glove. She didn't find a log.

She sat. The seat was cold, though the engine had been running the whole time. She put the new book on the dash and reached for the key, which was already in the ignition, and turned it past where it was already turned. The starter ground against a running motor.

The radio clicked on.

"Hello, Marisol," it said, in her own voice, tired and a little hoarse, with the flat Utah vowels she'd never been able to lose. "Your turn. Say hello first this time."

Scene 8

She didn't answer the radio. She put the truck in gear and let the clutch out, and the trailer dragged itself backward out of the ruts and found the pavement with a bump she felt in her teeth.

The reflectors stayed lit. She drove east between them, and they didn't pass like posts. They passed like a held breath. The radio said her name once, patiently. She turned the volume knob until it clicked off, and the voice kept talking anyway, just under the engine, too low to make out.

The new log lay on the dash with the pencil across it. She didn't open it.

The markers counted up in the headlights. 146. 147. Her mouth tasted of pennies and, faintly, of cream. 149.

At 150 a man stood on the shoulder, lit white by the post beside him. He had no truck behind him, no can in his hand, no bag. His hands hung empty at his sides, and he wasn't waving.

Her foot was already off the pedal. She noticed that and kept it there. The air brakes let go with a long sigh, and the truck rolled to a stop forty feet past him. She sat with the engine running and her hand on the door handle.

In the mirror he started walking toward her, unhurried.

The radio came on by itself, loud now, and her own voice laughed in it, warm and tired and glad.

"There it is," it said. "That was the choice, Marisol. It was always going to be his."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She pulls the truck back onto the interstate and drives east into the lit reflector line, ignoring the radio. At mile 150 a man stands on the shoulder with no gas can, and she chooses to stop. Her own voice on the radio laughs and says that this was the choice, and that it was always going to be his.

She grabs the mic and demands to know who it is, and the voice answers with the exact words she is about to say next, then goes silent, leaving her convinced the call is real.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

The Salt Fork Travel Plaza stood alone at the end of ninety miles of white, its sign still lit against a sky the color of dishwater. Dell parked beside the diesel island and sat a minute with the engine ticking. The CB had given her nothing but static since Wendover.

Inside, the attendant was a heavy man with a pencil behind his ear. He looked up from a crossword and then past her, out the window, at her truck.

"Thought you just left."

"Nobody's left. I just got here."

"Woman about your size. Gray braid, that canvas coat." He nodded at her coat. "Kenworth, red cab, Nevada plates ending four-one-seven. I read them off when she paid." He tapped the counter. "Had a heeler up in the passenger seat. One blue eye."

Dell's hand had gone flat against the cooler door. "What's the dog's name?"

"She called it Biscuit."

Biscuit had been dead since March. Dell had buried her in a wash outside Elko, wrapped in a moving blanket.

"She left something for you," the attendant said. "Said you'd come in asking." He slid a folded fuel receipt across the counter.

The front said *DELL* in blocky capitals, with the slashed D she'd made since third grade. Inside, under the pump total, four lines in the same hand. She read them standing there while the coffee machine hissed.

At dawn she reaches a truck stop where the attendant says a woman matching her description left an hour ago, driving her rig, with her plates and her dog. The attendant hands her a note the other driver left, addressed to her in her own handwriting.

Scene 2

Dell went out past the diesel island without looking at the attendant's window. In the cab she set the receipt on the dash, smoothed it flat with her thumb, and took the mic off its hook.

"Channel nineteen," she said, and then, because her voice came out thin, "This is Dell."

She hadn't let go of the button when the speaker opened up.

"Go ahead, Dell."

It was her own voice, a little rougher, like she'd been using it on long empty roads. There was no surprise in it. Somewhere behind it a dog's tags clinked.

"Who is this?"

"You know who. Don't waste the battery." Wind moved across the mic. "Listen. Mile marker 62, the road splits. Highway bends north, and it's smooth, and you'll want it. Take the old salt-works spur instead. Straight on, where the pavement quits."

"That's forty miles of washboard."

"Thirty-eight. Keep your speed under thirty-five and don't stop for anything white."

Dell looked at the slashed D on the receipt. Her thumb had left a gray print beside it.

"Why would I trust you?"

"You already read the paper twice." A pause. "I'm not asking you to like it."

The channel went to hiss. Dell hung up the mic, turned the key, and watched the odometer roll over to the next tenth.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Dell gets back in her cab and keys the CB, and the other Dell answers right away, calmly, as if she had been expecting the call. She says the road ahead splits at mile marker 62 and tells Dell to take the old salt-works spur and not the highway. Dell has to decide whether to trust a voice that knows her own handwriting.

Scene 3

Mile marker 62 came up green and bent, a bullet hole through the six. The highway swung north in a long clean curve, fresh paint on the shoulder line. Dell kept her foot steady and her hands at ten and two. Straight ahead the pavement ended in a lip of broken asphalt, and past it a pale track ran off toward nothing.

She downshifted and went over the lip.

The washboard took the truck at once. The trailer boomed behind her, the mirrors shook until the road jittered in them, and the receipt walked across the dash an inch at a time. She pinned it with two fingers. A cupboard door in the sleeper banged open and she let it bang. The speedometer needle trembled between thirty-two and thirty-four.

Twenty minutes in, the light went flat and strange. She saw a shape in the road a half mile ahead.

A woman stood dead center on the track, in white from shoulders to boots, with salt dust caked to her like flour. She had her arms at her sides. She wasn't waving.

Dell's foot lifted on its own. She pushed it back down. Thirty-three. Thirty-four.

The figure didn't step aside. At the last second Dell steered wide, the right tires dropping into soft crust, and the cab slid past close enough to hear the salt hiss against the door.

She looked in the side mirror. The woman had turned to watch her go. Under the white crust the face had a gray braid pulled across one shoulder, and a scar through the left eyebrow that Dell had gotten at nine, off a fence wire.

Scene 4

The right side of the truck dropped like a stair missing underfoot. Dell felt the crust break, a sound like a plate cracking under a rug, and then the cab tilted and the front axle settled into something soft and wet. The engine coughed once and quit. The washboard shudder left her hands all at once, and the quiet was worse.

She turned the key. The starter clicked and nothing caught. She reached for the mic. The CB's little red light was out, and the speaker gave her not even static.

"Come on," she said. "Go ahead, Dell. Say it."

Nothing. The receipt had slid off the dash into the footwell. She left it there.

Through the windshield the glare off the flat had thickened into a white wall, and the wall had shapes in it. One, then three, then more, rising out of the shimmer the way heat stands up off a road. She counted twelve. They walked in no hurry and in no line, arms at their sides, salt falling off their shoulders in pale smoke. Every one had a gray braid across the left shoulder. Every one had a scar through the left eyebrow.

The nearest was sixty yards out, and its boots made no sound on the crust.

Dell put her hand on the door latch, then took it off. She took the tire iron from behind the seat. She slid across to the passenger door, the high side, the one facing away from them, and thumbed it open.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The salt crust gives way under her right tires where she swerved. The truck sinks to the axle and stalls, and the CB goes dead. Through the windshield, a dozen white figures rise out of the glare and walk slowly toward her, all with her braid and her scar, and Dell has to decide whether to wait for the voice or climb out and get away from the cab.

Scene 5

Dell dropped from the high side into ankle-deep crust that held, barely. She had snatched the receipt out of the footwell on her way across, and now she crouched with it, then went flat on her belly and wormed under the cab, tire iron first. The frame dripped brine onto her collar. The crust here was gray and soft as wet cardboard.

Through the gap between the wheels she could see boots. They had stopped walking and then started again.

She held the receipt up to the light that leaked under the bumper. The four lines looked different from down here. Each one ended in a small slash she had taken for a smear. Between the words were pencil ticks, the kind she made on bills of lading to mark where to breathe. Her own marks. They were meant to be said aloud.

The nearest boots were thirty feet off. Twenty.

"I'm Dell," she read, and her voice came out dry as paper. "I'm the one who kept the speed down. Kenworth, four-one-seven, thirty-eight miles of spur. Biscuit rides on the seat."

The boots stopped.

She said the last line, and then said all four again because her mouth wouldn't quit.

Salt hissed. The women knelt in a ring, one after another, braids swinging forward. Then their hands went into the crust, bare and white, and began to dig around the tires.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Dell climbs down the high side and crawls under the cab, where she finds the receipt's four lines were written to be read aloud. She recites them as the figures close in, and the salt-women stop, then kneel and start digging at the crust around her truck.

Scene 6

Dell read the four lines a fifth time, and this time she was not the only one saying them.

The voices came in a half-beat behind her, from all sides of the truck. *I'm Dell. I'm the one who kept the speed down.* A dozen throats, and every one of them was hers. Some were rough and some were thin. One cracked on *Biscuit* the way hers had cracked in March. Above her the brine dripped steadily off the frame.

She stopped at the tick after *seat*. They stopped with her, all together, and the silence had a shape, like a held door.

Their hands had quit digging. Under the bumper she could see the kneeling women with their fingers buried to the knuckle. They waited like people at a crossing.

She turned the receipt to the light. Below the fourth line, past the slash she had taken for a smear, there was a fifth ruled line. It was empty. Only the first pencil tick sat on it, small and patient, where she'd have marked a breath.

It wasn't a warning. It was a part, and they had all stopped at the same place in it.

Her coat pocket held the grease pencil, the yellow one she used for marking trailer tires. She bit the cap off and spat it into the salt. The point dragged on the damp paper. She wrote the first word, and the slashed D came out of her hand without being asked.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Dell reads the four lines a fifth time and hears them echoed back in a dozen voices that are all hers. She realizes the receipt is a script the women need her to finish, and that the final line is blank, so she must write her own ending on it with the grease pencil from her pocket.

Scene 7

The grease pencil squeaked on the damp paper. *Dell.* She put the tick after it, and breathed there, and kept going.

*Mile 62. Take the spur. Don't stop for anything white. I'll keep Biscuit.*

She said it aloud, once, slowly, and the voices came in around her a half-beat late, steady now, no cracks in it. When she reached the last word the ring went quiet.

The women stood up out of the crust. Salt slid off their knees in sheets. They came to the truck and laid their hands on it, on the bumper and the fenders, on the dripping frame over her head. Dell felt the cold come through the steel into her shoulder blades, a cold like a cellar floor.

She wormed out the passenger side and climbed into the cab on her hands and knees. Tire iron on the seat. Receipt flat under her palm. She turned the key.

The engine caught on the first crank, loud as a dropped tray.

The front end rose. It came up with a long wet sucking sound, the axle clearing the brine, the cab tilting level, and all around her the women walked it forward onto hard crust and let go. They turned and went back out into the glare, one at a time, their white backs thinning, until the white took them.

The last one stopped at Dell's window. Her hand opened. A dog tag lay in it, one blue enamel bone, and it clinked against the glass.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Dell writes the fifth line as a promise to the next driver: a mile marker, a warning, and a dog's name. The women rise and press their salt-cold hands to the truck, and the engine turns over. They lift the cab out of the soft crust, then walk back into the glare one by one, and the last one hands her a clinking dog tag.

Scene 8

Dell took the tag. It was cold and wet, and it left a blue chip of enamel on her thumb. She hung it from the mirror stem by its ring and put the truck in gear.

The spur gave her the last of its washboard for six miles, and she held thirty-four the whole way. Then the pavement came up out of the salt in a clean black lip, and the cab went quiet under her. She eased onto it. The mirror tag swung once and settled.

The CB's red light came on by itself.

Static rose and fell. Dell watched the road. Then the speaker opened.

"You came through."

It was her voice, but older than before, worn down to the grain, with a wheeze under the vowels. No tags clinked behind it this time. Dell looked at the one hanging from her mirror.

"I wrote it," she said. "I said it back."

"You did. That was the first stretch." Wind crossed the mic. "Mile marker 211. There's a gate off the east shoulder, chained but not locked. Go through it."

"And then what?"

"Then you'll see."

The voice had never been wrong. Dell pulled the grease pencil from her pocket and held it over the receipt. A green sign rose out of the glare ahead: *Mile 163.*

She put the pencil to the back of her hand and wrote *211*, pressing hard, and kept her foot steady on the pedal.

Dell takes the tag and drives on. Past the end of the spur the CB wakes with her own voice, rougher still and clearly older. It says the part she just wrote was only the first stretch, and it gives her a new mile marker. She has to decide whether to keep trusting a voice that has never once been wrong.
