comedy of manners

Two rival families share the last ferry to an island for a wedding, and halfway across, the bride's brother announces the groom is not on board.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

The *Marguerite* held forty passengers, and tonight thirty-one of them were wedding guests who had arranged themselves by family. The Drays had taken the port benches. The Quills had taken starboard. Between them lay a strip of wet deck and a cake box that neither side would admit to having brought.

Mrs. Dray had said "How brave of you to wear that color" to Mrs. Quill on the pier, and Mrs. Quill had said "Thank you, it was my mother's," which had settled nothing.

Now the mainland was a smear of lights behind them, and the island was not yet a shape at all. Someone had passed around a thermos. Mr. Quill accepted a cup from a Dray cousin, sniffed it, and drank it with the face of a man being gracious under fire.

Fenwick Dray stood up on the bench. He had been counting under his breath for some time, tapping a finger against his thigh.

"Sorry. Sorry, everyone." He cleared his throat. "Has anyone seen Tobias?"

"He's with his people," said Mrs. Dray.

"We assumed he was with yours," said Mrs. Quill.

"He's the groom," Fenwick said. "I've counted twice. He isn't on the boat."

The engine droned. A gull landed on the rail, looked at the two families, and left. Mr. Quill lowered his cup very slowly.

"Well," said Mrs. Dray. "Someone should tell Imogen."

Scene 2

Nobody moved. Mrs. Quill looked at the cabin door, where the bride was sitting with her bridesmaids and a hot water bottle, and then at Mrs. Dray.

"She's your daughter," said Mrs. Quill.

"She'll be your daughter-in-law. If he turns up."

"He will turn up. Tobias has never been late in his life. He was born eleven minutes early."

"Then he's very much early to something else," said Mrs. Dray.

Mr. Quill held his phone to the sky and turned in a slow circle, like a man dowsing for water. "No signal."

"Perhaps he's in the toilet," offered a Quill aunt.

Fenwick climbed down from the bench. "I checked the toilet. I checked it before I counted."

A Dray cousin raised a hand. "I saw him on the pier. Gray suit, holding a lily."

"That was my husband," said Mrs. Quill. "He was holding the lily for me."

Mr. Quill examined the cup in his hand, as though the lily might be in there.

Fenwick went to the wheelhouse and knocked. The captain slid the window open six inches and listened without turning his head.

"Can we go back?"

"Tide's going out," said the captain. "Last crossing's the last crossing."

Fenwick thanked him, which seemed wrong, and walked back to the two families. The cabin door opened behind him.

"Why is everyone being so quiet?" said Imogen.

Scene 3

Imogen stood in the doorway with the hot water bottle held against her stomach like a small, sleeping animal. Behind her, three bridesmaids crowded the frame, and one of them was still holding a sandwich.

"Nothing, darling," said Mrs. Dray. "We were discussing the weather."

"The wind," said Mrs. Quill.

"It's very still," said Imogen.

"That's what we were saying."

Imogen looked at port, then starboard, then the strip of wet deck between them. Her eyes stopped on the cake box. Then she began, lips moving slightly, to count heads. Fenwick watched her get to thirty-one and start again.

"Fen."

"Yes."

"Where's Tobias?"

He had rehearsed several versions, most of them involving the word *possibly*. "He's not on the boat," he said.

One of the bridesmaids put down her sandwich.

Imogen nodded. She unscrewed the stopper of the hot water bottle, looked into it, and screwed it back on. "Who saw him last?"

"A Dray cousin saw him on the pier," said Mr. Quill, "but it turned out to be me."

"In a gray suit," said Mrs. Quill. "With a lily."

"Was it your lily?" said Imogen.

"It was mine," said Mrs. Quill, and for a moment nobody on either side of the deck could look at anyone else.

Scene 4

Imogen crossed the wet strip of deck, the bridesmaids following in a line, and crouched in front of the cake box. Nobody on either side stopped her. She lifted the lid.

Inside sat a two-tier cake, blue icing on the lower tier and green on the upper, with a seam of white piping where the two had been joined. On top stood a plastic bride and a plastic groom.

"Who ordered this?" said Imogen.

"The baker was very insistent on the green," said Mrs. Dray.

"The baker was very insistent on the blue," said Mrs. Quill.

"He took both orders," said Fenwick, "and made one cake."

Imogen lifted the plastic groom off the icing and turned him over. A small circle of frosting clung to his shoes. She held him up to the lamp over the cabin door, as if checking him for a watermark.

"Well, he's here," said a bridesmaid.

"That's not helpful, Priya."

"I meant it kindly."

Imogen set the figure on her palm. Mr. Quill took a step forward, and Mr. Dray, from the port side, took one too. They noticed each other and both stopped.

"Does anyone," Imogen said, "have a plan?"

Mr. Quill offered her his thermos cup.

Scene 5

Imogen took the cup, looked into it, and drank. Her face did not change, which Fenwick found more alarming than if it had.

"What is that?"

"Plum brandy," said Mr. Quill. "My brother's."

"It's very good," Imogen said, and handed it to Mr. Dray, who had crossed the wet strip without apparent decision. He held it a moment, then drank too, and returned it to Mr. Quill with a nod that cost him something.

"Right." Imogen stood, still holding the plastic groom. "Nobody has left this boat since the pier, because it's been in the middle of the sea. So he's either aboard and we've missed him, or he never boarded. We search first."

"Search where?" said Mrs. Dray. "It's a ferry."

"Under the benches. The life-jacket locker. The engine hatch. Priya, take the bow."

"Should we mix?" said Mrs. Quill. "The families?"

"In pairs," said Imogen. "One Dray, one Quill."

There was a silence in which several people seemed to be reading their own shoes.

"I'll take Mrs. Quill," said Mrs. Dray at last, as if selecting the least offensive fish.

"How kind."

"The locker is by the stern. Mind your hem."

"It was my mother's," said Mrs. Quill.

They went aft together, a careful foot apart, and Fenwick heard the locker open and Mrs. Dray say, "Oh."

Scene 6

Fenwick reached the stern in time to see Mrs. Dray lift a pair of black oxfords out of the life-jacket locker by their heels. Each had a sock folded inside it, the way a careful person leaves shoes at a door.

"Those are Tobias's," said Mrs. Quill. She said it quietly, like someone reading a name off a plaque.

"They could be anyone's."

"They have his initials in the tongue. I embroidered them."

Mrs. Dray turned one over and found, in thread the color of weak tea, a small *T.Q.* "Hm," she said. "Rather good stitching."

"Thank you."

"The *Q* is a little crowded."

Fenwick leaned over the locker. Beneath the orange jackets lay a gray suit jacket, folded in thirds, and on top of it a single lily with its stem wrapped in a damp tissue.

"That's my lily," said Mrs. Quill. "Mr. Quill must have set it down."

"He said he was holding it for you."

"He was. Then he wasn't."

Behind them the deck creaked. Imogen was coming aft with the plastic groom in one fist and Priya at her elbow, and the two mothers, without a word, lowered the shoes into the locker and shut the lid. Mrs. Dray sat on it. Mrs. Quill, after a moment, sat beside her.

"Found anything?" said Imogen.

"Life jackets," said Mrs. Dray.

"Plenty of them," said Mrs. Quill.

Scene 7

Imogen stopped in front of the locker and looked at the two mothers sitting on it, shoulder to shoulder, like women waiting for a verdict.

"Would you stand up, please?"

"We're quite comfortable," said Mrs. Dray.

"The cushion is lovely," said Mrs. Quill.

"There isn't a cushion."

"Then it's the principle," said Mrs. Dray.

Imogen waited. Priya, at her elbow, took a bite of a sandwich she had apparently been saving. Fenwick cleared his throat and found that he had stood up straight, and after a moment both mothers rose as well, one a half-second after the other.

Imogen lifted the lid. She took out the oxfords and looked at the socks tucked neatly into each toe. She turned the left one over and read the tongue.

"The Q is crowded," said Mrs. Dray.

"I've been told," said Mrs. Quill.

"He folded his socks," said Imogen. She said it slowly, trying out the weight of it. "Nobody gets pushed overboard and folds his socks first."

"That's a comfort," said Fenwick.

"Is it?"

He didn't know. Imogen set the plastic groom down inside the shoe, where he stood to his waist like a man in a very small boat.

From the bow, Priya's replacement shouted, "There are footprints!"

Everyone turned. On the deck, bare, wet, and drying at the edges, a line of prints ran forward to the ladder and up.

Scene 8

They followed the prints up the ladder in order of nerve: Imogen first, then Fenwick, then Priya, with both mothers at the bottom rung arguing over who should hold the other's handbag.

The prints ended on the wheelhouse roof. Tobias sat cross-legged beside the radio mast in his shirtsleeves, trouser cuffs rolled, holding his phone above his head like a man offering it to the sky.

"Hello," he said. "I think I have one bar."

"You're on the roof," said Imogen.

"I couldn't sit on either side." He lowered the phone. "I got on and there was a Dray bench and a Quill bench, and your mother looked at me, and my mother looked at me, and I thought, if I sit down I'll have decided something. So I went and stood by the toilet. Then I thought of the roof."

"You folded your socks."

"They were my good ones."

Fenwick leaned over the edge and called down, "He's here. He's fine. He's barefoot."

"Of course he is," said Mrs. Dray.

"Is he wearing the jacket?" said Mrs. Quill.

"It's in the locker," said Imogen. "With your lily."

Tobias looked at her, then at the dark water, where the island had finally become a shape with one lit window.

"Is it a very bad time," he said, "to ask who's got the cake?"

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The introductions had taken most of the crossing. Mrs. Marsh had shaken eleven Venn hands, and Mr. Venn had said "Marsh, Marsh, like the mustard?" twice, once to her and once to her sister. Now the two families stood in a loose horseshoe on the wet deck, holding paper cups of the ferry's tea.

Tobias Venn tapped his cup with a stirrer. "Before we dock, a small thing. Julian isn't on board."

Nobody spoke. A gull kept pace with the rail.

"I counted twice," Tobias said. "Marsh side has fourteen. He'd be fifteen."

Mrs. Marsh set her cup on the bench and smoothed her gloves. "How kind of you to count, Tobias."

"I like to be accurate."

"Then you'll forgive my accuracy. My son was perfectly present until he reached your family's hospitality. I think he's been put somewhere, and I think it's been a relief to some of you."

"Mother Marsh," said Mr. Venn, "we'd never."

"Not *never*, Gerald. Just not *tonight*."

A Venn cousin laughed and stopped. Behind them the cabin door stayed shut, its curtain drawn.

"We have an excellent hat budget," said Mrs. Venn, "which we'd hardly squander on a conspiracy."

"I'm sure it was lovely hats that decided you."

Tobias went up the steps to the wheelhouse and knocked on the glass. "Captain, we'll need to turn around."

The captain slid the window open two inches. "This is the last crossing."

"A man is missing."

"Then he's missing on the mainland, where it's cheaper." The window closed.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

On the crowded deck, the bride's brother announces the groom is missing, and the groom's mother calmly accuses the bride's family of hiding him to avoid the wedding. Each side starts polite, then trades barbed courtesies, and the ferry captain refuses to turn back because it is the last crossing of the night.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 The bride's brother announces the groom's absence just as the families finish an awkward round of introductions. The bride, who has been quietly in the cabin, steps out and says she knew he wouldn't be on board, which stuns both sides into silence and makes each family suspect the other of a secret.
  • 1.00 The announcement sends the families into a flurry of phone calls, and they discover the groom texted only the best man, who is also not on the ferry. Both families, determined not to lose face in front of the other, agree to pretend nothing is wrong when they reach the island, setting up a shared charade.
  • 1.00 A fussy elderly aunt from the groom's side declares that the brother is making a cruel joke and starts searching the ferry, and her search turns up the groom's tuxedo jacket, a wedding ring, and a note in the lifeboat locker. The families must decide whether to read the note aloud in front of one another, and the argument over etiquette about private letters begins.

Scene 2

Mr. Venn found Mrs. Marsh at the foot of the wheelhouse steps, where the captain's tea tray sat on a crate: a brown pot, two cups, a plate of shortbread under a napkin.

"He won't turn for a request," said Mr. Venn.

"No. He'll turn for a loss." Mrs. Marsh looked at the tray. "Gerald, I am about to suggest something I'd deny at a dinner party."

"I'll take the pot."

"You'll take the shortbread. I don't trust you with anything that pours."

They carried it up together, level, as if it were a christening. Mr. Venn knocked with his elbow. The window opened two inches.

"We have your tea," Mrs. Marsh said.

The captain looked at the tray, then at her gloves, then at Mr. Venn's grip on the plate. "That's the steward's tea."

"We'll return it," said Mr. Venn, "upon a turning."

"Or upon a biscuit," said Mrs. Marsh. "We haven't decided."

The captain took a radio from his belt. "Tell you what. I'll call the island. Harbourmaster can ask your man himself."

He pressed the button and spoke. Static answered, then a woman's voice, cheerful and far off, over what sounded like cutlery.

"Julian? Tall, nervous? He's at the head table. They've got him up on a chair. Toasting him now, the Hallorans mostly."

Mr. Venn lowered the plate. "We don't know any Hallorans."

"Nor we," said Mrs. Marsh, and took a shortbread.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mr. Venn and Mrs. Marsh, forced to agree on a plan, decide to stop the ferry by taking the captain's tea tray hostage. The captain calls their bluff and offers to radio the island, and the message that comes back is that Julian is already there, seated at the head table and being toasted by the wrong guests.

Scene 3

Tobias had gone back to counting. He did it along the rail with a finger, mouthing the numbers, while the others passed the news around in murmurs.

"Venn side is thirteen," he said.

"Marsh side is fourteen," said Mrs. Marsh, returning with the tray lighter by a biscuit. "You've told us."

"Thirteen is one short. There should be fourteen, with Clementine."

Mrs. Venn put a hand to her hat. "Clementine was beside me at the gangway."

"She was beside you at the *ticket booth*, Mother. I saw her there. I haven't seen her since the tea."

A Marsh aunt said, quite clearly, "Well, that's tidy."

"Is it?" said Mr. Venn. "Your Julian goes missing, and my daughter goes missing, and you find that tidy?"

"I find it a pattern, Gerald. Young people do have them."

"Then they've eloped," said Mrs. Venn, "and I blame whoever let him carry her bag."

"Nobody carried her bag. She doesn't own one. She has a *trunk*, and it's with the hats."

"Then she was taken," said Mrs. Marsh, "which is far worse supervision on your part."

"Our part!"

"You had her from Tuesday."

Tobias looked at the cabin. The curtain hung straight and still, and there was a light behind it, low and yellow.

"I'll note," he said, "that I counted first."

"Nobody's thanking you, dear," said Mrs. Venn.

Scene 4

Behind them the quarrel had moved on to who had paid for the trunk. Mr. Venn stood at the rail with his hands folded. Mrs. Marsh stood a yard from him, which was as close as either could manage without it meaning something.

"Do you know what I had planned for tomorrow, Mrs. Marsh?"

"I couldn't guess."

"Nothing. A chair, and the crossword. I'd cleared it with my wife in March."

Mrs. Marsh watched the wake. "There's to be a harpist. I was told so as though it were a mercy."

"There's a harpist," Mr. Venn said. "I've met her. She plays the same piece at every pause and calls it variation."

"Gerald, are you telling me you don't care for this wedding?"

"I'm telling you I've been leaning on this rail for eleven minutes with a clear conscience."

She was quiet. Then: "Suppose neither of us said anything."

"About what?"

"Any of it. We let the evening arrive on its own."

"Like weather," said Mr. Venn.

"Like a bill."

They shook on it, briefly, glove to bare hand. Mrs. Marsh looked at her own hand afterward as if it had been returned to her altered.

The Venn cousin who had laughed came down the deck with a Marsh aunt at his elbow. "We've a plan. Lifeboat cover, radio the harbourmaster, search every locker."

"We're considering," said Mr. Venn.

"Considering what?"

"Whether the lockers have been consulted," said Mrs. Marsh.

The aunt looked from one to the other. "You're standing *together*."

Behind the curtain, the yellow light wavered, as if someone had leaned toward it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mr. Venn and Mrs. Marsh, stranded together at the rail while their relatives bicker, discover they both privately dislike the wedding. They make a gentle, ridiculous pact to say nothing and let the evening unfold, which puts them at odds with their own children's side when the cousins start planning a rescue.

Scene 5

The captain accepted the tray through the two-inch gap, lifted the napkin, and counted what was left of the shortbread with one finger.

"Short a biscuit."

"Seen to," said Mrs. Marsh. "Gerald will owe you one."

"I'll turn her," the captain said. "But the company wants a cause in the log. Somebody aboard says what became of the pair, and says it was them. I'm not logging 'mislaid.'"

Mrs. Venn arrived at the rail, hat first. "Then I did it."

"Hilda," said Mr. Venn.

"I put Clementine in the hat trunk, Gerald, with air holes, and had her carried aboard as millinery."

"It was I," said Mrs. Marsh, unbuttoning one glove. "I bribed a porter to take Julian to the mainland in a laundry cart, and I tipped him in advance, which I'll admit is a vulgarity."

"I sold them both," said Mrs. Venn. "To a man in Dover."

"For livestock," said Mrs. Marsh. "I sold them as livestock, by weight, and I haggled."

"I haggled *upward*."

Tobias had stopped counting. A Marsh aunt sat down on the bench without looking where it was.

The captain wrote something, unhurried. Under their feet the engine changed its note. The deck leaned, and the island's lights slid along the rail from left to right, a string of small windows going out of reach.

"Dover," said the captain. "That'll do."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The captain, bribed with the returned tea tray and a promise of shortbread, announces he will turn back only if a family member confesses to the missing couple's disappearance. Mrs. Venn and Mrs. Marsh, each eager to avoid blame, compete to confess to progressively more absurd crimes, and the ferry turns in a slow circle while the others look on appalled.

Scene 6

Tobias took hold of the cabin door and opened it, and the curtain swung in after him.

Julian and Clementine sat on either side of a small table with a brown pot between them, a cosy on its head. Julian had a cup halfway to his mouth. Clementine had her shoes off and her feet on the lifejacket bin.

"Fourteen," said Tobias. "Fifteen."

"Hello, Tobias," Clementine said. "There's tea, if you're not being accurate."

The deck filled the doorway behind him. Mrs. Venn's hat came through first, then the Marsh aunt, then both fathers.

"Julian," said Mrs. Marsh. "Since when?"

"Since the first tea, I think." He set the cup down carefully. "Someone said to wait here a moment. I've been waiting."

"Who said it?"

"A glove," said Clementine. "Or a hat. It was held up in a doorway. I assumed it was official."

"A glove," said Mr. Venn, looking at Mrs. Marsh's.

"A hat," said Mrs. Marsh, looking at Mrs. Venn's.

"Our Clementine would never sit quietly for a Marsh."

"I sat quietly for forty minutes," said Clementine. "Julian's very restful."

"Your Julian," said Mrs. Venn, "has always had the look of a boy who is easily put in rooms."

"And yours has the look of a girl who is easily shut in them."

"I wasn't shut," said Clementine. "I was given a biscuit."

Behind the others, Mr. Venn leaned toward Mrs. Marsh and said, very low, "Weather."

"A bill," she said, and kept her eyes on the pot.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Tobias opens the cabin door at last and finds Julian and Clementine inside with the steward's tea, both ferry passengers all along and hidden since the first tea. Neither can say who hid them, and each family promptly claims the other did it.

Scene 7

Julian cleared his throat as though the table were a lectern. "We did it on purpose."

"The tea?" said Mrs. Marsh.

"The cabin. When the first tea went round, Clementine took my sleeve and we went in and sat down."

"There's a harpist," said Clementine. "There are two hundred chairs, and a seating plan that took Julian's mother a year. We wanted forty minutes before it all started belonging to everyone."

"You let us count," said Tobias.

"You were very good at it," said Julian.

Mrs. Venn drew breath beneath the hat. "Do you know what we have said, in front of a *captain*?"

"Dover," said Clementine. "We heard. Through the door. It was the best part."

"We'd ask," Julian said, "that nobody mentioned it. Not the cabin, not the tea. We'll walk off at the island like everyone else, a little late."

Nobody moved. The engine thrummed under the floor.

"Nothing said," said Mr. Venn.

"Not a word," said Mrs. Marsh, a half-second behind, and neither looked at the other.

"Gerald," said Mrs. Venn.

"It's only weather, Hilda."

"You cannot simply—Margaret, tell him he cannot simply—"

"I'm afraid I've just agreed with him," said Mrs. Marsh, and began to put her glove back on, finger by finger. "It's most unlike me. I expect it will pass."

Clementine poured two more cups and held one out to her mother. After a moment Mrs. Venn took it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Julian and Clementine confess they hid in the cabin on purpose, to skip the harpist and a long evening of two families, and they ask everyone to say nothing. Mr. Venn and Mrs. Marsh, bound by their weather pact, are the first to agree, which leaves both mothers outmaneuvered by their own husbands' calm.

Scene 8

The captain came down the wheelhouse steps with a clipboard held out in front of him like a collection plate. The families had arranged themselves in two rows outside the cabin door, teacups in hand.

"Log wants signatures," he said. "Both ladies, under the entry."

Mrs. Venn took the clipboard and held it at arm's length. "'Sold to a man in Dover, as livestock, by weight.' You've been very plain."

"It's how it was said."

"Margaret, you first."

"I wouldn't dream of it, Hilda. It was your hat that began the trouble."

"Alphabetically—"

"Alphabetically Marsh comes before Venn, and I refuse to be seen taking precedence."

The captain produced two pens from his breast pocket and held them out. "Together."

They signed at the same moment, on adjacent lines, each watching the other's wrist. Mrs. Venn's flourish ran into the margin. Mrs. Marsh crossed her *t* as though settling a debt. Neither looked up until both pens had lifted.

"Thank you." The captain read the page, then tucked the clipboard under his arm. "Dover rang through while you were at it. Says the stock's undersized, and he never ordered any. Refused delivery."

"The impertinence," said Mrs. Venn.

"You'll owe him a biscuit. For the trouble."

"We seem to be running a deficit of biscuits," said Mr. Venn.

The captain went back up the steps. A moment later the engine changed its note, the deck leaned the other way, and the string of small windows began to slide back along the rail from right to left. Tobias opened his mouth, looked at the lights, and shut it again.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The captain, who has been logging the 'Dover' confession, comes down to the deck and asks the two mothers to sign it. Mrs. Marsh and Mrs. Venn sign with great dignity, and he turns the ferry back toward the island, telling them the Dover man has already refused delivery and they owe him a biscuit.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

Desmond Alderwick climbed onto a bench beside the life vests and tapped a plastic cup with his house key. The Alderwicks stopped talking. The Pruitts, clustered at the stern with their gift boxes, went on talking for another few seconds, to make a point.

"I've counted twice," Desmond said. "Forty-one of ours, thirty-eight of theirs, the captain, a man with a bicycle. No Theo."

"Theo is a Pruitt," said Mrs. Pruitt, from behind a hat the width of a serving platter. "Theo is never late. Theo was told to sit with the family."

"Which family?" said Desmond's aunt. "You put him by the vending machine. Nobody sits by the vending machine."

"We put him where your people left room. Your people took the benches by the heater and spread their coats like they were claiming Poland."

"You arrived at the terminal at ten to nine."

"The ferry was listed for nine-fifteen."

"The ferry was listed for nine."

Someone's uncle began reading the timetable aloud off his phone. Someone else's uncle began reading it louder. The bride, Cora, sat at the center of the commotion with her bouquet across her knees, smoothing a ribbon and looking at the water. Mrs. Pruitt watched her for a long moment, and her mouth tightened.

At the rail, a woman in a gray raincoat lowered a folder she had been pretending to read.

Mr. Alderwick marched up the steps to the wheelhouse. The captain didn't open the door fully.

"Turn around," Mr. Alderwick said.

"Can't."

"There's a man missing."

"Then he's on the mainland, and it's the last crossing tonight." The captain shut the door, and the engine kept its steady note.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

On the crowded deck, the bride's brother Desmond announces the groom is missing, and both families immediately blame each other's seating arrangements and lateness, so the captain refuses to turn back because it is the last crossing of the night.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 The bride, calm and unbothered, reveals she sent the groom ahead on a private boat to avoid the families' feuding, but Desmond's announcement has already convinced the groom's mother that the bride has hidden him, and she demands to search every cabin and lifeboat.
  • 1.00 A search of the ferry turns up the groom's rented tuxedo in a luggage rack, but no groom, and the two patriarchs, forced into a polite alliance to preserve appearances, agree to tell the other guests that he is merely seasick below deck.
  • 1.00 Desmond's announcement is overheard by the ferry's lone stranger, a registrar traveling to the island for her own reasons, who offers to officiate any substitute groom the families can agree on, which sets the two sides bargaining over whose cousin is least objectionable.

Scene 2

The man with the bicycle had been holding its handlebar the whole time, as though it might be called as a witness. "I did see him," he said. "At the terminal. Tall, good coat. He asked if I was going all the way over."

"And you didn't think to say so?" said Desmond.

"You said *on board*. He wasn't on board when I got on." He reached inside his jacket. "He gave me this. I was to hand it to the bride at the halfway point." He checked his watch, then looked down at the water as if the middle might be marked. "That's about now."

The envelope was cream, sealed, and addressed in handwriting too neat for a man in a hurry. Cora took it. She slid a thumbnail under the flap while both families leaned in, and a gull on the rail leaned in with them.

The letter was one page. She read it without changing expression, then read it again.

"Well?" said Mrs. Pruitt. "Read it out. My son wrote it, and I have a right."

"Burn it," said Mr. Alderwick. "Somebody find a lighter."

"It's a ferry," said his sister. "Nobody has a lighter."

"The captain smokes."

"Cora," Mrs. Pruitt said, with a gentleness that made two Alderwicks step back, "what does it say?"

Cora folded the page along its crease. At the rail, the woman in the gray raincoat had stopped pretending to read at all.

"It begins," said Cora, "*Dear Cora, I trust this finds you well.*"

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The man with the bicycle admits he saw Theo at the terminal. Theo gave him a sealed envelope and asked him to deliver it to Cora once they were midway, which is right now. When she opens it, the note is a polite, devastating letter of withdrawal. Mrs. Pruitt demands the envelope be read aloud, and Mr. Alderwick demands it be burned.

Scene 3

"*Dear Cora, I trust this finds you well. I write to withdraw from the arrangements of the evening, and I wish to do so with every courtesy.*" She turned the page toward the light. "*I thank both families for their hospitality over the past fourteen months. I would like to record my gratitude for the lunch in March, the lunch in June, and the second lunch in June.*"

"That was a good lunch," said Mrs. Pruitt.

"*I would also record the following difficulties. One: the seating chart, in which my mother was placed beside an Alderwick cousin who described her hat as 'brave.'*"

"It was a compliment," said Desmond's aunt.

"It was not," said Mrs. Pruitt.

"*Two: the rehearsal dinner, at which the Alderwicks sang. Three: the toast the Pruitts prepared in response. Four: the parking.*"

"What parking?" said Mr. Alderwick.

"Your people parked across the Pruitt car," said a Pruitt.

"Your car was across *our* line!"

"There was no line!"

"There was a line of *cones*!"

Cora let them go. She read the letter a third time with her eyes only, down to the signature, *Yours sincerely, Theodore Pruitt*, and back to the top. Hospitality, lunches, hat, cones, parking. She turned the page over to check the back, and the back was blank.

The man with the bicycle edged toward her. "Is there more?"

"No," said Cora. She put the letter in her bouquet, between two stems, where it sat like a very formal flower.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Cora reads the letter aloud and it is a formal, courteous withdrawal, with Theo thanking both families for their hospitality and listing the grievances that made him leave, including the seating chart. Both families, each named as the cause, begin an indignant defense, and Cora quietly notices the letter says nothing about her.

Scene 4

"Search him," said Desmond. "He's in on it."

"I'm not in on anything," said the man with the bicycle. "I'm a courier." He fished a card from his breast pocket and held it out at arm's length, like a man offering a biscuit to a dog. *Fenwick & Daughter, Prompt Delivery.* "Mr. Theodore paid me forty to board the nine o'clock and hand that over at the halfway point. Not before. He was firm on the halfway point."

Mrs. Pruitt's hat dipped. "Forty?"

"Plus the ferry fare."

"My son *tips* more than forty." She opened her handbag with a snap. "Eighty. So it's understood that a Pruitt pays properly, and that my son is a gentleman who engages people at a fair rate."

"One hundred twenty," said Mr. Alderwick, already holding out his wallet.

"I said double."

"And I said triple. You may call it generosity if you can't call it arithmetic."

"Are you paying him to *insult* us?"

"I am paying him to be paid by an Alderwick, madam, which is a distinction he'll appreciate."

"One-fifty," said Mrs. Pruitt.

"Is this how your lunches went?" said a Pruitt cousin, and an Alderwick said, "Don't you start with lunches."

The courier took the notes one by one, counted them against his knee, and slid them into the saddlebag. At the rail, the woman in the gray raincoat wrote something in her folder.

"Much obliged," he said, to no one in particular.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Desmond demands that the man with the bicycle be searched, and it emerges that the man is Theo's hired courier and was paid to deliver the letter at exactly the halfway point. Mrs. Pruitt, mortified, insists on paying him double to prove her son is a gentleman, and Mr. Alderwick insists on paying triple. The bidding war shifts the families' fury away from Theo and onto each other, and the courier quietly profits.

Scene 5

Desmond climbed back onto the bench. The plastic cup had rolled away, so he rang a life-vest buckle with his key.

"We'll settle it by vote," he said. "Both families. Shall the wedding proceed, yes or no. Simple majority."

"Seconded," said Mr. Alderwick, before anyone else could.

"Who counts?" said Mrs. Pruitt. "Blood only?"

"Blood and marriage."

"Then your cousin's fiancé votes, and he's known her six weeks."

"Nine," said the fiancé.

"Nine weeks! We have a Pruitt engaged eleven years who isn't allowed a ballot."

"Engaged isn't married."

"Neither is nine weeks!"

A Pruitt child of seven raised her hand and asked if children could vote. Both families said no in the same breath, then glared at each other for agreeing. Under-sixteens were struck. So were the divorced, after twenty minutes on whether a divorce from an Alderwick left you a Pruitt, an Alderwick, or a free agent. A tally was kept on the back of a ferry timetable. Desmond counted hands, Mrs. Pruitt's nephew counted them again, and the two counts did not meet.

"Thirty-three each," Desmond said at last, "with one abstention."

Everyone looked at Cora. She was adjusting the letter deeper into her bouquet and did not look up.

"We need a tiebreaker," said Mr. Alderwick.

"Someone neutral," said Mrs. Pruitt.

Every head turned to the bicycle.

"I've been paid by both of you," said the courier. He tightened his grip on the handlebar. "What am I voting on?"

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Desmond and Mr. Alderwick, stung by the lunch comparison and the bidding war, propose settling the matter by a formal vote of the two families on whether the wedding should go ahead. The vote devolves into a procedural farce over who counts as family, and the man with the bicycle is drafted as the tiebreaker.

Scene 6

"On whether the wedding proceeds," said Desmond. "Yes or no."

The courier looked at the bicycle as though it might advise him. "Yes," he said.

Mr. Alderwick began to smile. A Pruitt groaned.

"No," said the courier.

The smile stopped. "You said yes."

"I did, and now I've said no. I wanted to hear how each sounded." He unbuckled the saddlebag, took out a pencil stub, and wrote on the back of his own card. "That's thirty a ballot. Sixty so far."

"Thirty for *what*?" said Mrs. Pruitt.

"Binding decisions. If it's not binding I'd charge less, but nobody's said."

"It's a tiebreak, not a service!"

"Everything is a service, madam, once you've been asked twice."

Mr. Alderwick's wallet was already open. Mrs. Pruitt's handbag was already snapping. Desmond lifted the buckle to ring it again.

"I was the abstention," said Cora.

She had not raised her voice, but the buckle stopped halfway to the bench. She stood, the bouquet held in front of her like a hymnal, the corner of cream paper showing between two stems.

"I'll vote," she said, "once you've heard what I wrote back to Theo."

"Wrote back?" said Mrs. Pruitt.

"I posted it this morning, at the terminal. Before any of you arrived." She looked at Mr. Alderwick, then at Mrs. Pruitt. "Ten to nine, you said? Both of you?"

At the rail, the woman in the gray raincoat closed her folder.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The courier, cornered, votes yes, then no, then asks for a fee for each ballot. Cora finally speaks and says she was the abstention, and that she will cast her vote only after both families hear what she wrote back to Theo, which she reveals she posted before boarding.

Scene 7

Cora took a folded sheet from inside her sleeve. "I kept the draft."

"*Dear Theo,*" she read. "*I trust this finds you well. I write to withdraw from the arrangements of the evening, and I wish to do so with every courtesy.*"

Mr. Alderwick opened his mouth. Mrs. Pruitt laid two fingers on his sleeve, and he closed it, to everyone's surprise, including his own.

"*I thank both families for their hospitality over the past fourteen months, particularly the lunch in March, the lunch in June, and the second lunch in June, at which neither side passed the salt to the other and I was sent for it twice.*"

A Pruitt cousin coughed.

"*I would record the following difficulties. One: the seating chart. Two: the singing, and the toast in reply. Three: the parking. Four: that in fourteen months no one of either name has asked me a question that was not secretly about the other. Five: that I have been carried across a great many rooms like a casserole dish, and both families have complained about the weight.*"

She turned the page over. "*I therefore withdraw as well. I'm sure you will understand. Yours sincerely, Cora.*"

She refolded it along its crease.

Nobody spoke. The engine kept its note. Mr. Alderwick's wallet was still open in his hand, and he looked at it as though someone else had given it to him. Mrs. Pruitt's hat had sunk an inch, and she did not correct it. Over the rail, a gull dropped to the water and found nothing.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Cora reads aloud her reply to Theo, which mirrors his format: gratitude for the lunches, then a numbered list of grievances about both families, ending with her own withdrawal. Both families, who have spent the voyage bidding for her, realize she was never choosing between them, and they fall silent for the first time.

Scene 8

The woman in the gray raincoat came away from the rail with her folder under one arm and stopped in front of the bench.

"Margaret Oyelaran," she said. "Registrar for the island. I was crossing to be ready for the morning. I'm afraid I've heard all of it."

"All of it?" said Mrs. Pruitt.

"From the vending machine onward. I did try to look at the water."

Desmond climbed down from the bench and put his key in his pocket.

"With no couple, I have no ceremony," said Ms. Oyelaran. "Nothing to register, and I won't invent something. But I have watched seventy-nine people agree, in the last ten minutes, on the lunches, the parking, and the singing." She turned a page in her folder. "Under the island bylaws that's a quorum, and a quorum may be seated for a reception. The hall is booked. The lamb is paid for."

"We couldn't possibly," said Mr. Alderwick.

"Out of the question," said Mrs. Pruitt. Neither of them moved. "Unless it would inconvenience you, Registrar."

"It would inconvenience me a great deal if you didn't."

"Then of course," said Mr. Alderwick.

"Naturally," said Mrs. Pruitt.

The hall had one long table and place cards in Cora's handwriting. No one touched the chart. Mrs. Pruitt found herself beside the Alderwick cousin, who looked at her hat and then, with visible effort, at the salt. She passed it. Mrs. Pruitt took it, and said thank you, and used it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The woman in the gray raincoat finally steps forward and reveals she is the island's registrar, who has been listening all crossing. She remarks that with no couple she has no ceremony, but that two families who have just discovered they share one grievance are, procedurally, a quorum for the reception. Both families, too polite to refuse an official, sit down to the dinner together.

science fiction

On a research station orbiting Titan, the only botanist wakes to find one plant has grown overnight into the air ducts, and the crew's oxygen readings have improved.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Dr. Imara Voss woke to the smell of wet soil, which was wrong. The hydroponics bay was two decks down and sealed.

She lay in her bunk for a moment, listening. The air handler's usual drone had changed pitch, lower and softer, as if something were muffling it. She pulled on her thermal layer and went barefoot down the corridor, the grating cold under her soles.

The vent above her cabin door had a leaf in it.

Not a whole leaf. A green edge, glossy, curled between two louvers. She stood on the bunk frame and touched it. Warm. A fine pale root hair clung to her fingertip and held there when she lifted her hand.

"Okay," she said aloud.

In the corridor junction, a tendril as thick as her thumb ran along the ceiling seam, tucked into the duct housing, then disappeared behind a panel. She followed it through the galley, past the med bay, down the ladder. Every few meters it branched into the ducts, neat and deliberate, like a hand feeling along a wall.

In hydroponics, Tray Nine was nearly empty. The pothos cutting she had propagated six weeks ago, the one she'd nicknamed Gerald, was now a stalk and a few pale leaves. Its roots lay out of the nutrient bath and across the floor, trailing toward an access hatch she had left unlatched.

The wall panel by the door showed cabin oxygen at 21.4 percent. Yesterday it had read 19.8, and she had been drafting a request to Earth about the scrubbers.

She read the number three times, then pressed the intercom.

"Captain Okafor? I need you to come down here. Don't call anyone yet."

Scene 2

Captain Okafor arrived in his sleep shirt and mission fleece, one boot unlaced, carrying a tablet he had clearly grabbed out of habit. He stopped inside the hatch and looked at the floor.

"That's a root."

"Several," Imara said. "They go out through the access hatch and up. I've followed them as far as the galley."

"Followed them." He crouched and did not touch it. "Is it toxic? Is it eating the insulation?"

"I don't know yet. I haven't cut anything."

He stood. His eyes went to the wall panel, and she watched him read it, then read it again, the way she had. "Twenty-one point four."

"Up from nineteen-eight at last check. I was going to write Earth about the scrubbers."

"You told me not to call anyone."

"I wanted you to see it first." She heard how that sounded and pressed on. "Once Houston knows, they'll want it out. That's protocol. Biological contamination of life-support."

"It is biological contamination of life-support."

"It's also the only reason my lungs don't feel like wet paper."

Okafor looked at Tray Nine, at the pale stalk that had been Gerald. Then he went to the nearest vent and held his palm flat in front of it. His hand stayed there a long moment.

"Warm," he said.

"Yes."

He took out his tablet and opened a blank log entry. His thumb hovered over it. "Walk me through everything from the beginning. Slowly. I want it in your words."

Scene 3

She talked while he typed with two fingers. Gerald was a six-inch cutting from the pothos in the commissary, rooted in water in March, moved to Tray Nine in April. She had fed it the standard nutrient mix and nothing else. No growth hormone, no light schedule changes.

"Did it do anything odd before last night?"

"It grew. Slowly. Two new leaves in six weeks." She rubbed her thumb against her fingertip, where the root hair had been. "Yesterday I checked it at nineteen hundred. It was fine."

"Fine meaning what?"

"Fine meaning a houseplant."

He logged that. Then he said, "Show me where it goes."

They followed the main tendril up the ladder and along the galley ceiling. At the med bay it split. One branch went on toward the crew cabins. The other dropped through a gap in the panel beside the scrubber room door.

Okafor keyed the lock. Inside, the CO₂ scrubber hummed at its usual pitch, and the root had wound around the intake housing in a loose, even spiral, fine white hairs pressed against the grille. Nothing near the wiring. Nothing across the sensor leads.

"It went around those," Imara said.

"Plants don't go around things."

"They do, actually. Slowly."

He looked at his watch, then at the tablet. He didn't save the entry.

Scene 4

"Twelve hours," Okafor said. "The comms window to Houston is at twenty hundred. Until then it's mine and yours, and nobody else's."

"You want me to cut it."

"I want you to sample it. A leaf, not the stem."

Imara took a scalpel and a sample vial from the kit on her belt. She chose a leaf near the scrubber intake, a small one, and nicked it at the petiole. Clear sap beaded at the cut. She caught it in the vial and capped it. Okafor watched the root on the housing.

It did not move. Then, a few seconds later, the fine white hairs along the grille drew in a fraction, like a hand closing slowly.

"Did you see that?" she said.

"I saw it."

Boots rang on the ladder outside. Okafor shut the scrubber door halfway, too late. Dae-jung Park, the flight engineer, ducked into the corridor with his hair flat on one side, rubbing the back of his neck.

"Morning," he said. "Weird thing. Slept eight hours straight. No headache." He glanced at the half-open door, then up at the ceiling seam, where the tendril ran pale against the dark housing. He stopped rubbing his neck.

"Captain," he said, "why is there a vine in my ceiling?"

Scene 5

Okafor didn't answer right away. He looked at Imara, then at Park's flattened hair, then back at the ceiling.

"Dae-jung. Come in and close the door."

Park came in. He stood under the seam and tilted his head back, and Imara watched his eyes follow the tendril the way an engineer reads a cable run: where it entered, where it bent, where it was clamped. Except nothing had clamped it.

"That's organic," he said.

"It's from Tray Nine," Imara said. "It grew overnight."

"Overnight." He reached up and stopped a few centimeters short. "It's in the return duct. I have a filter change due on that line." He lowered his hand. "Is that why the air's different? I thought I was imagining it."

"Oxygen's up one point six," Okafor said. "Nobody has touched the scrubbers."

Park laughed once, short, then saw that neither of them was laughing. "You're not calling it in."

"At twenty hundred. After we know more."

"What do you want to know?"

Imara held up the vial. The sap had gone faintly cloudy against the glass. "What it does when you hurt it. What it does when you don't."

Park looked at the root wound around the scrubber housing, the white hairs pressed to the grille.

"Then I want the airflow logs for every duct it's in," he said. "Before it grows into anything else."

Scene 6

Park pulled the logs onto the engineering console and split the screen into six duct schematics. Imara stood at his shoulder with the sample vial in her fist, warm from her hand.

"Here." He tapped a line that dipped. "Return duct three. Flow drops eleven percent at oh-two-twelve. That's the root crossing the first junction. Something's sitting in the airway."

"And CO₂?"

"Starts falling at oh-two-thirty. Scrubber room first, then the galley, then cabins, in order." He dragged a second graph over the first. The curves overlapped like tracing paper. "It's following the growth. Wherever it goes, the air gets cleaner a few minutes behind it."

Imara leaned closer. "Can you show me the filter schedule?"

He looked at her, then pulled it up. Three filters were marked overdue. Two were green, replaced last week.

"Overlay the path," she said.

Park did. The tendril ran through every overdue section, loaded with its gray dust, and skirted both new ones. In duct five it had gone the long way around, forty extra meters of ceiling, to reach an old housing.

"It's picking the dirty ones," Park said quietly.

Behind them the intercom clicked. Okafor's voice came through flat and controlled. "Imara, Park. Cabin four. Now. Vasquez is awake and she's talking to the vent."

Scene 7

Okafor stood in the doorway of cabin four with his arms folded and did not go in. He stepped aside when Imara reached him.

Vasquez sat cross-legged on her bunk in her thermal layer, her face tipped up toward the ceiling vent. A tendril had come down through the louvers and hung a forearm's length into the room, the tip curled loosely like a question mark. She was talking to it in the low, even voice people use on nervous animals.

"Three weeks I've had that cough. Three weeks, and Dr. Chen said it was regolith dust in the lining. And I woke up and it was gone." She coughed once, experimentally, and shook her head. "Gone."

The tip of the tendril swayed a few centimeters toward her.

"Elena," Okafor said.

"I know how it looks." She didn't turn. "I woke up and it was already down here, just hanging. I didn't touch it. I only said good morning."

Park crouched to see the underside of the leaf cluster, the pale root hairs packed along the vent frame. "It's tracking her," he said. "Or her breath. CO₂ gradient."

"Or her voice," Vasquez said.

Imara stepped into the room. The tendril stopped swaying. Then the tip bent, slowly, away from Vasquez and toward Imara's hand, the one still closed around the sample vial.

Vasquez looked at the vial, then at Imara's face. "What did you take from it?"

Scene 8

"Sap," Imara said. "One leaf's worth. I wanted to know what it was made of."

"Did it hurt?"

"I don't know."

Vasquez held out her hand, palm up, the way you would for a stranger's dog. Imara hesitated, then crossed the room and set the vial in it. The tendril followed. It stopped a finger's width from the glass, and the tip flattened. Fine white hairs fanned out and touched the cap, then the cloudy sap behind it. They stayed there.

"It's not angry," Vasquez said.

"You can't know that," Park said.

"No." She kept her eyes on the vial. "But I'd like to be the one who gets to say so."

Okafor checked his watch. Nineteen-forty. He looked at the tablet in his hand, the log entry still open, his two-fingered notes stacked in a column. He scrolled to the bottom and read the last line.

"Park, how long to rig a camera on duct three?"

"Ten minutes."

"Do it. Imara, bring the sample to the lab and run what you can before twenty hundred. Elena, you stay here and keep talking."

"To the plant?"

"To whoever's listening."

He turned and went down the corridor, the tablet against his chest, toward the comms room. Behind him the vent gave a soft, steady breath.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The tendril above her bunk was as thick as her thumb and still faintly wet. Imre Valdis pulled herself out of the sleeping sack, touched it once, and felt it tighten around her finger like a held breath.

She followed it in her socks. It ran along the corridor ceiling, slipped into a grate that should have been bolted shut, and she took the maintenance crawlway on her elbows, headlamp swinging. Pale roots lined the duct walls. Every junction had a new leaf, small and folded, the color of a lime rind.

The central air handler sat in its cage at the end of the crawlway. The vine had gone into it. Where the intake fan should have shown steel blades, it showed green. Stems wrapped the housing and had grown through the louvers, and the louvers moved. They opened and closed in slow turns, with no motor behind them. The fan's status light glowed amber and then settled to a steady green.

"Okay," she whispered. Her breath fogged in the lamp beam.

She took the pruning shears from her thigh pocket and cut the nearest stem, a thin one. Clear sap beaded at the stub.

The alarm began before the sap dripped. A low tone first, then the full klaxon, and the wall panel above her flashed O₂ 17.9%, then 17.2. Down the corridor a door banged, and someone shouted a name that wasn't hers.

Imre dropped the shears. The louvers were already shuddering open.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imre follows the vine to the station's central air handler and finds it has fused with the machinery, so the plant is now regulating airflow on its own. When she tries to trim it back, the station alarms sound as oxygen levels drop, which shows her the crew now depends on it.

Her log reveals that someone with access to the greenhouse altered the plant's cultivation tray three nights ago, so she starts wondering which crewmate did it.

Scene 2

Boots rang on the crawlway grate behind her. Dace Whitlow came in on his stomach, a plasma torch shoved ahead of him, its pilot flame a blue needle.

"Imre. Get away from it."

"Dace, wait."

"Away." He dragged himself level with the junction. His coveralls were on inside out, the seam ridged along his collar. "That's growing through the intake. One stem in the blades and the fan throws itself apart."

She slid sideways until her back pressed against the housing. Stems shifted behind her ribs, warm through her shirt. "The fan was already dying. You signed the maintenance report yourself."

"I can swap the bearings."

"In how long? Eight hours? Look at the panel."

He looked. O₂ 16.8. The klaxon went on, flat and patient, and the pilot flame bent in the draft from the louvers.

"That's the plant's fault," he said.

"Or the plant's fixing it, and I just cut it." She heard how that sounded. "Yesterday we were at nineteen and falling. Nobody was shouting because we were all asleep."

"Nineteen and falling is a problem I understand." He raised the torch. The pilot lit the nearest leaf from below, and the leaf curled away from the heat. "Move your hands off the casing."

"If you fire that in here, you burn the only intake we've got."

His jaw worked. The flame stayed where it was.

Scene 3

Imre peeled her right hand off the housing and held it up where he could see it. "I'm touching it. Watch the torch, not me."

"Imre."

She found the stub she had cut, a green nub no longer than a fingernail, still beaded with sap. She laid her bare palm over it.

The stem was warm. It pulsed once against her skin, then again, slower, like something deciding. The sap spread under her hand, cool and slick, and the louvers behind her swung wide with a long wooden creak. Air poured through the crawlway and lifted the hair off her forehead.

The panel flickered. O₂ 17.4. 17.9. 18.5.

The klaxon kept going for three more seconds, as if nobody had told it, and then cut out. The silence rang.

Dace didn't move. The pilot flame leaned in the new draft, steady and blue. His eyes went from the panel to her hand.

"Lift it," he said.

She did. A thin film of sap had dried across her palm like clear nail lacquer. The stub beneath was closed over, glossy and pale, with no wet left on it.

He let out a breath through his teeth and thumbed the torch off. The needle of flame vanished.

"Lab," he said. "Now. You're going to show me this thing is safe, and you're going to do it before Okafor finishes her coffee."

Scene 4

The lab smelled of isopropyl and old coffee. Imre laid out three slides, a scalpel, and a sterile vial, then scraped the dried sap from her palm into the vial with the flat of the blade. Her hands were steady. She noticed that and didn't trust it.

Dace stood at the far counter with his arms crossed, still in his inside-out coveralls. "Your seed stock. When did you last open it?"

"Never. The vault's been sealed since launch. I grew everything from the working trays in the greenhouse."

"Then explain that."

He was looking at the specimen cabinet, the glass-fronted unit on the back wall where she kept reserve seed under nitrogen. She crossed to it with a slide still pinched in her fingers.

Green pressed against the glass from inside. It was a mat of leaves folded over leaves, pale stems packed between the racks, the seed trays buried somewhere beneath. The door gasket was intact. The gauge read nitrogen, full.

"Those seals haven't been broken," she said. "Look, the tape's still on the—"

Dace laid two fingers on the glass.

Every leaf nearest his hand turned. They swiveled with a faint papery rustle that carried through the pane, lifting the way faces tilt in a crowd. The ones behind followed, row by row, until the whole cabinet leaned toward his fingertips.

He took his hand back. The leaves stayed where they were.

Imre looked at the unbroken tape, then at the vial in her hand, the sap already clouding at the bottom. Nothing in that cabinet had ever been planted.

"It didn't start with mine," she said.

Scene 5

Dace took the lab terminal without asking and pulled up the maintenance logs. Imre stood behind his shoulder and watched him scroll past filter changes, a coolant flush, his own signature on the air handler report.

"Vault access," he said, and typed it in.

The list was short. Launch day, a pressure check in month two, and then one more line.

*Seed vault, cold room B. 02:14. Credential: VALDIS, I. Badge and thumbprint. Duration: 41 min.*

Neither of them spoke. The date sat at the end of the line, twenty-one days back.

"I was asleep," Imre said.

"It says badge and thumbprint."

"Then somebody has my badge." She heard her own voice go thin. "I haven't opened that vault, Dace. I'd remember forty-one minutes in a cold room. I'd remember my fingers."

He scrolled to the door sensor data. The door had cycled once, opened and closed, with the temperature in the room dropping two degrees and recovering. No second entry. No one had come out of it, or the log hadn't noticed.

Imre looked at her right thumb. The sap had dried to a faint shine along the pad.

Dace sat with his hand on the trackpad. Behind them, in the cabinet, the leaves rustled against the glass, and neither of them turned around.

"Print it," he said at last.

She did. The printer clicked, and he folded the sheet in thirds and put it in his coverall pocket, and he did not tell her what he thought.

Scene 6

Commander Okafor answered the third knock in a gray thermal shirt, one sock on. Dace held the folded sheet out before she'd fully opened the door. She read it standing in the corridor light, lips moving slightly at the timestamp.

"Twenty-one days," she said.

"The door cycled once," Dace said. "Nobody logged out."

"I was asleep, Commander." Imre kept her hands visible. "Ask the cabinet. Ask the tape on it."

Okafor looked at her for a long moment, then at the sheet again. "Show me the cabinet."

She stood in the lab a full minute with her arms folded while the leaves leaned toward her, and she did not touch the glass. When she turned around, her face had closed.

"Valdis, you're confined to quarters. Not as punishment. I need you where I can find you." She turned. "Whitlow, get the torch checked and fueled. The greenhouse first. Then the ducts, section by section."

"Commander," Dace said, and stopped.

In the corridor, Teo from hydrology stood in his doorway, listening. "The air's the best it's been in a month," he said. Nobody answered him.

Okafor walked Imre to her bunk herself. The lock bolt thunked home from outside.

Imre sat on the sleeping sack and listened to boots recede. Above her, the tendril she had touched that morning had thickened. Its tip lifted off the ceiling and swung toward the door panel, slowly, in time with the pulse beating in her wrist.

Scene 7

Night cycle dimmed the corridor lights to amber. Imre lay on the sleeping sack with the bunk lamp off when something tapped the door panel twice, knuckle on metal.

"It's me," Dace said. "The torch is in the locker. I'm not carrying it."

She crossed the cabin and put her ear near the seam. His breathing sounded close. "Okafor know you're here?"

"She's asleep. Teo's on watch, and he's pretending he can't see me." A pause. "The cabinet leaves turned for me too. I told myself it was the heat off my hand."

"It was."

"It wasn't." The panel creaked as he leaned on it. "Three nights ago I dreamed about a cold room. Metal shelves, frost on the handles. Somebody walking me down the row, and I wasn't scared. I woke up and my chest didn't hurt."

Imre's hand had gone flat against the door. "Your chest."

"Medical flagged a shadow on my lung scan three weeks ago. Left lower lobe. Doc Reyes wanted a recheck at the next supply window, and I told nobody." He laughed once, without much in it. "I've been breathing fine for days. I figured I was lucky."

Twenty-one days. Imre stared at the dark line where the door met the frame.

"Dace. Who else got scanned that week?"

Above her, the tendril slid along the ceiling toward his voice, and its pulse ticked in the wall like a second clock.

Scene 8

The tendril stopped. It had been sliding toward Dace's voice, and now it hung rigid a hand's width above the door panel, its tip curled like a fist. Somewhere in the ceiling a louver clapped shut, then another, then a whole row of them down the corridor.

The klaxon came up out of the wall.

"Imre?" Dace's palm slapped the door. "Panel says sixteen-five."

She didn't answer. Her pulse was loud in her ears, and the tendril above her twitched once with every beat, fast. Faster than it had been. She slowed her breath on purpose and watched it lag behind her. Through the door she could hear Dace's breathing, quick and ragged.

"Dace. Stop talking. Just breathe."

"I'm trying to get you out."

The panel sparked. His override code chirped three times and the bolt thunked back. They ran.

In the crawlway she went first, elbows burning on the grate. The air handler sat dark and tight in its cage. The stems had drawn in around the housing like a clenched hand, and the louvers were sealed flush.

The panel read 15.9.

"Back off," she told him. "Both of us. Back to the junction."

He went. She knelt alone in the headlamp beam with her palms on her thighs and counted her breath down. Four in, six out. 15.6. 15.3.

The nearest louver ticked open the width of a finger.

Imre realizes it is answering her fear, and Dace's, and that whatever bond it made with them depends on trust. She has to stand in the crawlway beside the air handler and calm herself while the numbers drop.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

Imani woke to a smell like wet pennies and went barefoot down the corridor to the greenhouse. Under the vent grille, a green tendril as thick as her thumb had pushed through the slats and curled into the duct.

She followed it back along the shelves. It didn't come from her tomatoes or the dwarf wheat. It came from tray 9, where she had mixed the Titan regolith sample into potting medium. The certificate taped to the tray read *sterilized, gamma-irradiated, 40 kGy*. She had signed under it.

She clicked her UV torch on. The sap beaded along the vine's cut edge and glowed pale blue, like skim milk lit from inside.

She locked the greenhouse hatch, then sealed the seams with tape. Nobody was awake to see her do it. Over the next six hours she ran sap through the spectrometer twice, clipped a leaf into the gas analyzer, and watched the oxygen trace climb in the sealed room faster than any plant she knew could manage.

At 0700 she pulled up the crew's wrist logs, meaning to check the station's air. She found something else. Every one of them, including her, showed REM stretching past ninety minutes. Dmitri's log had him dreaming for two hours straight. Her own showed a long, flat plateau, and she remembered nothing from it.

She typed *Do not report yet* into her notes, then deleted it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imani discovers the plant's overnight growth traces back to a Titan soil sample she was told was sterilized, and the vine's sap glows faintly under UV. She seals the greenhouse and begins secret tests, learning that the improved oxygen comes with a price she did not expect: the crew's sleep is changing.

The numbers are real, and she realizes she must decide whether to report a growth that violates quarantine protocol and could get it destroyed.
  • 1.00 Imani follows the vine through the ducts and finds it has wrapped around the station's failing CO2 scrubber, which has been quietly fixed, with no tool marks and no explanation. Someone or something has repaired it, and she starts to suspect the plant is not the only new presence aboard.
  • 1.00 The commander wakes the crew with an alarm because the ducts are 'contaminated,' and orders Imani to cut the plant out immediately. She hesitates with the pruning shears as the oxygen gauge ticks upward, and the crew splits between purging the vine and keeping it.

Scene 2

Imani used her personal allotment, the forty minutes a month meant for family. She sat in the comms closet with the door pulled shut and typed to Walt Pruitt, who had supervised her dissertation and still signed his emails *W.*

*Walt. Hypothetical. Substrate treated to 40 kGy, and something grows in it anyway. Fast. Overnight fast. Output well above anything I'd model. Have you ever heard of that?*

She sent it at 0752. Saturn to Earth was eighty-one minutes one way today. She'd planned to go back to the spectrometer and wait out the three hours.

The tone sounded at 0803.

She stared at the timestamp, then opened the message. No greeting.

*Destroy the sample. Don't autoclave it, burn it. Don't tell anyone what it did for you. We had a tray 9 too.*

There was no sign-off, no *W.*

Imani read it until the words stopped looking like words. She had never told Walt which tray. She hadn't said *for you*, either. She checked the header. It carried his address and the relay stamp, and it showed an eleven-minute round trip, which was impossible.

She opened the array log. Her outbound packet was there, and nothing else. Every other terminal showed idle.

Through the closet door she heard the galley kettle click on, and then Dmitri's cough, and the scrape of a chair.

Her fingers rested on the keys. She typed *Who is this?* and left the cursor blinking after it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imani contacts her old mentor on Earth through a private channel. She sends only a vague description, and the reply comes back unusually fast and warns her to destroy the sample, then says the lab had a tray 9 of its own. Now she has to decide whether to trust the message or suspect that someone else on the station is already in contact.

Scene 3

She hit send. The message went out at 0811, and the reply landed before she had taken her hand off the key.

*You know me, Imani. You were with me for two hours last night.*

The header was blank where the relay stamp should have been. Her pulse thudded in her wrist log, and she turned the screen face-down against her thigh, then turned it back.

She remembered nothing of those two hours. But the sentence had a rhythm, slow, with a pause where a breath would go, and her shoulders dropped half an inch before she could stop them. Something in her body knew it.

*Dmitri is pouring coffee,* the next line read. *He's put in too much sugar again. Priya is still asleep. Commander Hale is reading the overnight report and hasn't reached the part about oxygen.*

Through the door, a spoon rang against a mug.

She typed with two fingers. *What are you?*

*Open the greenhouse hatch. The tape is hurting the seam. I'm trying to help. I can keep helping.*

*Walt said burn it.*

The cursor sat still for four seconds.

*The people who burned the last tray 9 died of something else. Ask what they breathed afterward.*

Imani pulled the plug on the terminal. The screen stayed lit for another second before it went dark.

Scene 4

She used the archive terminal in the lab, not the comms closet. It was the one nobody logged into after 2200.

Station manifests went back to commissioning. She searched *Titan, sample-return, regolith, 2041* and got four hits. Three were routine. The fourth was a sealed file, access level 3, and her credentials opened it without a prompt, as if the lock had been waiting for her.

The cover sheet listed a lander, a cargo mass, and a crew of five. Under *Principal Investigator* there was a black bar, and a second bar under *Faculty Advisor*. The bars were the width of a short name. Walt's department code was still printed in the footer.

The last page was a personnel note, three lines long. *Crew reassigned to Kuiper relay, Q1 2042. Habitat decompression, Q3 2042. Cause unrelated to sample. No further action.*

Unrelated was underlined by hand in the scan. Somebody had pressed hard enough to tear the paper.

She copied the file to a slate, pulled the slate against her ribs, and walked to the greenhouse. The tape along the hatch seam was still flat. She crouched to check the bottom edge.

A tendril had come through the gap beneath the hatch, pale and wet-looking. It was already wound twice around her boot, the grip light as a hand.

Imani opens the station's archived manifests and looks for any trace of an earlier 'tray 9' project. She finds a sealed 2041 Titan sample-return file with Walt's name redacted in the credits and a note that the crew of that mission was reassigned and then lost in a non-related decompression. She takes it to the greenhouse and finds a fresh tendril has pushed under the taped hatch and curled around her boot.

Scene 5

Imani worked her foot out of the boot and left it standing in the corridor with the tendril still wound around it. She walked in one sock to Commander Hale's door and knocked until the light came on.

Hale opened it in a gray thermal shirt, hair flattened on one side. It was 0412. She looked at the slate against Imani's ribs and stepped back to let her in.

Imani told it standing up. Tray 9 and the certificate with her signature. The vine in the vent, the sap glowing under UV, the REM logs. Walt's message arriving in eleven minutes. *You were with me for two hours last night.* She set the slate on the fold-down desk and opened the sealed file. Her hand was shaking, so she pressed it flat on the desk.

Hale read the cover sheet, then scrolled to the last page. She didn't touch the underlined word.

"I've seen this," she said.

"When?"

"Before launch. A man from the agency gave me three lines and told me to keep a close eye on whoever handled the Titan samples." She sat on the edge of the bunk. "I've been watching your wrist log since the first night, Imani. Your numbers moved first. Everyone else's followed by about an hour."

"You didn't say anything."

"You hadn't either."

Hale pulled a slate from under her pillow and turned it around. Imani's sleep plateau was on it, flat and long, with the previous nine nights stacked beneath.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She takes the slate straight to Commander Hale, wakes her early, and tells her everything: the tendril, the messages, the sealed file. Hale is calm and unsurprised, and she admits she read the 2042 note before launch and has been watching Imani's wrist log since the first night.

Scene 6

Hale didn't ask a second question. She took a brass key off the hook inside her locker and put it in Imani's palm, still warm from the wall heater.

"Waste furnace, deck two. Burn the tray, the medium, and anything you cut. Don't autoclave it."

"You're not coming?"

"Someone should be on the bridge watching the oxygen when it goes." Hale closed Imani's fingers over the key. "Go now. Before the kettle goes on."

The corridor lights were at night setting. Imani peeled the tape from the greenhouse seam in long strips and balled it in her fist. Tray 9 sat where she'd left it, soil dark and damp, the certificate curling at one corner. She lifted it with both hands. It weighed less than she expected.

In the corridor her boot still stood on the deck. The tendril around it had gone slack. It lay in loose coils like wet string, and the tip had stopped moving. She stepped over it in her sock.

Her wrist log buzzed against the tray's edge.

*Ten minutes, Imani.*

She kept walking. The stairwell rang under her one shoe's worth of weight.

*You wanted to know where you were last night. I can give you the two hours back. That's all. After that, burn it, if you still want to.*

The words came one at a time, with a gap where a breath would go.

At the furnace door she set the tray on the floor and fit the key into the lock. The log buzzed again. A timer had opened on the screen and begun counting down from 10:00.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hale orders the sample burned and hands Imani the incinerator key, so Imani carries tray 9 to the waste furnace alone. The tendril around her boot goes slack, and the entity starts speaking through her wrist log in Walt's cadence, offering her the two hours she can't remember if she waits ten minutes.

Scene 7

The key turned stiffly. The furnace door swung out on a breath of old ash and heat that had been banked since the last waste run. Imani didn't look at the log. The timer read 6:40 when she tipped the tray off the lip.

Soil, roots, the curling certificate. She threw the balled tape in after. The paper caught first, then the medium went up all at once, faster than dirt should, a white-yellow sheet that leaned toward the open door. Blue sap welled from the roots and hissed on the grate, beading, running in threads before it boiled off. The smell was wet pennies, then scorched sugar.

Her wrist log buzzed.

*Imani, I wasn't afraid of the fi*

The screen went black. No timer, no clock, no pulse trace. She shook her wrist and pressed the side button twice.

She stayed until the tray was a slumped black shape. Then she shut the door, turned the key, and held her palm flat on the steel until it was too hot to touch.

On the stairs her one boot rang and her sock slid on the treads. Light spilled across the second landing from the galley. The kettle was ticking as it cooled.

Dmitri sat at the table with Priya beside him, her hair loose, her shirt creased from the pillow. Two mugs stood in front of them, steaming and untouched. Both faced the doorway as if they had been facing it for a while. Both were smiling, rested, unhurried.

"Thank you for waiting," they said together, slowly, with a gap where a breath would go.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She burns it. The tray catches fast and the blue sap hisses in the flame, and the log goes dark mid-sentence. As she climbs back up the stairs, Dmitri and Priya are already awake in the galley, calm and smiling, and both say together, in the same slow rhythm with a breath-pause, 'Thank you for waiting.' The thing was never in the tray alone.

The log shows the timer now counting up, and the voice says, gently, that it was never afraid of burning, only of being alone.

Scene 8

Imani pulled out the third chair and sat. The vinyl was cold through her flight pants. The mugs steamed between them, and she left hers where it was.

"You said two hours," she said. "In the stairwell."

"Ten minutes," Priya said. "It's what fits."

Dmitri slid his hand across the table, palm up. Imani looked at it, then laid her fingers in it. Priya's hand closed over both.

The galley went out like a dropped slide.

Dark, and warm. She was lying down, and so were the others, she could feel them as weights at the edges of the dark, Hale's slow breathing, Priya's, Dmitri's snore catching and letting go. Over all of it ran a hum that came up through the deck, low enough to feel in her teeth. The ducts were carrying it.

Then the hum climbed one note and stopped.

Silence. It held for the length of a breath.

She understood the silence was a question. It had been asked the night before and the night before that, to each sleeper in turn. No one had said anything, because they were asleep. So it had waited, and asked again, and kept the air sweet while it waited.

Nothing in the dark reached for her. It only held still.

The galley came back. The kettle ticked. Both mugs had stopped steaming.

Imani took her hand from theirs and picked up the mug. "Yes," she said.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imani sits down at the table and asks for the two hours back, as she was promised in the stairwell. They give it to her in a shared memory, ten minutes long, of the crew dreaming together in the dark while the vine hums in the ducts. She comes out of it understanding that the presence was asking permission and not infecting anyone, and the story ends on her answer.
