cozy detective

A retired postal inspector is asked by a ten-year-old neighbor to find out who has been stealing the racing pigeons from the rooftops of their block.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Walter Pruitt was on his stoop with the crossword and a cold cup of coffee when the Okafor boy came up the walk and stopped exactly one step short of the porch.

"Mr. Pruitt, you used to investigate mail crimes."

"Mail fraud, mostly. Some theft." Walter set the pencil down. "Good morning, Desmond."

"Good morning." The boy had a spiral notebook under one arm and a shoebox under the other. He held out the shoebox with both hands. "This is a retainer."

Inside, on a folded dishtowel, lay four dollars in quarters, a pigeon feather, and a leg band stamped with a number and the letters *AU*.

"Where did you get this?"

"It was on the gutter outside Mr. Delacroix's loft. That's the number of Pickle. Pickle was his best bird. There were eleven birds on our block and now there are six." Desmond flipped open the notebook. The first page was a hand-drawn map of the block, rooftops shaded in pencil, with small x's. "Mr. Delacroix says they got lost. Pigeons don't get lost. That's the whole point of them."

Walter turned the band over under the light. The edges were clean. No scratch marks, no bend.

"This wasn't pulled off a bird in a struggle," he said. "Somebody cut it, or slipped it off a leg with care."

Desmond's eyes widened. He wrote that down, pressing hard.

"I'll need to see the roofs," Walter said, and reached for his cane.

Scene 2

The fire stairs behind Delacroix's building climbed four floors, and Walter took them one at a time, cane first. Desmond waited on each landing with the notebook open, pretending not to wait.

The loft sat at the back of the roof, a plywood box on cinder blocks with a slanted tin lid and a little landing board out front. A padlock hung on the hasp. Walter crouched, knee complaining, and examined it. No pry marks in the wood. No fresh bright scratches around the keyhole.

"Locked when you found the band?" he asked.

"Locked. Mr. Delacroix checks it every night. He keeps the key on a nail by his refrigerator."

Walter ran a thumb along the landing board, where the birds came in through a row of hanging wires that swung one way only. Then he stopped. Scattered in the gravel near the roof's edge were a few pale yellow kernels.

"What does Mr. Delacroix feed them?"

Desmond checked a page. "Peas and the little red seeds. Milo."

"Not corn."

"No, sir."

Walter picked up a kernel, cracked and dry, and then another. A thin trail of them led toward the parapet, spaced a hand's width apart. He slid them into an envelope from his jacket pocket and licked the flap.

Desmond wrote *CORN* and underlined it twice.

Scene 3

The kernels led along the parapet, one every hand's width, as if someone had walked there with a hole in a pocket. Walter followed with his cane tapping the gravel. Desmond came behind him, holding the notebook to his chest.

At the corner the wall dropped to knee height where Delacroix's roof met the next building's. Walter stepped over it the way a man steps over a sleeping dog. Desmond hopped it.

"We're on Mrs. Haskell's building now," Desmond whispered.

"You needn't whisper. Nobody's home on a roof."

The trail ended at the stairwell bulkhead, a squat brick box with a steel door. Against its shadowed side sat a plastic milk crate turned on its end, a square of chicken wire bent over the top and fastened with two twists of bread-bag tie. Walter lifted the wire. The crate was empty. Three gray feathers stuck to the bottom, and a few more kernels of corn lay in the corners.

"They were in here," Desmond said.

"For a little while, I'd say."

Walter tipped the crate toward the light. The bottom was lined with a sheet of folded paper, soft with damp. He drew it out and smoothed it against his knee. A church bulletin, St. Brendan's, with BINGO FRIDAYS 7 PM circled in blue ballpoint.

Desmond copied the circle into the notebook, carefully, ink and all.

Scene 4

Walter turned the bulletin over. The back was blank except for a torn corner of white label, stuck on with a smear of old glue, and printed on it in dot-matrix type:

*ECRWSS C014* *14 ALD*

"What's that?" Desmond asked. He had come around to read over Walter's elbow, which Walter allowed.

"Carrier route sort code. The post office prints it on bulk mail so the carrier doesn't have to sort by hand." Walter held it at arm's length, then close. "C014 is the route that covers Alder Street and the two blocks behind it. Not ours. Ours is C009."

"So whoever had this lives on Alder."

"Whoever *received* this lives on Alder. It might have blown up here. It might have been lining a crate for a week before anyone moved it." He eased the paper into a second envelope. "But it was dry in the middle and damp at the edges. Somebody put it down recently."

Desmond flipped to a clean page and wrote *ALDER*, then, after a moment, *14?*

"Don't write the number as a fact."

The boy added a second question mark, smaller than the first.

Below them, a pigeon landed on the parapet, looked at the crate, and walked away along the wall.

Scene 5

The mail carrier on Alder Street was a broad woman in a pith helmet, sorting a bundle against her hip at the corner box. Walter knew the walk before he knew the face: the slight forward lean, the satchel strap worn across the chest, not the shoulder.

"Retired," he said, when she looked at his cane. "Inspection Service. Twenty-six years."

"Rosalind Baptiste." She shook his hand and then Desmond's, gravely. "What can I do for the Service?"

He showed her the label through the envelope's cellophane window. She tilted it out of the glare.

"That's the parish mailing. Goes to every box on C014, all three hundred. St. Brendan's pays bulk." She squinted. "Fourteen Alder, though. That's Mrs. Lindqvist. She's been at her sister's in Duluth since March. I'm holding her mail at the station."

"So she wouldn't have received this week's."

"Not unless somebody's been picking up for her. I haven't released anything."

Desmond's pencil stopped. "Then how did the label get on a bulletin?"

"Could be a neighbor had hers forwarded, could be it came off the pile at the station." Rosalind shrugged and slid a flyer into a slot. "Or somebody took a bulletin off her porch. They sit on the step if the box is full."

Walter thanked her. At the end of the block he looked back at number 14: green shutters, a porch light on in daylight, and a folded paper on the top step.

Scene 6

Walter did not go up the walk. He stood at the gate with both hands on the head of his cane and looked at the paper on the top step, and Desmond stood beside him and looked at it too.

"It's the same one," Desmond said.

"It's the same kind. Folded the same." Walter lifted his chin. "Read me the circle."

Desmond squinted. "There's one. Blue pen. Around the bingo."

"Is the circle closed, or does it have a tail?"

"A tail. Like a little hook at the bottom."

Walter took out the damp bulletin from the crate and passed it down. Desmond held it up beside the step, one eye shut, as if sighting a rifle.

"A hook," he said. "Same hook."

A newspaper-colored curtain moved in the front window, then settled. Walter noted it and said nothing. Along the side of the house ran a strip of dirt and a wooden gate, latched but not locked, and through the slats he could see a green hose coiled on a spigot and a feed sack leaning against the garage wall, its mouth rolled down and clipped with a clothespin. The print on the sack was too far to read.

Then, from somewhere behind the garage, came a low, rolling sound, soft and unbothered, repeated and answered.

Desmond's pencil stopped above the page. He looked up at Walter and did not write anything.

Scene 7

The front door opened before Walter had decided whether to knock at the gate. A boy of about sixteen stood in the doorway in socks, holding a dish towel. A few yellow kernels clung to the cuff of his sweatshirt.

"I'm not selling anything," Walter said.

"I know who you are." The boy looked at Desmond. "You're the one with the notebook. Mr. Delacroix's neighbor."

"Desmond Okafor." Desmond lifted the notebook slightly, as if presenting credentials.

"Anders." The boy wiped his hands on the towel, slowly, for longer than they needed. "My grandmother's house. I'm watering the plants."

"And the bulletins," Walter said. "You've been bringing in the parish mailing."

Anders glanced at the step. "It piles up."

"It does." Walter nodded toward the side gate. "Do the plants need corn?"

The boy's mouth opened and shut. Behind the garage, the rolling sound came again, three notes, and a fourth answering from farther back.

"They were hungry," Anders said. "Nobody was feeding them. Mr. Delacroix only goes up there at night."

"Five birds," Desmond said. "Are there five?"

Anders looked at him for a while. Then he unlatched the gate, stepped into the dirt strip, and held it open with his hip. Walter went first, cane tapping on the flagstones past the hose and the feed sack. At the corner of the garage he stopped.

An old loft stood against the back fence, paint peeling, its door propped wide. Five gray birds sat along its landing board, and one of them had a bare leg.

Scene 8

Walter crouched, knee complaining, until the bare-legged bird was level with his eye. The skin above the foot was pink and slightly swollen, with a thin pale line where something had pressed for a long time.

"That's Pickle," Desmond said. "Isn't it?"

"His band was too tight," Anders said. "It was cutting in. I tried to tell Mr. Delacroix, but he doesn't answer the door in the daytime." He pulled a pair of nail clippers from his sweatshirt pocket and held them out on his palm, like evidence he'd been saving. "I did it slow. I put the band on the gutter so he'd know it was Pickle."

"That's why the edges were clean," Walter said.

"They kept coming over here anyway. Even before. Grandpa Lindqvist had birds. I think they remember the loft." Anders looked at the ground. "I only meant to keep them till the leg healed."

Desmond walked the length of the landing board with his pencil raised, touching the air above each bird. "One, two, three, four, five." He turned to a fresh page and wrote the number, then looked at Walter. "That's all of them. Eleven."

"Six and five."

"Mr. Delacroix is going to be loud."

"Probably," Walter said, straightening. "I'll walk over with you."

Anders reached into the feed sack and scattered a handful of corn. Pickle came down off the board and ate it.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

Walter Penhale had the Columbian issues in tweezers when the knocking started, three quick raps, low on the door. He knew it was a child before he opened it.

Dilly Okafor stood on the mat with an empty wicker basket on one arm and a folded paper in her fist. "Mr. Penhale, somebody's stealing Grandpa's pigeons. Four so far. I drew where everything is."

"Dilly." He kept the tweezers raised, like a man holding a thought. "I'm retired. I sort stamps now. Take it to the police."

"They said birds aren't a priority." She unfolded the map anyway. Rooftops in green marker, chimneys as squares, a skull and crossbones drawn on the laundromat. "You were an inspector for thirty-one years."

"Of mail. Mail fraud, mostly. I'm done with all of it."

"Okay." She dug into her jacket pocket and held out a small brown envelope, soft at the corners. "This came Tuesday. No return address."

He took it because his hands were already open. Inside lay a pale blue aluminum leg band, bent slightly, stamped *NPA 19 · 2207*. The envelope was addressed in block capitals to *Mr. Emeka Okafor, Loft Keeper*. The postmark was smeared, the stamp used twice, once, he noticed, and then cancelled again.

"That's Coco's band," Dilly said. "She went missing Sunday."

Walter turned the envelope over. Nothing on the flap. He set the tweezers on the album page.

"Come in," he said. "Don't touch the Columbians."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Dilly catches the retired inspector sorting his old stamp collection and asks for help, but he refuses, claiming he's done with investigations, until she shows him a ring band from a missing pigeon that arrived in the mail with no return address, which pulls him back in as a postal matter.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 The ten-year-old neighbor, Dilly, knocks on the retired inspector's door holding an empty pigeon basket and a hand-drawn map of the rooftops, and he reluctantly agrees to take the case after noticing a single odd feather on her sleeve that doesn't match any local breed.
  • 1.00 While watering his tomato plants on the fire escape, the retired inspector watches Dilly's grandfather's loft from across the alley and sees the latch is unbroken, so when Dilly arrives to plead for help he tells her the thief must be someone the birds trust, and she hands him a list of everyone on the block who feeds them.
  • 1.00 On the morning of a big club race, the retired inspector joins Dilly on the roof to count the remaining birds and discovers a tiny brass tag tied to a loft door with a note in careful cursive, making him realize the theft is not random and that the thief wants someone to notice.

Scene 2

They did the block in an hour. Mrs. Adeyemi at the bakery had seen nothing but pigeons, which she considered the problem. The barber had seen a man with a ladder, but it turned out to be the barber's cousin. Only the girl at the dry cleaner's offered anything. "Mr. Bautista's on the roof at dawn. Every day. I see him from my window."

Dilly looked at Walter with enormous restraint. "The skull and crossbones," she said.

The laundromat smelled of hot lint. Mr. Bautista was folding a stranger's sheets at the counter, a short man with forearms like rolled dough. When Walter asked about the roof, he stopped folding.

"Come," he said finally, and led them up a back stair past the water heater.

On the tar paper sat three produce crates turned on their sides, lined with towels. Perhaps fifteen pigeons, mismatched, gray and rust and one nearly white, shuffled inside. A coffee can of cracked corn stood by the vent.

"Strays," Bautista said. "Hit by cars, mostly. That one has half a foot." He did not look at Dilly. "I don't take anybody's birds. Nobody's with a band."

Walter crouched and checked every leg. Bare, all of them.

"Thursday, though." Bautista wiped his hands on his apron. "Six in the morning. A man on Emeka's roof, brown uniform, the cap, the whole thing. He had a bird against his chest like a football. Gray, with a white tail patch."

"Biscuit," Dilly whispered. "Coco's best friend."

"Delivery," Walter said. He touched the envelope in his pocket.

Scene 3

The sorting annex smelled of paper dust and floor wax. Walter signed Dilly in as his guest, and the guard didn't look up from his crossword.

Lorraine Voss sat at the back table under a gooseneck lamp, sorting undeliverables into gray tubs. She had been his deputy for nine years. She looked at Dilly, then at Walter. "You said you were done."

"I am. This is a favor." He laid the envelope on her blotter.

Lorraine pulled a loupe from her cardigan and bent over it. The lamp buzzed. "Used stamp, recancelled. Somebody's cheap, or somebody's careful." She tilted the envelope. "But look at the bars. Wavy lines, and the fourth one breaks and blobs at the end, see? Like a hair in the ink."

"A machine?" Dilly asked.

"A hand-cancel. Lever type, forty years old if it's a day. Nobody runs those anymore." Lorraine tapped the smear. "Except Marlow Street Station. Postmaster there won't give his up. Says the new ones jam."

"Across town," Walter said.

"Forty minutes on the 12 bus." She slid the envelope back with one finger. "Whoever mailed this dropped it at Marlow Street, or works there, or knows someone who does."

Dilly had taken a pencil stub from her pocket and was writing *MARLOW ST* on the back of her map, beside the laundromat.

Walter looked at the envelope a long moment. "Is the Marlow counter open Saturdays?"

"Till noon."

He put the envelope in his breast pocket and buttoned it. "Then we'll need to leave early."

Scene 4

At ten to six the fire escape was cold enough to print its grating into Dilly's knees. Walter sat on an upturned bucket with the thermos between his shoes and a pair of opera glasses he had not used since a *Tosca* in 1998. Across the alley, Emeka's loft was a dark box on a gray roof.

"You said six," Dilly whispered.

"Mr. Bautista said six. Pigeons keep their own time." He poured her half a cup of cocoa he had made in the thermos and pretended not to see her taste it and grimace at the lack of sugar.

At six exactly, the roof door across the alley opened. A figure came out in a dark jacket and a peaked cap, shoulders hunched against the wind. Walter lifted the glasses. The cap had a badge, or something that caught the light like one.

The figure went to the loft, unhooked the latch without hurry, and reached in. When the hands came out, they held a gray bird with a pale patch at the tail.

"Biscuit," Dilly breathed, and gripped the rail.

The figure walked to the roof's edge, held the bird out at arm's length, and opened both hands.

Biscuit dropped, caught air, and circled the water tower once. Then she flattened out and flew east, small and steady, until the chimneys swallowed her.

"He didn't keep her," Dilly said. "He just *sent* her."

Walter lowered the glasses. The roof across the alley was empty, the door swinging shut.

Scene 5

The roof door of Emeka's building was propped with a folded paper plate. Walter took the stairs one hand on the rail, Dilly two steps ahead of him, and by the top he was breathing like a man who had decided not to.

The roof was empty. Wind moved a plastic bag along the parapet.

Dilly went straight to the loft. "It's not broken," she said. "It's never broken."

Walter crouched at the latch. A bright smear of oil darkened the hinge pin, still wet enough to take his thumbprint. He sniffed it. Machine oil, the kind that comes in a thin red-nozzled can. Beside the loft door sat a tin of feed with its lid pressed on crooked. He lifted the lid. Under the tin, flattened by its weight, lay a paper bus transfer, punched at 5:12 and printed *ROUTE 12 · MARLOW ST*.

"Marlow Street," Dilly said, reading over his arm.

"Don't touch it."

"I'm not touching it, I'm reading it."

The roof door banged open. Emeka Okafor stood in an undershirt and unlaced work boots, a long man with gray stubble and a flashlight he held like a club. "Who is that? Penhale?" He crossed the tar paper in four strides. "On my roof? At six in the morning? That's trespass, sir."

Walter stood slowly, transfer still pinched in his fingers. "Mr. Okafor, I can explain."

"Grandpa." Dilly stepped between them, chin up, basket hugging her ribs. "I hired him."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Walter and Dilly cross the alley and climb to Emeka's roof, where they find the loft latch freshly oiled and a small tin of feed with a Marlow Street bus transfer tucked under it. When Emeka himself appears, furious, he accuses Walter of trespassing. Dilly has to confess she hired the inspector behind his back.

  • 0.26 While watering his tomato plants on the fire escape, the retired inspector watches Dilly's grandfather's loft from across the alley and sees the latch is unbroken, so when Dilly arrives to plead for help he tells her the thief must be someone the birds trust, and she hands him a list of everyone on the block who feeds them.
  • 0.26 On the morning of a big club race, the retired inspector joins Dilly on the roof to count the remaining birds and discovers a tiny brass tag tied to a loft door with a note in careful cursive, making him realize the theft is not random and that the thief wants someone to notice.

Scene 6

"I'll see that," Emeka said, and held out his hand for the transfer. "Whatever you're hiding in your fingers."

"I'm not hiding it. I'm preserving it."

"Grandpa, it's from the bus," Dilly said. "It says Marlow Street, and the latch has oil on it, and you never oil it on Saturdays, you said Saturdays are for scraping."

Emeka's mouth opened and his voice came up with it, big enough for the whole block. "Nobody on my roof, nobody, in my own—"

The stairwell door banged against the paper plate. A small woman in a quilted robe and one slipper stood there, gripping a dish towel. "Emeka Okafor, you'll wake Gus."

"Mrs. Rafferty, these two are trespassing—"

"I heard. Everyone heard." She looked at Walter, then at the basket on Dilly's arm. "Is this about the birds? Because that boy's been up here at dawn for weeks. The one from Marlow Street, with the cap. He comes down the stairs after, quiet as a cat, and sits with Gus an hour. Gus hasn't left his bed since March. He raced for thirty years." She twisted the towel. "He holds one in his lap. Gus does. Says it smells like his own roof."

Emeka's hand dropped.

Walter looked at the oiled hinge, and at the cap, and the bird carried against a chest like something that might break.

"Mrs. Rafferty," he said, "might we come in?"

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Emeka's shouting draws a neighbor out of the stairwell, and she announces that the postal carrier from Marlow Street has been coming to the building at dawn for weeks, visiting her bedridden husband, who used to race pigeons. Walter realizes the "thief" may be carrying the birds to someone who needs them, and the scene ends with Walter asking the woman if they might come in.

Scene 7

"Not in," Mrs. Rafferty said, and pulled the door of 4B shut behind her until the latch clicked. "He's asleep. He sleeps badly and then he sleeps well, and it's the well part I'm guarding."

So they stayed on the landing, under a bulb that hummed. Walter lowered his voice and she lowered hers to match.

"The boy. Has he a name?"

"Teo. Teodoro, I think, but Gus calls him Teo." She wound the dish towel around her wrist. "Nineteen, twenty. Thin as a rake. He doesn't talk much, he just sits."

"Does he say where he works?"

"The post office on Marlow. He told Gus once he sorts in the back and does the counter when they're short." She frowned. "The cap's too big for him. It was somebody's before."

Walter heard Emeka shift behind him, boots scuffing. He took the envelope from his breast pocket and looked at the smeared wavy bars through the cellophane of his own thumb. Lever type, forty years old. Marlow Street.

"Does he ever come empty-handed?"

"Never." She almost smiled. "Sometimes there's a paper bag of seed."

Walter buttoned the pocket. Not here, then. Not in a sickroom, with the boy cornered between a bedpost and a flashlight.

"We'll speak to him at the station," he said.

"We," Emeka said. He had stopped bristling and begun tying his laces, one knee on the stair. "The 12 leaves at twenty to eight. I'm coming."

"Mr. Okafor—"

"My birds, Penhale." He pulled the knot tight. "I'm coming."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Walter stays on the landing and quietly questions Mrs. Rafferty about the boy, learning his name is Teo and that he works at Marlow Street Station, where the lever cancellation stamp is. He decides the confrontation should happen there, and Emeka, still bristling, insists on coming along on the 12 bus.

Scene 8

Teo was at the back table at Marlow Street, cap pushed up, a tub of flats beside him. He saw Emeka's flashlight, still in Emeka's fist, and went the color of paste.

Walter spoke before anyone else could. "Mr. Rafferty has been waiting on a delivery. I understand there's one bird outstanding."

The boy looked at the three of them. Then he reached under the table and lifted a shoebox with holes punched in the lid. "She's got a bad wing," he said. "It's mending."

"Then she'll want carrying."

At 4B, Mrs. Rafferty opened the door six inches and stepped aside. Walter put a hand on Emeka's sleeve, and the big man stayed on the landing with his boots planted, breathing through his nose. Teo went in alone.

Through the gap Walter saw the bed, the oxygen line, a face like carved soap. Teo set the bird in Gus's lap. Coco shuffled, tucked her wing, and settled. The old man's hand came down over her back, and the fingers knew exactly where to go.

"There you are," Gus said. "There you are, girl."

Emeka's flashlight dipped until it pointed at his own boot.

Dilly opened her notebook against the wall, wrote *CLOSED* and underlined it twice, and put the pencil behind her ear.

At home Walter hung up his coat. On the mat lay a small envelope, addressed in block capitals to *Mr. W. Penhale, Inspector*. He did not pick it up yet. He stood over it with his hands at his sides.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Instead of questioning Teo, Walter arranges for Teo to deliver the last bird, Coco, to Gus's room while Emeka waits outside the door. The old racer holds his bird, Emeka sees what the birds have done for his friend, and Dilly quietly closes the case in her notebook. Walter goes home to his Columbians and discovers a small envelope on his mat, addressed in block capitals.

Scene 1

Odette took Walter's sleeve at the third-floor landing and did not let go until the roof door, which she shouldered open with her whole body.

Mr. Alvarado sat on an upturned paint bucket beside an empty coop, a cardigan buttoned wrong over his undershirt. Tar paper softened under the afternoon heat. Six cubbies, six open doors.

"They didn't fly off," he said, before Walter could speak. "People say a hawk, people say they got lost. Forty years I've flown birds off this roof. A bird that's lost comes home hungry and embarrassed. Mine are not embarrassed. They're taken."

"How many?"

"Eleven since spring."

Odette held up a finger. "Three of those were Mr. Okafor's, across the street. I counted."

Mr. Alvarado pointed with his chin at the coop door. "Look at the latch. Go on."

Walter crouched, knees complaining. The hasp hung clean from the frame. No splintered wood, no bent metal. On the ledge below, four brass screws sat in a row, heads all facing the same way.

He didn't touch them. "Somebody had a screwdriver and some patience."

"A bad man," Odette said.

"A careful one. That's worse, and more useful." He stood. "I'll look into it. But you follow my rules. You touch nothing until I say. You write down what you see, not what you think. And you accuse no one."

Odette pulled a pencil from her braid. "Can I write the rules down too?"

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Odette drags Walter up to the roof of her building to meet the grieving pigeon keeper, old Mr. Alvarado, who insists the birds were stolen and not lost, then shows them a coop latch that was neatly unscrewed rather than broken. Walter's trained eye sees a methodical thief, and he accepts the case on the condition that Odette follows his rules of investigation.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 The ten-year-old, Odette, knocks on retired inspector Walter Pruitt's door holding an empty pigeon basket and a hand-drawn map of the rooftops, and he reluctantly agrees to take the case after noticing she has already marked three coops with red crayon X's. Her map reveals the thefts all happened on Thursdays, giving him his first thread to pull.
  • 1.00 While watering his tomatoes at dawn, Walter finds a single banded pigeon feather and a torn scrap of brown paper twine on his fire escape, and Odette appears below, insisting these are clues to the thefts. Recognizing the twine as an old postal-grade type he hasn't seen in decades, he is drawn into the case against his better judgment.
  • 1.00 Walter opens a long-sealed shoebox of his old inspector's tools when Odette arrives at his door, and she pays him a retainer of seven dollars and a jar of buttons to find the thief. Touched, he agrees, but as she leaves he spots a figure on the opposite rooftop watching them through binoculars, hinting that someone already knows the investigation has begun.

Scene 2

By eleven Walter had learned the roof's sounds: the water tank ticking as it cooled, a television two buildings over, Mr. Alvarado's birds shifting and muttering in the one coop still occupied. He sat on a folded raincoat behind the tank with a thermos between his shoes and a view of the roof door.

The coffee had gone lukewarm when something scuffed behind him.

"It's me," Odette whispered. She wore pajama pants printed with moons, sneakers with no socks, and a blanket around her shoulders like a cape.

"Your mother—"

"Thinks I'm asleep. I put the pillows in." She lowered herself onto the tar paper beside him. "Rule one was I touch nothing. I haven't touched anything."

Walter looked at the stairwell door, then at her. He unscrewed the thermos cap and poured an inch of coffee into it, then, after a moment, tipped half back. "You sit there. You don't talk."

She mimed zipping her mouth.

At eleven-forty the door latch clicked. It was a small sound, a careful one. The door opened barely a foot. A flashlight beam came out low, its lens covered with something that turned the light red, and crossed the roof toward the coop.

Walter had pictured a man with a toolbag, someone with shoulders. The figure under the beam came up only to the top of the coop. A hood, thin wrists, a screwdriver held in a fist like a spoon.

Odette's fingers closed on his sleeve.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

That night Walter stakes out the roof with a thermos, and Odette sneaks up to join him despite her mother's rules. Near midnight they hear the roof door click and see a small figure with a flashlight go to the coop, but it is a child's silhouette, which complicates what Walter expected to find.

He finds that Mr. Alvarado has been receiving unusually large, unexplained offers from a buyer for his best birds, offers he never mentioned, and wonders why the old man kept them quiet.

Scene 3

Walter kept his hand flat on Odette's blanket until her fingers loosened.

The figure crossed to the coop without hurry. It crouched, set the flashlight on the ledge, and fitted the screwdriver to the first screw. Each turn was a soft rasp, and each screw went onto the ledge in a line, heads all facing the same way. Four. The hasp swung down.

A hand went into the cubby. The bird made one low complaint and then went quiet, the way they do when held right. The hand came out with a gray pigeon pressed against a sweatshirt, thumb stroking its neck.

Walter switched on his flashlight.

"Evening."

The figure didn't drop the bird. It stood very straight, caught in the white beam, and the hood slid back on its own. A boy, twelve at most, with a shaved head and a chipped front tooth, blinking hard.

"That's Mr. Okafor's grandson," Odette said, forgetting the zipped mouth. "Daniel. Rule one, you said—"

"I'm not stealing them," Daniel said. His voice cracked in the middle. "I'm not. I'm moving them."

"Moving them where?" Walter asked.

"Somewhere safe."

"Safe from what?"

The boy looked at the stairwell door, then at the bird, then at the four screws lined up on the ledge. He tucked his chin down against the pigeon's back and said nothing at all.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Walter keeps still and lets the small figure unscrew the hasp and lift out a bird. Then he switches on his own flashlight and says calmly, "Evening." The hood falls back to show a boy of about twelve, Mr. Okafor's grandson, who says he isn't stealing the birds, he's moving them somewhere safe, and he won't say from what.

Scene 4

Walter kept two fingers on Daniel's shoulder the whole way down, not gripping, just present. The boy carried the pigeon against his stomach with both hands. Behind them Odette's blanket slid down each stair with a soft *flump*, and she stepped on it twice.

Across the street the Okafors' lobby smelled of floor wax and fried plantain. Second floor, the door at the end. Walter pressed the bell once and heard a chair scrape inside.

Mr. Okafor opened the door in a plaid robe, reading glasses pushed up into his gray hair. He looked at Walter, then at the girl in moon pajamas, then at his grandson.

"Daniel. It is midnight."

"Yes, sir," Walter said. "I think you should look at what he's carrying."

Daniel held the bird out without raising his eyes. The old man bent to it, annoyed, and then he stopped. The pigeon shifted, and the band on its left leg caught the hall light, a thin green ring.

Mr. Okafor lowered his glasses onto his nose. His thumb found the leg and turned it, very gently, until he could read the numbers. His lips moved over them once, then again.

The color left his face from the forehead down. He put a hand flat against the doorframe.

"This is Ifeoma's bird," he said. "Ifeoma's blue-gray hen. A hawk took her. I found the feathers myself."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Walter marches Daniel and the pigeon down to the Okafor apartment, with Odette trailing and the blanket dragging. Mr. Okafor opens the door in his robe, sees the gray bird, and goes pale, because he recognizes a band number that belonged to his late wife's champion, a bird he thought was dead.

Scene 5

"Who told you a hawk?" Walter asked.

Mr. Okafor didn't answer at first. He took the pigeon from Daniel, cradled it against his robe, and ran a thumb down its breast. "Chidi. My sister's boy. He came to the door in March with the feathers in a paper bag. He said he found them by the water tank." He frowned at the bird. "He manages the roof door for the building. Him and the super's ring are the only keys."

Daniel's chin dropped further. He studied the doormat.

Odette drew a breath. Walter could feel the whole sentence building in her, and he turned his head just enough to catch her eye. He lowered his hand an inch, palm down, the way you settle a dog.

She let the breath out through her nose.

"Mr. Okafor," Walter said, "may we come in? I think this bird wants water, and you want to sit."

"Yes. Yes, of course." The old man shuffled backward, still holding the hen, and Daniel slipped in after him.

Walter bent toward Odette as she passed. "Pencil," he murmured. "What Chidi said, the paper bag, the water tank, March. Everything Mr. Okafor just told us. Exactly as he said it."

She pulled the pencil from her braid, looked around for paper, and found a pizza menu on the hall table. She turned it over and wrote, tongue between her teeth.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mr. Okafor, shaken, says the hawk story was told to him by his nephew Chidi, who manages the building's rooftop access and has the only spare keys. Walter, remembering the rule about accusing no one, quietly asks Odette to write down what Chidi said and when, so they can check it before anyone confronts him.

Scene 6

The bell rang before Mr. Okafor had found a saucer.

Walter was nearest the door. He glanced down the hall: the old man at the kitchen counter with the hen in the crook of his arm, Daniel frozen beside the refrigerator, and Odette folded down behind the sofa with the pizza menu on her knee, only the top of her braid showing. He opened the door.

The man in the hall was broad through the middle, fortyish, in a pressed short-sleeved shirt. He held a white bakery box by its string. A ring of keys hung from his belt loop.

"Oh," he said. "I saw the lights on from the street. Is Uncle all right?"

"Chidi, isn't it?" Walter put out his hand and smiled the way he used to at counters, when a man arrived to claim a package. "Walter Pruitt. I live across the way. Your uncle's fine, just up late. Please, come in."

Chidi shook it. His palm was damp. "I brought cake. Lemon. He likes the lemon." His eyes went past Walter's shoulder to the kitchen, to the shape in the old man's arm, and stayed there a half second too long.

Behind the sofa a pencil stopped scratching.

"I have a menu," Odette said, standing up, "with all your lies on it."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Before anyone can settle, the doorbell rings and Chidi is standing in the hall with a cake box, announcing that he saw lights on and wanted to check on his uncle. Walter greets him warmly and says nothing about the pigeon, but Odette, forgetting rule three, announces from behind the sofa that she has a menu with all of his lies written on it.

Scene 7

Nobody moved. The bakery box tipped in Chidi's hand, and he caught the bottom of it with his other palm.

"Odette," Walter said, mildly.

"It's okay," Daniel said.

He came out from beside the refrigerator one step at a time, the way he had crossed the roof. Dust still grayed the cuffs of his sweatshirt. "Chidi's not the thief, Grandpa. I am. I moved all of them." He swallowed. "Chidi was only trying to protect them. I think."

"You think," Mr. Okafor said.

"Daniel," Chidi said, "you don't need to say anything."

"Yes, I do." The boy's voice cracked and he pushed on through it. "In March I was on the back stairs and he was on the phone. He said a number. He said the blue-gray hen was the best one, and the old man wouldn't notice a few missing." He looked at the floor tiles. "So I took them first. Where he couldn't find them."

Chidi laughed, short and dry. "A boy hears half a phone call through a stairwell door."

"You were holding the bag of feathers when you said it. I saw."

Mr. Okafor stood very still at the counter with the hen against his robe. Her head turned toward the light. He looked at his nephew's damp collar, then at his grandson's chipped tooth, and last at the thin green ring on her leg. Nobody spoke. The refrigerator hummed, and the saucer in his free hand began to tremble.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Daniel, who has been silent all night, steps out from beside the refrigerator and says Chidi isn't the thief, because Daniel is the one who moved the birds and Chidi was only trying to protect them. He admits he took the birds after overhearing Chidi on the phone with a buyer, so he hid them where Chidi couldn't sell them. Mr. Okafor must now decide which of the two relatives he believes.

Scene 8

"Mr. Okafor," Walter said, "nothing can be proved tonight. A bird, a band, half a phone call through a door. Put the hen down and sit."

The old man sat. Daniel set a saucer of water on the counter, and the hen drank, tipping her head back after each sip.

"At first light," Walter said, "take her up to Ifeoma's coop yourself. Let her walk in on her own." He glanced at the wall clock. "Odette and I will keep an eye on the roof until then. Nobody gets near those birds."

Odette, still holding the pizza menu, nodded hard.

Chidi had set the bakery box on the counter. He cleared his throat. "Well. Cake, then. Uncle, you should eat something."

"Yes," Mr. Okafor said, without looking at him. He took a bread knife from the drawer, slipped the string off, and lifted the lid. The cake was whole and glazed, a little lopsided. He pressed the blade through the middle.

It stopped with a small click against metal.

He worked the knife around it and tipped the slice onto a plate. A brass key slid out of the crumb, trailing yellow glaze, and lay on the china. A cardboard tag hung from its hole, lettered in block capitals: ROOF – SPARE.

Walter didn't pick it up. He heard the refrigerator hum and the hen's feet on the counter.

Chidi's hand went to his belt loop and closed on his own ring.

He offers to stay up with Odette watching the roof, and when the lemon cake is cut open a small brass key falls out. It is the missing spare, and it makes Chidi's guilt clear without anyone accusing him.

literary mystery

A bookkeeper at a failing salt mine finds that the company has been paying wages to forty workers who died in a collapse six years ago.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Marta Eklund was reconciling the March payroll when she noticed that Dyer, Hollis, was paid twice a month and had been for as long as the ledger went back. She had typed his name herself, a hundred times, without reading it.

She turned the page. Dyer was in Section C, along with Okafor, Pruitt, Lasko, and thirty-six others. Each drew the same flat rate, with no overtime and no sick days. Each was paid by direct deposit on the fifteenth and the last day of the month.

Salt dust had worked into the seams of the ledger again. She wiped her thumb on her skirt and looked at the window. Beyond it the headframe stood against a white sky, its wheel still.

She took the stairs down to the lobby. The brass plaque hung beside the time clock, polished every spring by someone who was not on her payroll. She read it from the top. Dyer, H. Okafor, S. Pruitt, W. The dates beneath the names were all the same: 11 October, six years ago.

She counted the names with her finger. Forty.

Back upstairs, she opened the bank portal and typed Pruitt's account number from the ledger. The balance came up before she had finished breathing out. Last Friday's deposit was there, and above it, the Friday before that. Someone had been withdrawing the money in cash, at a branch in Karsten, every week.

Scene 2

She opened Dyer's account next, then Okafor's, then Lasko's. The portal listed each as a company sub-account, opened at the Karsten branch, with Eklund Mining Services, Inc. as co-signatory. She had never been told that. She had never been asked to sign anything.

The pattern held in all three. A deposit on the fifteenth or the last day. A withdrawal on the following Thursday, in cash, for the exact net amount, to the cent. The portal gave a time for each: 10:12, 10:40, 10:07. Every slip carried the same teller number, 0417.

She took an envelope from her bag and wrote the numbers on the back. Forty accounts, twenty-four deposits a year, six years. She stopped doing the sum when it passed a figure she recognized from the annual report, the one the board had called unrecoverable.

Down the hall a door opened. Brandt's shoes came along the linoleum, slow, the left one dragging a little. He stopped at her doorway with his coat already on.

"Still at March?"

"It doesn't balance yet," she said.

"It never does in March." He looked at the screen, then at her hands. She had not touched the mouse. "Lock up when you go. The heat cuts out at seven."

When his steps reached the stairs, she minimized the window and put the envelope inside her shoe.

Scene 3

The records room was in the basement, behind the boiler, and the key hung on a nail where it had always hung. Marta turned on the single bulb. The cabinets were gray steel, labeled by section. She pulled the drawer marked C and walked her fingers back to Dyer.

His folder was thin. A hiring form, a boot-size card, a photograph of a man squinting under a hard hat. A death certificate had been stapled to the inside cover, the county seal pressed through three layers of paper. She turned it over. Nothing on the back.

Behind it sat a sheet she did not know. *Direct Deposit Authorization — Annual Renewal.* Six of them, one for each January, clipped together. The account number matched the one in her ledger. In the box marked *Payroll Approval* each form carried the same initials in blue ink: *M.E.*

She held the top sheet under the bulb. The M had a small hook at the start of its first stroke. She made that hook. She had made it since the fourth grade, when Sister Anne tried to break her of it.

She opened Okafor's folder. Six forms, six sets of initials. Then Pruitt's.

Upstairs the pipes knocked as the heat came on, an hour early. Marta put the forms back in order and closed the drawer without a sound.

Scene 4

On Thursday she told Brandt's secretary she had a dentist appointment and drove forty minutes to Karsten with the heater off. The bank sat between a feed store and a closed pharmacy. She parked across the street at 9:50 and watched the door.

At 10:06 a man in a canvas work jacket went in. He wore a cap low and carried nothing. She could not see his left foot or his face. She crossed the street.

Inside, he was already at the third window, his back to her. The teller's placard read *D. Voss, 0417.* Voss counted bills onto the counter in stacks, squared each one with two fingers, and slid them into a bank envelope. The man took it without speaking and turned. Marta looked at the rack of loan pamphlets until his boots had passed her and the door had closed.

She waited for the next customer to finish, then stepped up.

"I'm with Eklund Mining Services," she said. "I'm asking about the Section C accounts."

Voss did not look at a screen. "You'd be Mrs. Eklund."

"Miss."

"There's a letter on file." Voss opened a drawer, took out a single page, and turned it to face her. It authorized one bearer to withdraw. At the bottom, in blue ink, was her signature, the hooked M.

Scene 5

"I didn't write this," Marta said.

Voss looked at the page, then at her. "It came in January six years ago, with the account papers. I notarized nothing. I'm not a notary." She said it flatly, like a line she had practiced. "The bank accepted it."

"Who brought it in?"

"The bearer's not named. That's what bearer means."

"Who comes on Thursdays?"

"Someone with the letter." Voss slid the page back into the drawer and shut it with her hip. "He's never given me trouble. Forty envelopes, same count, same time. You'd be surprised how much I appreciate a customer who doesn't talk."

Marta's palms had gone damp. She pressed them against the counter, and a thin grit of salt, carried in on her own sleeves, came away on the laminate. "If I close the accounts today?"

"You're a co-signatory. You can." Voss paused. "Then I'd have to ask you to sign."

Marta looked at the pen on its little chain. She left it where it was.

Outside, the cold had sharpened. At the end of the block a gray pickup idled in front of the feed store. The man in the canvas jacket was climbing in. He did it carefully, right leg first, and then lifted the left in after it with both hands. A permit hung from the mirror, white with a red stripe, the kind the mine had printed for its lot.

The truck pulled out. She wrote the plate on her palm.

Scene 6

She drove back with the plate smearing on her palm and wrote it again on the envelope in her shoe before it was gone.

The guard shack at the mine gate had a space heater and a radio playing farm prices. Halvorsen had worked the gate for twenty-two years and did not get up when she came in. She said she was auditing parking permits. He shrugged and pulled the binder off its hook.

The permits were numbered in red pencil, one line each. She ran her finger down to the plate. Permit 31. *Pruitt, W.* Beside it, six small checkmarks in a column, one per January.

"Pruitt's been dead six years," she said.

"Has he?" Halvorsen turned the page toward himself, as if it might say otherwise. "I just check the sticker. Sticker's current."

"Does that truck come through on Thursdays?"

"Most weeks." He scratched his jaw. "He doesn't stop at the window. I lift the arm, he lifts two fingers."

"Do you see his face?"

"Cap. Collar up." The radio gave a price for hogs. "He doesn't park in the lot, though. Goes around the back, past the old hoist house, where the road ends."

"What's back there?"

"Nothing. Fence." Halvorsen closed the binder. "Your hand's all ink, Miss Eklund."

She looked down. The plate had run into her lifeline.

Scene 7

She left the car at the gate and walked, because the road behind the shaft house was rutted and she did not want to hear her own engine. Past the headframe the gravel gave way to packed salt, gray and crusted, and it squeaked under her shoes.

The gray pickup stood at the end of the road with its nose to the fence. She put her hand on the hood. It was still warm. The cab was empty, the permit swinging a little from the mirror.

The hoist house had a steel door painted the same green as the lobby. It was not locked. Inside, the cold smelled of brine and machine oil. A work lamp hung from a nail, and under it was a folding table with forty bank envelopes laid out in four rows of ten.

Each had a name on it in pencil. *Dyer. Okafor. Lasko.* Beside every envelope sat a smaller one, stamped and addressed, with the flap still open. She read the nearest. *Mrs. Ruth Pruitt, 14 Alder Lane, Karsten.* The one beside it went to a post office box in a town she did not know.

A thin line ran across the dust of the floor, from the door to the table and back. It was a boot print, then a long smooth drag, then a boot print.

Marta counted the envelopes again. Forty. Somewhere behind the building, gravel turned over under a slow step.

Scene 8

The door opened behind her and the cold moved. Marta did not turn right away. She watched the lamp swing on its nail.

"You're early for Thursday," Brandt said.

He stood in the doorway in the canvas jacket with the cap in his hand. The left boot scraped once on the salt as he came in. He did not look at the envelopes. He looked at her shoes, then at the hand she had put flat on the table.

"You signed my initials," she said.

"You were signing them anyway. Every pay period, forty lines." He pulled the folding chair out and did not sit in it. "I only did the January forms. The company stopped the death benefit the week after the collapse. Counsel said any payment was an admission. Ruth Pruitt had three kids."

"It's the company's money."

"It's the company's wages. For work they did." He set the cap on the table beside *Lasko*. "I figured six years was about what the lawyers would call a gift."

She lifted the Pruitt envelope. It was heavy and soft, the bills banded in twenties. Beneath the lamp the pencil letters were small and square, the same hand that had written *Lock up when you go* on a sticky note in March.

"The fifteenth is Tuesday," she said.

Brandt nodded once.

Marta took the pen from his shirt pocket, opened the ledger she had not brought, and then remembered that and laid the pen down on the table instead.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

Mr. Pruett did not look at the page Ida set in front of him. He looked at her, then at the door, which she had closed behind her.

"Forty lines," she said. "Same deposit day, same amounts, no changes in six years. No sick leave, no tax adjustments. Every name is on the plaque in the lobby."

"Yes."

"They died in the collapse."

"They did." He squared the page against the edge of the blotter, as if it were something he might sign. "It's an old arrangement, Ida. It predates you. It predates me, in its way. It's handled."

"By whom?"

"By people who aren't asking you to handle it." His voice stayed level, the voice he used for late freight and broken pumps. "Leave the lines as they are. Reconcile around them. Your numbers will tie out; I've seen your quarterlies."

He opened the drawer and took out a cream envelope, unsealed, and slid it across the desk with two fingers. She knew what it was before she touched it. Inside was a slip with a new figure for her salary, typed, already initialed.

She stood there. The radiator ticked. She could hear the hoist grinding somewhere below the floor.

"Thank you," she said, and was sick at how quickly it came out.

That night, at her kitchen table, she pulled the deposit records again. She wrote out the forty account numbers by hand. Each began with the same six digits, and each routing slip named the same place: the Corrick branch, eleven miles down the valley road.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The bookkeeper brings the anomaly to her supervisor, who calmly explains it is an 'old arrangement' and instructs her to leave it alone, then slides an envelope with a raise across the desk. She accepts it, ashamed at how easily her silence has been priced, and that evening finds the bank account numbers for the dead men all lead to one branch in the nearby town.

Scene 2

Row Nine had been painted the same gray since Ida was a girl. Odalys Marren's door stood open behind the screen, and a radio inside was reading grain prices.

"Survivor records," Ida said, holding up her ledger folder like a permit. "The office is updating them."

"Is that what the office is calling it." Odalys let her in anyway. The kitchen smelled of onions and coal smoke. A man's work jacket still hung on the hook by the stove, the elbows gone shiny.

Ida did not sit until she was told to. "Are you receiving anything from the company? Since Tomas."

Odalys turned the radio off. She took her time. Then she reached up to the shelf over the bread box, moved a tin of buttons, and brought down a small brown envelope, soft from handling. Nothing was written on it.

"First of the month," she said. "Through the mail slot. No stamp. Cash." She tipped it so Ida could see the bills, flattened and counted. "A man told me at the funeral not to speak of it, and I haven't. Not to my sister."

"What man?"

"A man in a good coat." She set the envelope down between them. "It paid for the roof last spring."

Ida looked at the figure Odalys named, then at the number she had written in her own hand the night before. The two did not match. She said nothing, and Odalys watched her say it.

Scene 3

The archive was a cage of wire shelving at the far end of the basement, lit by one bulb on a pull chain. Ida found the box by its label, EAST GALLERY, INQUIRY, in a hand she didn't know. It weighed almost nothing.

Inside were a fire marshal's sketch of the gallery, a list of names on company letterhead, and a single typed page of findings. She read it standing up. *Roof failure consistent with undetected brine intrusion. No negligence found.* Three signatures. One date.

"They did it in an afternoon."

She turned. Hobart stood at the cage door in his cardigan, a thermos under his arm. He had worked the night desk when she was in grade school and still kept a key to everything.

"Pruett's office said you'd gone down," he said. "I didn't think they'd say it so quick."

"An afternoon?"

"Sat at one o'clock. Rose by five. I brought them sandwiches." He set the thermos on a shelf and unscrewed the cup. "Nobody asked me anything, and I'd have told them something."

"Told them what?"

"I ran the night batch, Ida. Punched the cards for the pay run." He poured, and the steam rose past the bulb. "Your forty lines. They weren't added after. The first deposit went out the Friday before the roof came down."

She still held the findings page. The sketch had a date penciled in its corner, and she looked at it, then at him.

Scene 4

The valley road ran along the dry creek bed, and Ida kept the window down so the cold would keep her alert. Corrick had one street. The bank sat between a feed store and a shuttered barber, its brass door handle worn pale.

The teller was young, with a name plate that read D. Fenn and a pencil she kept turning end over end. Ida gave her the account numbers on the sheet, not the folder.

"Reconciliation," Ida said. "I only need to see the file."

"Mr. Alder handles the files." Fenn glanced at the office door. It was dark. "He's at lunch."

"Then you can tell me who's on them."

The pencil stopped. "It's one person. All forty. They were opened the same week." She said it quickly, the way a child reports a broken window. Then she went into the back and returned with a gray card in a paper sleeve. "I'm not supposed to take these out."

"I won't ask you to."

Ida laid it flat on the counter. Under *Authorized Signatory* the ink had gone slightly brown. She knew the capital W before she read the rest, the loop that closed on itself, because it had been on every shift sheet that crossed her desk her first year. *A. Weir, Foreman.* Beneath it was the opening date, typed by the bank's machine.

Eleven days after the roof came down.

"Has he been in?" Ida asked.

Fenn looked at the door again. "I only started in the spring."

Scene 5

The lobby was empty at five-forty. Ida stood before the bronze plaque with her handwritten list and read down it, name by name, touching nothing. Forty names, in alphabetical order. Tomas Marren was the twelfth. Between *Wasik* and *Yerby* there was no Weir, and no space where one had been cut.

The company cottage stood past the last streetlamp, where the valley road bent toward the tailings. Smoke came from the chimney. Ida had her hand raised to knock when the door opened.

Alder Weir was heavier than on the shift sheets, his hair gone white at the temples. He wore his boots indoors. He looked at her folder, then at her face.

"You're quicker than I figured," he said. "Come in. I've kept the stove going."

She stayed on the step. "The accounts at Corrick. You opened them eleven days after the roof came down."

"I did."

"Forty accounts, and the money's swept out every month. Odalys Marren gets an envelope through her slot. It doesn't match the ledger."

"No." He said it without hurry. "The ledger's what the company pays. The envelope's what I can get out to them."

"And the rest?"

He held the door wider. On the table behind him she saw a cashbox, a pencil, and a column of figures in the same closed-loop hand.

"Sit down, Ida. Check my arithmetic."

Scene 6

"I'll stand," Ida said. "I'm not checking anything."

Weir nodded as though she'd remarked on the weather. He left the door open, and the stove's heat leaned out around him onto the step.

"You're not on the plaque."

"No."

"You were foreman of the East Gallery. Your hand is on every shift sheet I inherited."

"I was in the hoist house that Saturday. Marren's crew went down without me." He rubbed his thumb along the doorframe, where the paint had worn to wood. "Nobody puts a man on bronze for standing above it."

"Then explain why every line in your cashbox has a name there."

He took longer than she expected. Behind him the pencil lay across the column, exactly where he'd set it down.

"Two of them weren't under it either," he said.

The wind moved the tailings fence, a long dry rattle. Ida kept her eyes on his face.

"Alive?"

"Alive. They drew on two of those accounts, and I send it where they are, under other names. They've never come back down this valley." He said it plainly, the way he might have read out a tonnage. "I didn't put them on the plaque. I never saw the plaque until it was hung."

She thought of the lobby, the letters cut so clean. Somebody had handed an engraver a list, and the list had been right about every name but two.

"Who gave it to him?" she said.

Weir looked past her at the road. The stove ticked behind him.

This makes her wonder whether the plaque, the inquiry and the dead are all arranged to cover something else.

Scene 7

Ida sat. The chair was still warm from him. Weir took the other one and folded his hands and did not speak, and she understood that was the whole of his answer for now.

She picked up the pencil. His columns ran in three: *Ledger*, *Envelope*, *Difference*. Forty rows, a month to a page, six years of pages held with a bulldog clip. Odalys Marren's line was there, her envelope smaller than her wage by a little more than half. She added the differences down the last page twice. Both times the total came to the same figure, and under it he had written a short line and an account number.

"That isn't yours," she said.

"It's never been mine."

"You carry it to Corrick."

"First Monday. I put it in at the window and take the slip."

She knew the number. She had typed it herself, month after month, on the transfer sheet headed *Operating Reserve*, never wondering why the reserve was kept eleven miles off. She pulled her folder open and found the last sheet. The deposit from the cashbox sat above the draw that covered the office payroll.

She turned to the raise slip, still folded in her coat pocket. The new figure was typed and initialed. She set it beside the ledger. The month on the slip was the month the Reserve draw grew.

The stove ticked. Ida laid the pencil down parallel to the page.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ida finally sits and checks Weir's column, as he asked. She finds that the gap between the ledger and the envelopes does not stay in the cashbox. It goes out each month to a Corrick account that traces back to the company, and her own raise has been coming from the dead men's wages.

Scene 8

Ida laid the cream envelope on the blotter, then the bulldog-clipped pages on top of it. Pruett looked at the clip, at the closed loops of Weir's handwriting, and then opened the drawer.

His hand stayed inside. She could see the edge of a second envelope, the same cream. The radiator ticked twice. He slid the drawer shut and set both palms on the desk.

"Weir showed you the Reserve."

"I typed the Reserve for six years."

"Yes. You were good at it." He did not reach for the pages. "You asked me once who handles it. Counsel handles it. A Mr. Calloway, who wears a very good coat. He typed the roster of the east crew the Sunday after, and I drove it to the engraver myself. Nobody counted anyone. The roster was the list."

"Two of them are alive."

"Then the roster was wrong about two." He said it like a late shipment.

"And Friday?"

Pruett looked at the window, where the headframe stood against a white sky. "The brine report came Thursday. The gallery was worked Saturday regardless. Calloway wanted the wage paid out Friday, early, to every man on that roster, so the books would show the company paying them before the roof, and not after."

Below the floor the hoist started up. Ida did not pick up the envelope.

He opens the drawer for a second envelope, then closes it, and finally tells her who handed the engraver the list and why the first deposit went out the Friday before the roof fell.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

The box had been wedged behind the boiler in the records room, its lid furred with salt dust. Inside were payroll stubs from the spring before the collapse. Nora Vance was only checking them against the archive index, a job nobody had asked for. Then she noticed that forty lines on the current register had the same routing number as the stubs in her hand.

She ran her thumb down the column. Forty names, forty deposits, every other Friday, all into one account at Harlan County Savings in Pruett. The current register called them "legacy hourly." She had signed off on the total three quarters running without looking at the lines.

She copied the account number onto the back of her hand, then onto a notepad, then drove the forty minutes to Pruett with the heater rattling.

The bank was one room with a clock over the door. The teller, a young man with a lanyard, took her ID and her story about a payroll discrepancy and typed for a while.

"That's a business sub-account," he said. "Opened nine years ago. Signature card says Walter Prosser."

"He was my predecessor. He died in March."

"Then he's not who's been in." The teller turned the screen slightly, then seemed to think better of it. "Someone comes every Monday and checks the balance. Always pays the fees in cash, exact change. Never gives a name."

"What do they look like?"

He looked at the clock. "Like someone who comes every Monday."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

While auditing a dusty box of pre-collapse records, the bookkeeper finds that the forty wages are still being routed to a single account at a small-town bank. She pulls the account number and drives there, only to learn that the account was opened under her late predecessor's signature and is checked weekly by someone who always pays in cash.

She realizes they are the collapse dead, and when she quietly asks the pay clerk about it the next morning, he abruptly asks her to drop it and leaves the room.

Instead he invites her to dinner, explains that the payments are a 'private arrangement' with the widows, and offers her a raise to keep the books exactly as they are, leaving her torn between his sympathy and the sense that something is off.
  • 1.00 A widow arrives at the office to ask why her husband's pay envelope stopped coming last month, which makes the bookkeeper realize that the dead men's wages were actually reaching families, and that someone has just cut them off. She checks the ledger and finds that the wage lines are still booked as paid, so the money is going somewhere else.

Scene 2

Nora took a room at the Kessler Motel for two nights and spent Sunday in the diner across from the bank, nursing coffee until the waitress stopped refilling it. On Monday she was back at the corner table by eight-thirty, watching the door under the clock.

The bank opened at nine. At nine-forty a woman crossed the street from the direction of the feed store. She was sixty or so, in a canvas work jacket gone pale at the elbows, gray braid over one shoulder. She did not look at the diner. She went in, and she came out six minutes later, tucking something small into her breast pocket.

Nora left a five on the table and followed half a block behind. They passed the post office, a shuttered laundromat, a church with a hand-lettered sign about a fish fry. The woman turned down Alder, walked to the fourth house, a white one with a sagging porch, and went in without a key.

Nora stood on the sidewalk for a full minute. Then she climbed the steps and knocked.

The woman opened the door with a dish towel in her hand. She did not ask who Nora was. She looked at her shoes, then her face, then stepped back.

The kitchen was small and smelled of onions. On the wall by the stove, thumbtacked in two columns on lined paper, was a list of names in blue ballpoint. Nora knew the first one before she had read the second.

Nora stays in Pruett and waits across from the bank until Monday. She watches a woman in a faded work jacket enter, and she follows her to a small house where a handwritten memorial list of the dead is pinned to the kitchen wall.

Scene 3

"Sit," the woman said, and Nora did not.

"I don't know what that list is," Nora said.

"Neither do I." The woman folded the dish towel in thirds and laid it over the oven handle. "Who've you told?"

Nora thought of the notepad in her coat, the box behind the boiler, the teller's lanyard. "No one."

The woman watched her the way Nora had watched the bank door, steadily and without hurry. The refrigerator hummed. Somewhere in the house a clock ticked a half-second off from the one in the hall.

Then the woman opened the drawer beside the sink, moved aside a tangle of rubber bands and a roll of stamps, and took out a brass key on a loop of green yarn. She held it out across the linoleum.

"Pruett Self Storage, out on 9. Number fourteen. It's the only lock that isn't a Master."

"What's in it?"

"His handwriting."

Nora took the key. The yarn was warm from the drawer.

The woman drove, a tan Buick that smelled of wintergreen, and said nothing for eleven minutes. The facility was a row of orange doors behind a chain-link fence, one floodlight on a pole. She parked facing number fourteen and left the engine running.

Nora walked the gravel alone. The padlock was old and stiff. She turned the key and it gave. With her hand flat on the cold ribbed door, she looked back. The woman sat behind the windshield with both hands on the wheel, not leaving and not looking away.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The woman admits nothing and asks Nora whom she has told. Nora lies and says no one, and the woman answers by taking a key from a drawer and handing it to her. It opens a storage unit where Walter Prosser kept his own records. The scene ends with Nora at the unit door, aware that she is now complicit and that the woman is watching from the car.

Scene 4

The door rattled up on its track and cold air came out of the unit, smelling of cardboard and old pennies. Nora found the light switch for nothing; there was none. Just a desk against the back wall, a steel one with a rolled blotter, and on it a gooseneck lamp whose cord ran down and along the floor to a plug lying loose on the concrete.

An outlet box was bolted to the wall outside, under the floodlight. She pushed the plug in. The lamp came on yellow.

Ledgers stood in a row along the desk's back edge, green cloth spines, years inked on masking tape. She pulled the first. Walter's hand was small and upright, the sevens crossed like his old payroll memos. Columns ruled by hand: date, deposit, balance. Then two more he had added himself, headed *Out* and *To*.

*To* was initials and towns. *R.T., Dunmore. 140. M.&L.O., Pruett. 90 cash.* Every Friday deposit matched a line on the register in her car. Every withdrawal was accounted for to the dollar.

She turned to the last ledger and the last written page. The final entry was dated the eleventh of March, five days before the funeral program she had kept on her corkboard. A deposit. A balance. Under *Out*, a single figure, and under *To*, nothing.

Nora tipped an empty crate on its side, sat, and opened the first ledger to its first page. Behind her the gravel was quiet, and then the Buick's engine stopped.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Nora rolls up the door and finds a desk, a lamp on an extension cord, and ledgers in Walter Prosser's hand. They show he kept a second set of books recording every deposit and where each withdrawal went, and the final entry is dated the week he died. She sits on an upturned crate and starts at the first page, and the woman finally cuts the engine.

Scene 5

Boots on gravel, then the roll of the door track as the woman ducked under it. She looked at the lamp, the desk, the row of green spines. Then she pulled the other crate close, sat, and put her hands on her knees.

"Ada Lindqvist," she said. "Erik was my husband. Fourth name on the wall."

Nora kept her thumb in the ledger. "You've been collecting since the collapse?"

"Since the May after. Walter came to the house with an envelope. Said it was what Erik was owed. The next month there was another." Ada's breath showed faintly in the lamplight. "I never asked him why. I had two boys and a mortgage on a house with no one earning in it. You don't question the hand that's holding the bread."

"Did he say who it was from?"

"He said it was from the books."

Nora looked down. The first page was ruled in pencil, the margin measured with a straightedge. Where she had expected a date and a deposit there was one line of ink, pressed hard enough to emboss the paper beneath.

*June 2. I am sorry, Ada. I put my name where his should have been.*

Nora read it twice. Whose name was on the register, on the signature card, on every transfer? Walter's. She turned the page and the next one began, plainly enough, with a number.

Ada was watching her face, not the book. "Is it long?" she asked.

Scene 6

"Longer than I'd like," Nora said, and closed the first ledger on her thumb.

She reached for the last one, the one with the blank beside the eleventh of March. She had read that page already. This time she looked at the book itself. The cloth on the back cover had lifted at one corner, and under the lamp she saw a rectangle of masking tape, yellowed at the edges, the same tape as on the spines.

She pressed it with a fingernail. It was an envelope, flat against the inside board, taped on all four sides.

*To whoever finds the box.*

Ada leaned forward on her crate. "That isn't for me."

"No."

Nora worked the tape loose in strips. The flap had never been licked; it was folded under. Inside was a single brass key, small and flat, stamped 212, and one sheet of ledger paper folded in thirds.

The writing was the same small upright hand, but the lines slanted downhill.

*Harlan County Savings, Pruett. Box 212, in my name. Everything I could not say aloud is in it. I did not keep the legacy line open for myself. Gerald Stroud, VP Finance, told me in the spring of the collapse that if it closed, I would be the one who had closed it. Every quarter after, he asked me for the total.*

Nora read it through again. The key was cold in her palm.

"Who?" Ada said.

Nora told her.

It holds a key to a safe deposit box at Harlan County Savings and a note naming the one executive who forced him to keep the false hourly line open.

Scene 7

The teller kept the key a moment longer than he needed to. Then he checked the card, and his eyebrows moved. "Second signer's on file. A. Lindqvist, added in February."

Ada stood very straight at Nora's elbow. "He said it was for the mail," she said.

The vault was cold. Box 212 was long and shallow, and inside it lay two narrow black ledgers and nothing else. Nora carried them to the little booth with the frosted door, and Ada sat across from her with her purse in her lap.

The first page was headed *G.S. — Totals*. Walter had ruled it into three columns: date, figure, what was said.

*Jul 9. $61,480. Asked at my door, not by memo. "So we both know the number."*

*Oct 11. $61,480. Asked whether Ada L. still collects in person. I said I did not know who collected.*

*Jan 15. $61,480. Did not ask the total. Asked what I would say if the state called.*

Nora turned pages. Every quarter, the same figure, and under it Stroud's sentences in Walter's upright hand, each one mild.

The last entry was alone at the bottom of a page.

*Feb 26. Asked who else has the account number. Said no one. He said good. Offered to drive me home, since my car was in the shop. I said I would walk.*

Nora counted the days without wanting to. Two weeks, near enough. She remembered the line in the program: *Walter passed suddenly, of his heart.*

Ada was looking at the frosted glass. "Read the date again," she said.

Nora opens box 212 and finds not a confession but a second set of ledgers recording every quarterly total Gerald Stroud requested, each with a date and a note in Walter's hand about what Stroud said. The last entry shows Stroud asked about the account two weeks before Walter died, which turns the mystery from fraud into possible murder.

Scene 8

"Every page," Nora told the teller. "Both books, front and back."

He fed them through the copier in the back office one sheet at a time. It was an old machine and it ground at every page. Ada stood beside the tray and squared each copy as it came out. By the time he finished, the stack was as thick as a phone book, and the teller had to find a rubber band for it.

The state auditor's office was on the third floor of a sandstone building in the capital, past a metal detector and a guard who made Nora open both ledgers. A clerk named Mr. Oyelaran took them to a desk with a glass top. Nora set the black books down, then the copies beside them, then the green ledgers from the storage unit, stacked by year. Then she laid out the brass key and the folded letter with its downhill slant.

Mr. Oyelaran read the first page of Walter's totals without sitting. Then he sat.

"The originals stay with you," Nora said. "I'll sign for them leaving my hands."

He pushed a form across for her and a second one toward Ada. "A witness to the payments?"

"I was paid them," Ada said.

She uncapped the pen, wrote her full name, *Ada Marie Lindqvist*, and read it back to herself. Then she turned to the first page of the form and began, without being asked, to list the dates she remembered.
