psychological thriller

A string quartet's second violinist starts receiving letters that describe mistakes in performances before those performances take place.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

The envelope was under the doormat, not in the mailbox. No stamp, no address, just *Tessa Marrin* in blue ink, the letters upright and careful.

She read it standing in the hallway with her cello-less shoulder still aching from yesterday's rehearsal.

*Thursday, Halloran Hall. Beethoven, Op. 132, the slow movement. In bar 41, after the fermata, you will enter a sixteenth early. Your A will be sharp. Pavel will look at you. Marcus will not.*

There was no signature. The paper was cream, heavy, torn along one edge as if from a pad.

Tessa turned it over. Blank. She smelled it and caught nothing but paper.

At ten she was in Ines's living room, where they rehearsed because the piano had been sold and the space was left over. Marcus tuned. Pavel ate half a clementine and set the other half on the radiator. Ines was talking about her landlord.

"You're quiet," Marcus said.

"Slept badly."

They started with the Beethoven. Tessa kept her eyes on the page and felt the letter folded in her case pocket like a second, smaller part. When they reached the slow movement she counted rests she didn't need to count. Bar 41 came and she waited out the fermata until Marcus's bow lifted, then entered with him. Her A sat dead center.

Pavel was peeling the clementine's other half, not looking at anyone.

She took her pencil and wrote *41* in the margin anyway.

Scene 2

On Wednesday she opened her case in the practice room at the conservatory to rosin her bow, and the second envelope was already in the pocket, lying flat against the first.

She had not put it there. The case had been locked in her hall closet overnight. She checked the latch anyway, turning it with her thumb. It clicked the way it always did.

Same blue ink, same upright hand. This one was folded in thirds.

*You wrote 41 in the margin of your part on Tuesday. It will not help. You will be thinking about the number when the fermata ends, and not about Marcus's bow.*

Below that, a second paragraph.

*After the concert Ines will say it was a small thing. She will say it kindly.*

Tessa sat down on the piano bench. Through the wall someone was working the same four bars of a Chopin étude, stopping, starting over.

She pulled her part from the case and found the pencil mark. It was small, in the upper corner, and she had made it while Pavel peeled his clementine. Nobody had been looking at her. Nobody had been behind her.

She took the eraser from her pencil case and rubbed out the 41 until the paper went gray and thin. Then she held the page to the window. The number was still there, pressed into the paper, legible as a scar.

Scene 3

They ran the Beethoven at Halloran Hall at six, in the empty room with the chairs stacked along the walls. The stage lights made the varnish on Marcus's cello look wet.

Tessa had decided on the walk over to play bar 41 late rather than early. She would count the fermata twice. Let the A come after Marcus's bow had been up a full second.

It came a full second after. Her pitch was fine.

Pavel lowered his violin. "You hung back."

"Did I?"

"A little." He looked at her the way he looked at a passage he intended to fix. "It's better early. It's a breath. You know that."

"I'll watch it."

Ines wrote something in her part. Marcus tightened his A string a hair, though nothing had gone flat, and kept his eyes on the scroll.

They took the movement again. This time Tessa entered with the bow lift, exactly, and her ears rang with the effort of not thinking *sixteenth*. The A was clean. Pavel nodded once at the floor.

At the break she crouched by her case. She had put a strand of her own hair across the latch that morning. It was still there, pale against the black.

"Everything all right?" Ines asked from above her, kindly.

Tessa closed the lid. "Fine. Just tired."

Scene 4

Thursday, in the second half of the program, the slow movement opened out under the lights. Tessa could see the first rows: a woman with a program folded into a fan, a man whose eyes were closed.

Bar 41 approached. She did not count. She watched Marcus's right hand, the hair of his bow, the small tremor in his wrist. The fermata held and held. His bow lifted and she entered with it, not early, not late, the A placed under her finger like a coin on a table.

It sounded true. She would have sworn to it.

Pavel's head turned a few degrees. His eyes found her for the length of half a beat, then went back to the page. Marcus stared at his scroll as if it were speaking to him.

The movement went on. Her hands were steady. She noticed that, and noticed that she was noticing, and played the next phrase half a second behind her own attention.

Backstage the corridor smelled of dust and hot lamps. Marcus walked past her to the water fountain. Pavel was already on his phone.

Ines caught her at the coat rack and put a hand on her sleeve.

"It was a small thing," she said. "Truly. Nobody heard it."

"Heard what?"

Ines smiled, and her thumb moved once over the fabric of Tessa's cuff.

"Bar 41, darling. Don't think about it."

Scene 5

The reception was in the lobby, with plastic cups of white wine and a donor holding Pavel by the elbow. Tessa watched Ines laugh at something, head tipped back, and then watched her turn toward the stairs with a woman in a green scarf.

The green room was empty. Ines's tote bag sat open on the couch, her folder of parts on top.

Tessa told herself she was looking for her own pencil. She lifted the folder. Under it was a pad of paper, cream, heavy, the top edge ragged where sheets had been torn away.

She did not breathe in. She held the pad to the light of the makeup mirror and tilted it until the bulbs raked across the surface.

Grooves. Upright, careful, pressed deep. She followed them with her eyes, line by line.

*Saturday. Ravel, the pizzicato. Marcus will break a string in the*

The rest was too faint, lost under the hollow of a thumbprint.

Footsteps on the stairs. Two voices, one of them Ines's, saying *no, no, it was lovely*.

Tessa set the pad back in the bag, squared the folder over it, and straightened the strap the way it had been. She was at the sink running water over her wrists when the door opened.

"There you are," Ines said. "We were about to send a search party."

Her eyes went to the couch, and then, easily, to Tessa's face.

Scene 6

"Delia, this is our second violin," Ines said. "Tessa, Delia wants to hear the Ravel on Saturday."

The woman in the green scarf shook Tessa's wet hand without remarking on it. "I'll be in the third row," she said. "I always sit in the third row." Then someone called her name from the stairwell and she was gone, scarf last.

The door swung shut on its slow hinge. Ines crossed to the couch and sat beside her tote. She did not look inside it. She drew the strap straight with two fingers, though it already was, and rested her hand on the folder.

"You're pale," she said.

"It's the lights."

"Come here." Ines patted the cushion. Tessa dried her wrists on her skirt and sat. The couch was still warm from the lamps.

"Marcus's strings are ancient," Ines said conversationally. "I've told him and told him. He thinks they're fine until they're not." She unzipped the tote four inches and took out a pencil, yellow, sharpened to a fine point, and held it out. "You were looking for one."

Tessa hadn't said so.

She took it. The wood was dented near the end by someone's teeth.

"Thank you."

"Keep it," Ines said. "Write whatever you like."

Scene 7

Saturday, she was at the hall by four. The side door was propped with a folded program, and the dressing room held only Marcus's cello, laid in its open case like something sleeping.

She knelt and ran her thumbnail along the D string, from the bridge down toward the pegs. Near the nut it caught. A nick, clean-edged, the winding parted over a hair's width of core. A bend would finish it.

Her own case was on the chair. She opened it, and the envelope lay on her part.

*You will tell Marcus. He will thank you and then he won't believe you.*

She read it twice. The blue ink had a faint sheen on the downstrokes.

Marcus came in with a paper bag of almonds. He saw her kneeling and stopped.

"Your D," Tessa said. "Look at the nut."

He crouched and looked. He pressed the string with a fingertip, and his face went still.

"Thank you," he said.

She waited.

"Ines told me Thursday you'd been looking at my strings," he said, quietly, to the cello. "Said you were upset. That you'd say something like this before Saturday."

"Marcus, it's cut."

"It's frayed. They fray." He took the almonds off the lid and set them on the floor. He did not touch the peg. "I'll change it at intermission."

Down the corridor Ines was laughing at a stagehand.

Scene 8

Intermission came and Marcus did not change the string. Tessa watched him through the dressing room door. He sat with the cello between his knees, eating almonds one at a time, the new D coiled in its envelope on the shelf beside him.

In the Ravel, the second movement began with Ines's pluck, dry and bright. Tessa counted. Delia sat in the third row, scarf bright as a lit signal, hands folded.

Bar 60. Marcus's fingers dug in on the D.

The string went with a crack like a dropped plate. The loose end whipped across his cheekbone and a line of red opened there. In the third row, someone gasped. Marcus's hand stayed on the fingerboard. He looked at it, then at Tessa.

She kept her pizzicato going. Every note landed where it should. Pavel, startled, dropped a beat and found it again.

Across the stand, Ines was not looking at Marcus. She was looking at Tessa, with her head slightly tilted, as though waiting for a reply.

Tessa held her gaze through two bars. Then she took the yellow pencil from behind her ear, bent, and wrote a number in the margin of her part, small and upright, pressing hard enough to dent the page beneath.

Ines's smile stayed where it was. Her left hand tightened on the neck of her violin.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The envelope came between a gas bill and a flyer for roof repair. Cream paper, a first-class stamp, her name in blue ink. Mara read it in the hallway with her coat still on.

*Tomorrow, in the slow movement, your E string will split under the third finger on the high G. Not a squeak. Two pitches at once. You will want to blame the rosin.*

There was no signature. She turned the page over and found nothing. The sevens in her house number had little crossbars, the way she made them.

In the kitchen she held her violin under the lamp and ran a thumbnail along the E. New in September. No fraying, no kink. She slid the letter into the drawer with the takeaway menus.

At rehearsal, Tomas asked if she'd slept. "Fine," she said. Ines tuned to the A and frowned at her own pegs. Mara changed nothing about her fingering, her bow hold, or her strings. She told herself that was the point.

The next night, in the Adagio, the hall was so quiet she could hear the radiators. Her third finger came down on the high G and the note cracked open, a whistle on top of a rasp. Ines's eyes flicked toward her. Tomas's bow never paused.

In the dressing room he was already coiling a cable around his elbow. "Strings do that," he said. "Even new ones."

"They do," Mara said, and zipped her case.

Mara receives the first letter by post the morning before a concert. It names a specific error, a split E-string note in the slow movement, and she hides it from the others, so when it happens on stage exactly as written, she alone knows it was foretold.

She decides to defy the prediction by playing flawlessly, but her fixation on the bow causes her to break the quartet's rhythm in a way the letter never mentioned.

Scene 2

Mara spread the last six programs across the kitchen table and put the recordings on, one after another, with the score open at her elbow. She found her own small errors easily: a late shift in the Ravel, a smeared run in the Haydn. They were the ordinary kind. None of them told her anything.

At Thursday's rehearsal she asked Tomas for his Beethoven score. "Mine's got coffee on it," she said.

He handed it over without looking up. She turned to the second violin lines in the score, and there they were: tiny pencil ticks in the margin, each with a date. Bar 47 had two. The Adagio in the Schumann had one dated three weeks back, before the new E string had even been bought.

"You've been keeping count," she said, lightly.

"I mark everyone's." He took the score back and closed it. "It's how I rehearse."

"There's nothing by Ines's part."

"Ines doesn't need it." His thumb pressed the cover flat. "Is this about the string? I told you, it happens."

"I'm only asking."

"And I'm only working." He turned to his stand and slid the score into his folder.

The folder was open wide enough for her to see. Under the photocopied parts lay a sheet of cream paper, folded in thirds, its edge a shade yellower than the music around it.

"Mara," Ines called. "A, please."

She tuned.

Scene 3

The bell over the door of Halloran's Strings still had its flat note. Mara waited while Mr. Halloran finished tightening a bridge on a viola, then put her receipt on the glass counter.

"September," she said. "The E. I'd like to see the order slip, if you keep them."

"We keep everything." He pulled a ledger from under the till and licked his thumb. "Here. Ordered the ninth, came in the nineteenth, you collected the twenty-first."

The slip was a carbon copy. Her name, her phone number, the string's brand. She read it twice, looking for something that wasn't there.

"Is there a problem with it?"

"It split. I'm just trying to understand when it was handled."

He frowned and tapped the nineteenth. "Handled by me. Though someone did ask about it before you came in. Day or two before. Tall fellow, with a cello case on his back. Wanted to know if your string had arrived and what kind it was."

"Did he give a name?"

"I assumed he was in your group. He knew your name." Mr. Halloran shrugged. "I told him it was in the drawer. He looked at the box and thanked me."

"Looked at it. Did he touch it?"

"I didn't watch him. I was ringing up rosin."

Mara folded the receipt into her wallet. Outside, a bus went by, and she stood with the cold on her face, seeing the folder open on Tomas's stand and the yellowed edge of paper under the parts.

Scene 4

The envelope was propped against the milk bottle on the step, not posted, though the stamp was there, uncancelled. Cream paper. Blue ink.

*Saturday, in the Beethoven, Tomas will stop in the middle of a phrase. He will lower the bow and carry the cello off through the stage-left door. Ines will keep playing. So will you, for two bars.*

Mara read it in the kitchen and then laid it beside the first letter. The same slant. The same hard downstroke on the *T*. She opened the drawer, set the two pages on top of the takeaway menus, and shut it again.

At rehearsal Tomas was already there, tightening his bow, the folder square on his stand. He nodded at her. His hair was damp from the rain.

"Tomas," she said.

"Mm?"

The folder was closed. Ines was in the corridor, laughing at something on her phone.

"Could we take the Beethoven from the top today? I want to hear the middle again."

"We always do." He drew the bow across the C, a long note that filled the room and held. "Why?"

"No reason."

They played. In the passage she'd read about, he did not stop. His shoulder rolled with the phrase, his eyes on the page, and she counted the bars out loud in her head, one hand tight on the neck of her violin.

Scene 5

The café on Pell Street smelled of wet wool. Ines had taken the table by the radiator and ordered tea she didn't touch.

Mara laid the two letters on the table, then the envelopes beside them, then the receipt from Halloran's with the nineteenth circled. "Read them."

Ines kept her hands in her lap. "Is that Tomas's paper?"

"I don't know whose paper it is."

"I mean, it looks like it." She went pale in stages, the color leaving her cheeks first and then her mouth. She looked at the blue ink, the slanted *M* in *Mara*, and pushed her chair back an inch from the table. "I don't need to read them."

"Why not?"

"Because I get them too."

The milk jug on the next table clinked against a saucer. Mara waited.

"Since August. Cream envelopes, my name, that ink." Ines's voice was level, the voice she used to count rests. "Eleven. I put them in the kitchen sink and light them. I haven't opened one."

"How do you know what they say?"

"I don't. I know what they are." She finally looked at the pages. "Does yours say what I do wrong?"

"It says what I do."

Ines took a sugar packet from the bowl and folded it in half, then in half again, pressing the crease flat with her thumbnail.

"Eleven," Mara said.

"Last one came Tuesday. It's still on my piano."

Scene 6

Ines's flat was on the third floor, and the piano took up most of the front room. The envelope sat on the music desk, squared to the edge, as if she'd been practicing from it.

"Tuesday's," Ines said. "Go on. I can't."

Mara slit it with her thumbnail. Cream paper, blue ink, the hard downstroke. She read it aloud, standing, one hand on the closed lid of the keyboard.

*Saturday, bar 47 of the Beethoven, Mara will come in early. Ines will hear it and follow her, a half beat behind, because she trusts her. Tomas will not look up.*

Neither of them spoke. A tap dripped in the kitchen.

"Tomas wrote that," Ines said. "He has to have."

"He's written nothing about Saturday that came true yet."

"The string came true."

"Yes." Mara set the page on the desk. "Ines, in the eleven you burned. Did you ever play something differently afterward? Even a little?"

Ines sat down on the bench and pressed one key without sounding it. "I count more. I count everything. In the Haydn last month I came in so carefully I was late." She looked at her hand. "I thought that was nerves."

"Bar 47 has two ticks in Tomas's score."

"I saw."

Mara read the line again. *Because she trusts her.* Ines was watching her mouth, waiting to see what she'd do with it.

Scene 7

Bar 47 came after a page and a half of rests. Mara counted them with her bow hovering, the hall dark past the stage lights, a cough somewhere in the stalls. Ines sat to her left with her eyes on the page. Tomas sat to her right, his cello angled toward the stage-left door.

She had decided in the cab. Not a half beat, not a slip. A full, clean early entrance, chosen, the way a person steps off a curb.

On the last beat of 46 she let her bow drop onto the string.

The sound was strong and wrong, and it ran ahead of the pulse by an eighth. For a moment it was only hers. Then Ines's A came in under it, a hair behind, bright and obedient, and the two of them were a half beat off the barline, together and wrong.

Tomas looked up.

He looked at the music first, as though it had misprinted. Then at her. His bow stayed on the string. His face had no anger in it. It looked closer to someone hearing his name called in a crowd.

Mara held his eyes for the length of the phrase. She did not know what she had expected: the page was supposed to say he wouldn't look. Beside her Ines kept counting, her lips moving.

Tomas dropped his gaze, caught the downbeat, and pulled them back in.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mara decides to test the letters by deliberately playing bar 47 exactly as the letter says, coming in early, to see whether the prophecy comes from the paper or from the person who wrote it. Ines, who doesn't know, follows her half a beat behind and Tomas does look up, and the break in the pattern leaves Mara unsure who was manipulating whom.

Scene 8

The final chord of the Beethoven died into the rafters, and for a second the hall held its breath. Then the applause broke over them, warm and ragged.

Tomas stood before it finished. He did not bow. He lifted the cello by the neck, tucked the endpin against his shin, and walked behind Ines's chair toward the stage-left door. His bow hung from two fingers. The door swung shut on its pneumatic arm, slowly, and clicked.

Ines's lips were moving. "Bar 47," she whispered. "That's not what it said."

"It said he'd leave."

"In the middle of a phrase."

"A movement late." Mara heard her own voice from a distance. The applause thickened. Someone in the front row was half standing, unsure whether to continue. Ines gripped her bow with both hands.

Mara laid her violin on the chair and went.

The corridor behind the door was cold and smelled of dust and hot lamps. A stagehand flattened himself against the wall to let her pass. At the end, under the exit sign, a trestle held Tomas's cello case, lid thrown back. The velvet was dented in the shape of the instrument. Nothing else. No scarf, no rosin, no coat.

Through the wall, the clapping dwindled and began again.

On the lid, squared to the edge, lay a cream envelope. *Mara*, in blue ink. The ink at the bottom of the *M* had pooled, and when she touched it, it came away on her thumb.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Tomas leaves the stage without a word after the final chord and carries his cello through the stage-left door, just as the letter said he would in the Beethoven. Mara and Ines stay seated in the applause, stunned that the prediction came true a movement late. Mara goes after him and finds the cello case open and empty, with a cream envelope on the lid addressed to her.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

The envelope had no stamp. Mara noticed that after she'd already slit it with a butter knife and unfolded the single sheet beside her cold tea.

*Tomorrow, in the Andante, you will shift from third position to the high B in bar 41 and land flat of it. The note will crack on the up-bow. A man in the balcony will cough twice, and the cough will cover most of it. Only Teodor will turn his head.*

The handwriting was small and upright, in blue-black ink. She didn't know it.

She read it three times, then laughed once, a short sound in the empty kitchen. She got her violin from its case by the door.

Bar 41 was nothing. She had played it a thousand times. She played it now, and it was clean. She played it again, slower, watching her left hand. Clean. By eleven she had played it forty times, then fifty. She wrote tick marks on the back of the envelope. She tried the shift with her eyes closed, then with the metronome at half speed, then with her elbow lowered a centimeter. Her neighbor knocked on the wall at midnight, and she switched to the practice mute and kept going.

In the morning her shoulder ached. Her phone lit up on the table with the quartet's group chat. *Call is 6:30. Don't forget the black shoes, Dani.* Four people were typing replies.

She thumbed the screen dark and put the letter back in its envelope.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mara opens a letter at her kitchen table that describes in precise detail a flubbed shift and a cracked note she will play tomorrow night, down to the cough from the audience that covers it. She decides to say nothing to the quartet and practices the passage obsessively, and the next morning she realizes she has isolated herself with the secret.

Scene 2

In the Andante she counted the bars the way she had counted tick marks. Thirty-nine. Forty. Teodor's phrase swelled above her, and she thought: *you don't get me.*

At bar 41 she shifted to third and aimed her finger a half-step low, on purpose, a clean small rebellion. She even felt pleased.

The note cracked. The up-bow skidded on the string and the sound split into a rasp with a whistle on top of it. Two coughs came down from the balcony, dry and ordinary, and swallowed most of it. In the second before the next phrase, Teodor turned his head. He looked at her for half a beat, then back to his page.

She finished the movement without hearing it.

Backstage, in the corridor that smelled of steam and carpet glue, she set the violin on a road case and stared at her left hand. Flat. The letter had said flat. She had been so sure she was choosing it, and the letter had known she would choose it.

Dani passed behind her, humming the finale, and didn't stop.

Mara opened her case for the rosin. A cream envelope lay under the neck of the instrument, her name on it in blue-black ink. In her coat pocket hung the one she had found under her door that morning and hadn't opened. She took out neither one, only stood with her thumb on the latch.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

During the performance, Mara deliberately plays bar 41 a half-step off to prove the letter can't control her, and the note cracks on the up-bow exactly as described, with the cough covering it. Backstage she realizes that her defiance was the thing the letter predicted, and she finds a third envelope tucked into her violin case.

Scene 3

Her room was on the fourth floor, facing an air shaft. She put the chain on, sat at the foot of the bed with the case across her knees and her coat still buttoned, and took out the cream envelope.

*You are sitting on the bed in your coat. Your thumb is on the left latch of the case, not on the envelope. You have just noticed this, and you will move it. The radiator under the window will tick twice before it settles.*

The radiator ticked. Twice.

*Tonight you will not sleep. Tomorrow you will make a mistake, and you will make it on purpose. You will know it is wrong while you do it. Knowing will not help.*

She looked at her thumb. She lifted it off the brass.

She checked the bathroom, behind the shower curtain, under the bed. She opened the closet, saw four wire hangers and a folded luggage rack, and shut the door until the latch clicked. She pushed it with her palm to be sure.

Then she propped her phone against the desk lamp, framed the whole room, bed, window, desk, the closet at the right edge, and pressed record.

She practiced under the mute until two. She ate hotel crackers. Whenever the battery warning came she plugged in and started a new file.

At six she sat on the floor and scrubbed through the first file at triple speed. Herself jerking across the room. Herself at the window. Herself on the bed, asleep, which she didn't remember.

At 3:12 the closet door stood open the width of a hand. Nothing moved in the gap.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mara opens the second envelope alone in her hotel room and finds it contains no prediction, only a description of what she is doing at that exact moment, down to the hand on the latch, and a line saying the next mistake will be one she makes on purpose. She spends the night recording herself in the room with her phone, then plays the footage back and finds, in the corner of the frame, the closet door standing slightly open when she is certain she shut it, pushing the story toward paranoia and the question of whether she is being watched or breaking down.

Scene 4

She came back from the rehearsal at four, and the corridor carpet muffled her steps. She did not take off her coat. She dropped the case on the bed, crossed to the closet, and pulled the door so hard the hangers shrieked along the rod.

Four wire hangers. The folded luggage rack. A smell of cedar spray over something older.

She shoved the hangers left in one armful. Behind them the back panel was a sheet of veneered board, and along its right edge ran a dark seam as thin as a pencil line. She put two fingers in it. The panel slid with a dry whisper, and cooler air touched her wrist.

Another closet, identical, lit by the gray of another air shaft. A single cream envelope stood propped on the shelf at eye level. *Mara*, in blue-black ink.

Below it, on the carpet, lay a stack of letters held with a rubber band gone brittle. She crouched and lifted it. The top envelope read *Second Violin, Ines*. Under it, *Second Violin, Paul*. Under that, a name she couldn't make out, and then another. She thumbed down through them to the bottom. The postmark on the oldest was eleven years gone.

The band snapped when she tried to slide it off. She unfolded the top sheet. Her eyes went to the last line first.

*You will not be the first to leave.*

Mara returns to the hotel and tears the closet open, finding it empty except for a thin gap behind the wire hangers where the back panel slides aside into the adjoining room. A fresh envelope lies on the other side, along with a stack of earlier letters addressed to different second violinists. The oldest is dated eleven years ago, and the last line of the top one reads: *You will not be the first to leave.*

Scene 5

Teodor's room was two doors down from the lift. He opened it in shirtsleeves, a pencil behind his ear and the Ravel part open on the bed. She walked past him and set the stack on the desk. The rubber band lay in two pieces on top.

"Read the first one," she said. "Then the last line of any of them."

"Mara."

"Please."

He sat. He took the top sheet by its corners, as if it were hot, and read with his lips pressed flat. She watched the color leave him from the forehead down. He set it aside and took the next. Then he turned the stack over and looked at the postmark on the bottom envelope, and his thumb stopped moving.

"They're addressed to the second violin," she said. "Yours would be..."

"First Violin." He said it to the desk. "Since my second year. Three or four a season. They described my mistakes. Small ones, mostly. I burned them in the sink at my flat." He pinched the bridge of his nose. "I told myself it was a joke somebody had been running for a long time."

"Ines left. Paul left."

"Ines went to Lyon. Paul stopped playing." He squared the edges of the stack. "Eleven years, and every one of them has gone. I have never once asked why."

Down the corridor a door shut. Neither of them turned.

"Dani doesn't know," he said. "Neither does Wen."

He held the top letter out to her, then pulled it back.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She carries the stack to Teodor and asks him to read it. He goes pale and admits he has received letters like these for years, addressed to 'First Violin,' and burned them. He says the quartet has always lost its second player, and that he has never asked why. Now he must choose whether to help her or protect the group.

Scene 6

The argument went on down the corridor, low and fast, because the walls were thin.

"Eleven years," Mara said. "You burned them in a sink."

"I was twenty-three."

"You're thirty-four. You pulled that letter back just now."

"I pulled it back because I wanted to read the rest of it first."

"That's what I said."

"It is not what you said."

In her room she dragged the hangers left, and the rod shrieked. The panel stood open a hand's width where she had left it. Teodor looked at the gap, then at her, and went through first, turning his shoulders to fit.

The shelf was bare. The brittle rubber band and the stack were in his room, so she had expected nothing. Then she saw the corner of cream paper wedged behind the shelf bracket, flat against the wall, and she pointed.

*Teodor*, in blue-black ink.

He read it under the gray light from the air shaft. His jaw moved. "Listen to this." He read in a flat voice. "*You will say you never once asked why. She will say that is not the same as not knowing. You will hold out a letter and pull it back.* There's the pencil. It says pencil. It says behind my ear."

He gave her the sheet. She read the last line twice.

*Mara will break first. She will say his name before he says hers.*

Neither of them spoke. In the shaft, a pipe knocked once.

Mara and Teodor go to the hidden closet together and find a fresh envelope on the shelf, addressed to Teodor in the same blue-black ink. It describes in exact detail the argument they just had in his room, and ends with a line predicting which of them will break first.

Scene 7

"Give it here," Mara said.

Teodor folded the sheet in thirds and put it in his shirt pocket, behind the pencil he'd moved from his ear. "No. Listen. It's a script, so we don't follow it. I go to the hall. You go back to your room. Whatever it says we'll do, we do the other thing."

"And if it says that too?"

"Then we'll know something." He ducked out through the panel. She heard his shoes on the carpet, then the lift button's soft click.

She slid the panel shut, dragged the hangers back along the rod, and turned around.

A cream envelope lay on the bedspread, square in the center, her name on it. The chain on the door was still hooked. She had not been gone ten minutes.

She opened it standing up.

*You will read this on your feet. You will cross to the closet and stop with your palm flat against the panel. Then you will turn and take the violin case by its handle.*

She sat down on the floor, away from both.

Below a ruled gap, the ink changed pressure, harder.

*In the corridor Teodor stands at the lift with his thumb on the button. He has not pressed it. He is looking at the pencil in his pocket, not at the doors.*

Her mouth had gone dry. She listened. Past the wall, past the shaft, a long way off, the lift chimed once and did not open.

She didn't move her hand toward the case.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Teodor pockets the letter and suggests they test it: they will separate, he to the hall and she to the room, and each will do the opposite of whatever the letter says. Alone in the hotel room, Mara finds a new envelope on the bed describing her walking back to the closet and, below that, her reaching for the violin case, and she realizes the writer is describing Teodor's actions too.

Scene 8

Mara slid the panel shut behind her, and the seam closed with its dry whisper. The gray from the air shaft was the only light. She sat down on the carpet with her back against the shelf and her knees up, and she did not touch the case, because she had left it on the bed.

The pipe knocked once. After that she heard only her own breath.

She counted. At some number past four hundred, a line of yellow showed along the floor at the far end of the closet, where she had taken the wall for plain board. A latch turned. A second panel opened inward.

Dani stepped through in her black shoes, carrying a thermos and a small brass lamp with a cord wound around its base. She set the lamp on the shelf, clicked it on, and sat on an upturned crate that Mara had not noticed. Her coat was buttoned wrong by one button.

"You waited," Dani said. "Paul never did. He went looking for me."

"You were at every one of them," Mara said.

"Eleven. I found each of you a room. I sat with each of you after." Dani unscrewed the thermos and poured tea into its lid. She didn't drink it. From her inside pocket she took a pen, blue-black barrel, cap already off, and held it out across the lamplight, nib down, the way you pass scissors.

"Do you want to write the next one?"

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Mara goes back through the panel and slides it shut behind her, then sits in the other closet and waits in the dark. quiet horror

A night cleaner in an office tower notices that a desk on the tenth floor is used every night, though the floor has been empty for a year.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Marguerite pushed the cart off the freight elevator at ten past eleven and the motion lights on the tenth floor came on in sections, one bank after another, the way they had every night since the lease ended. Bare carpet tiles. Cubicle frames with the fabric panels stripped. A whiteboard someone had forgotten to wipe, its blue marker faded to the color of a vein.

She did the floor in the usual order: bathrooms first, then the kitchenette, then a pass with the dust mop down the center aisle. Nobody had touched it in a year, and the work was mostly for the log. Her supervisor wanted a checkmark beside every floor.

The desk was by the east windows. She had walked past it a hundred times. Tonight she stopped because the chair was pulled out.

It was the only chair left on the floor, black mesh, one armrest missing. It sat angled away from the desk, as though someone had just stood up. The desktop was clean. She ran a gloved finger across it and the glove came away without any dust at all. Four feet to either side, the carpet tiles had a gray film she could write her name in.

She looked at the chair for a while. Then she pushed it in, square to the desk, and went to empty the bins that had nothing in them.

When she came back around at half past one, it was pulled out again, and the seat was warm when she laid her palm flat against it.

Scene 2

Marguerite left the cart by the elevator and took the stairs down to the lobby, ten flights, one hand on the rail. Tomás sat behind the security desk with his shoes off, watching a soccer match on his phone propped against the monitor.

"Ten," she said. "Anyone badge in up there?"

"Ten's dead." He didn't look up. "Lease ended, they pulled the access. Only the freight key gets you there, and that's you."

"Somebody's been using a desk."

"Homeless, maybe. They come in behind deliveries." Now he looked at her, and then reached over and clicked through the camera feeds with a mouse worn smooth at the edges. Lobby, garage, loading dock, stairwell B. The tile for ten was a gray rectangle with a line of white text across it. NO SIGNAL.

"Since when?"

"Since they left. Nobody's paying to fix a camera on an empty floor." He pulled his phone closer. "You want, I'll walk up with you."

She looked at his socks, one with a hole at the heel. "No. It's fine."

"Probably the vents," he said. "Air moves things."

She stood a moment longer at the desk. On the dead tile, her own reflection showed faintly, a woman in a gray smock, holding the strap of her bag with both hands.

She took the freight elevator back up.

Scene 3

The motion lights came on in their usual order, bank after bank down the aisle, except for the last one by the east windows. That one was already lit when she stepped off the elevator.

The chair was pulled out again. She stood at the end of the aisle with her hands on the cart and counted to twenty. Nothing moved. The air smelled of carpet glue and, faintly, of coffee.

She wheeled the cart down, took a bucket of sweeping compound from the lower shelf, and scooped a handful. It was the green sawdust kind that smelled of pine and made her eyes itch. She sifted it over the carpet in a ring around the desk, a yard wide, the way she'd seen her mother lay salt across a doorway. The tiles went the color of a pond.

Then she opened the desk drawers, one at a time. Top: empty. Middle: empty. Bottom: a single pencil, sharpened, the shavings still pale and curled beneath it.

She closed the drawer with two fingers.

At the elevator she looked back. Her own boot prints ran out to the desk and back in two neat lines, and there was nothing else in the green. The chair sat angled toward the window. The bank of lights above it stayed on after hers had gone dark.

Scene 4

She did the bathrooms, the kitchenette, the center aisle. She did them slowly, and she did not look east until the mop had reached the far wall and there was nothing left on the floor to put off.

At half past one the lights over the desk were off. She wheeled the cart down anyway.

The ring was whole. Her boot prints ran in and out, two neat lines, and nothing else crossed the green. But the chair had moved. It sat square to the desk, pushed in the way she had pushed it the first night, and behind it, in the sawdust, ran two curved tracks from the wheels, out toward the window and back. The chair had gone somewhere and returned, and there were no feet beside it.

She stepped over the ring's edge. It crunched. The pine smell rose around her.

The bottom drawer was open an inch. She hadn't left it that way. The pencil lay on the desktop now, worn to a flat gray nub, and beside it, drawn in a column down the clean wood, were short upright strokes. They were grouped in fives, each group slashed through. She counted the groups with her finger hovering above them. Forty-one, and a last group of four.

The fourth stroke was still bright. When she tilted her head, it caught the light from the elevator.

She put her hands in her smock pockets and stood there, listening to the carpet glue tick in the walls.

Scene 5

She did not finish the floor. She wheeled the cart back to the freight elevator, rode down to the basement, and unlocked the supply room, where the log hung on a nail by the mop sink in a clear plastic sleeve.

It was a grid, one page per month. Floors ran down the left side, dates across the top, and she had put her initials in every box for as long as she had worked the building. M.D., M.D., in blue ballpoint. Her supervisor drew a line under each week.

She laid the pages on the lid of the laundry hamper and counted the boxes beside Ten with the tip of her pen. Nights she had worked, nights she had been sick and someone covered, a week in March she had gone to her sister's. She skipped those. She started over twice because she lost her place when the compressor kicked on behind the wall.

Two hundred and eight.

She counted again, slower, touching each set of initials, and got the same number.

On the shelf above her was the stack of gray pads she used under the bucket. She took one down and set it on the page, then took it off again. Tonight's box was empty. The pen was already in her hand.

She stood with the point resting on the paper, a small blue dot spreading in the white square.

Scene 6

She wrote the initials. M.D., in the square for tonight, over the blue dot, and the second letter came out heavier than the first.

Then she stood there with the sleeve in her hands. Two hundred and nine, if you counted the box she'd just filled. She counted it. The compressor behind the wall shuddered and went quiet.

She hung the log back on its nail, took it down again, and carried it to the freight elevator under her arm, tucked against her ribs the way she carried the mail at home.

On ten, every bank of lights was on. She had not seen that before. The aisle ran bright and flat to the windows, and the green ring around the desk looked like something spilled.

She crossed it without stopping. The chair was pulled out. The pencil lay in the groove at the edge of the desk, no longer than her thumb, and the column of strokes ran down the wood where she had left it. She counted the groups with the sleeve still under her arm. Forty-one. Then four.

She laid the log flat beside them, opened to the right page, and held her gloved finger over the last box of initials.

The seat of the chair was warm when the backs of her knees touched it. She had not decided to sit.

Scene 7

The lights went out behind her first, the bank by the elevator, then the next. Motion sensors, set to ten minutes. She had sat that long without moving.

The dark came down the aisle toward her one section at a time. She watched it in the east window, which had turned to a mirror as the room dimmed: the long floor, the cart small and pale by the elevator, a woman in a gray smock at a desk. The chair held her without creaking. The missing armrest left her right elbow hanging in air.

The last bank over the desk stayed on.

She did not look at the log. She looked at her hands, in their yellow gloves, resting on either side of it. Then she peeled the right glove off finger by finger and laid it on the desk, and the wood under her bare palm was warm too, evenly, like a table where someone had just finished eating.

The pencil lay in its groove. She picked it up. It was shorter than she'd thought, the flat gray nub rubbed smooth on one side, and her thumb went to the smooth place without searching. Her first two fingers closed where the paint was worn through.

Down in the green ring, nothing shifted. The compressor started somewhere under the floor, ten stories below, and she felt it in the soles of her boots.

Scene 8

The pencil would not take a point anymore. She set the flat gray nub against the wood below the last group and drew the fifth stroke, and it went down easily, as if the line had been waiting there.

Then she laid the slash across all five, corner to corner, and the group stood complete beside the other forty-one. She put the pencil in its groove.

Her bare hand stayed on the desk. The warmth in the wood had not changed.

Behind her the freight elevator opened. She knew the sound, the rubber lip of the door and the small chime that Tomás had never gotten fixed. A cart wheel with a bad bearing started up the carpet, ticking every third turn.

The lights came on in sections. She watched them arrive in the east window: the bank by the elevator, then the next, then the next, each one laying a pale square over the green ring and moving on. The reflection of the floor grew longer and brighter, and in the middle of it sat a woman in a gray smock with one glove off.

The cart stopped at the end of the aisle.

She did not turn around. She picked up the pencil again, though there was nothing left to count, and held it over the wood. Nobody said her name. Somewhere below, the compressor shut off, and the chair took her weight evenly, the way it always had.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

At eleven she carried the cart up the stairwell instead of taking the elevator, because the elevator no longer stopped at ten. The key to the stairwell door was still on her ring, between the supply closet and the loading dock.

The floor smelled of carpet glue and shut-up air. Cubicles stood in rows with their monitors gone. Only the desk by the east window had a chair, and the chair was pulled out from it by a hand's width, as it had been every night that week.

Marta tore a strip of masking tape from the roll in her apron. She pressed it across the seam of the top drawer, one end on the frame, one on the drawer front, and smoothed it flat with her thumb. Then she went back to the stairwell door. She tied a length of black sewing thread to the push bar at ankle height and ran it across the landing to the railing, pulled tight enough to hum when she flicked it.

She did not look back at the desk when she left.

She mopped eight and nine, emptied the bins on seven, and stayed away from the clock until it said ten past six. Then she climbed.

The thread was still taut. She touched it with one finger and it sang.

Inside, the chair was out. The tape on the frame had curled up, its sticky side gray with lint, and the end on the drawer front was still pressed down flat.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Marta sets a small trap, placing a strip of tape across the desk drawer and a thread across the stairwell door, then finishes her shift on another floor. Returning at dawn, she finds the thread intact and the tape peeled back from the inside, which suggests whatever uses the desk never came through the door.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 During her usual rounds, the cleaner, Marta, finds the tenth-floor desk warm, with a fresh coffee ring on the wood and the chair pushed out. She wipes it away and tells no one, but when she returns the next night the ring is back in exactly the same place.
  • 1.00 Marta asks the day security guard about the tenth floor, and he flatly insists the floor was sealed and the elevator locked out a year ago. When she checks her keycard log, it shows her own stops on ten every night, including nights she swears she skipped it.
  • 1.00 Marta finds a stack of paperwork on the desk that has been updated nightly, in handwriting that slowly begins to resemble her own. She takes one page home to compare it, and the next night a new note on the desk says only, 'You kept my place.'

Scene 2

She told the dispatcher she was sick and then did not go home. At ten to eleven she let herself into the supply closet on seven, pulled the door shut, and sat on an upturned bucket between the floor wax and the paper towels. She left the light off. A strip of gray came under the door from the emergency lamp in the hall.

The building ticked as it cooled. Pipes knocked once and went quiet. She checked her watch by its green face: midnight, then one, then ten past. Her knees ached. She ate a mint from her apron pocket and held the wrapper in her fist so it wouldn't crackle.

At two the chair scraped.

It came from directly overhead, thin and dragging, carried down through the building's ductwork and out of the vent grille in the closet ceiling. Marta stopped breathing through her nose. Wood on carpet, then the small creak of weight settling into a seat.

Nothing for a long time. Paper turned, once.

Then the chair eased back, and steps started across the floor of ten. They were slow and even. They did not go toward the stairwell door. She followed them by the sound, past where the cubicles would be, past the columns, until they stood somewhere above her and the duct began to hum faintly in its throat.

The steps stopped. Something leaned close to the vent, and the grille over her head gave off a soft, wet sound, like a mouth opening.

Scene 3

She was out of the closet before she knew she had stood. The bucket rang against the shelf behind her. She hit the stairwell door with both palms and took the steps two at a time, one hand dragging the rail, her breath loud in the concrete shaft.

On the ninth landing her shin broke something fine and taut. She felt it part, a small give, and did not stop.

The door to ten was shut. She pushed it open.

Light. Not the gray of the emergency lamps but a yellow pool at the east window, small and steady. The desk lamp. She had coiled its cord on Tuesday and left the plug lying on the carpet, and it lay there now, three feet from the outlet, its prongs bare.

The floor was empty. The chair was pulled out. She walked the length of the cubicle rows with her keys clenched between her fingers and heard only her own shoes.

On the blotter lay a facilities form, the pink carbon kind. Half the boxes were filled in. *Reported by:* M. Ilves. *Location:* 10, east. The sevens had the little bar through them. The 4 was open at the top, the way she had made it since school.

*Date:* the next day.

The pen lay across the form with its cap off. She touched the seat of the chair with the back of her hand. It was warm.

She stood over the form for a while with her keys still bunched in her fist. Then she opened her hand and let them drop into her apron, and picked up the pen.

It was warm too. The barrel was a cheap blue plastic one with the end chewed flat. She bent over the blotter, and the chair, when she put her knee against it for balance, shifted a little under her.

*Description of problem.* The box was small. She printed in it the way she did on every pink form: *Chair moved nightly. Drawer opened. Noise in vent, 7th fl closet, approx 2 a.m. Person unknown.* Her sevens had their little bars. Halfway through *unknown* the ink began to skip, and she pressed harder and finished the word in grooves.

The lamp dimmed. It did not flicker. The yellow simply drew back across the blotter, over the form and her wrist, as if someone were turning a dial with great patience.

Behind her the carpet creaked.

It creaked again a pace later, and then again. The weight was unhurried and it was coming up the aisle between the cubicles. She kept the pen on the paper. Her thumb was cramped white around it.

She turned.

No one stood in the aisle. The chair was pushed in under the desk, flush, its back square against the edge, and the lamp had gone down to a dull orange thread.

Scene 5

She left the form where it was, pen laid across it, and went out through the stairwell door without looking at the lamp.

On the landing the thread hung from the railing in two short lengths, stirring slightly. She started down. One flight, the turn, a second flight. Where the door to nine should have been there was only a wall of painted concrete, the same gray as the rest, with no handle, no hinge, no stenciled 9. She laid her palm flat against it. It was dry and cool. The paint had no seam.

"Okay," she said. Her voice went down the shaft and did not come back.

She kept going down, and the stairs turned and rose. She counted twenty steps up, then another twenty, her hand sliding on the rail, until a landing opened under her and there was a door with a 10 on it, steel, with her own smudged thumbprint low on the push bar.

Beside it stood another door. It was the same steel, with the same stencil and the same dent in the corner.

She stood between them with her keys out. Then she took the second one.

It opened without a sound. The lamp was lit, yellow and full. At the desk a woman sat with her back to the aisle, in a gray apron with the pockets sagging. Her head was bent. A pen scratched steadily across a pink form.

She takes the second, and it opens onto the same floor with the lamp lit and a woman in her apron sitting at the desk with her back turned, filling in a form.

Scene 6

She crossed the floor without letting her shoes land heavy. The carpet took each step and gave nothing back. Past the columns, past the cubicle where the ceiling tile hung crooked, the lamp grew warmer on her hands. The woman did not turn.

Marta stopped an arm's length behind the chair. She could see the woman's hair, pulled back with a black elastic, the same kind she bought in packs of twenty. Beneath the gray apron the shoulder blades moved with each stroke of the pen, small and steady, like someone sewing.

She leaned and read over the shoulder.

*Chair moved nightly. Drawer opened. Noise in vent, 7th fl closet, approx 2 a.m. Person unknown.* The word *unknown* ended in grooves. Every seven had its bar.

Below it, in the box marked *Action taken*, the pen was still moving.

*Cleaner crosses floor. Keys in left hand.*

She looked down. The keys were in her left hand, the ring cutting into her palm. She opened her fingers and they hung from her thumb, ticking against each other.

*Stops behind chair. Reads.*

The ink was wet and very black. It had not skipped once. The pen reached the end of the line and dropped to the next without a pause, and Marta watched the letters coming, one after another, a little ahead of her breath.

Scene 7

She did not decide. Her hand went over the woman's shoulder and closed on the pen, and it came out of the fingers easily, as if it had been waiting to be taken. The barrel was warm and the chewed end pressed into her palm.

The woman did not flinch. Her head stayed bent.

Marta leaned down and put the tip to the form, just under *Keys in left hand*, and wrote hard, in the same square print. *Cleaner walks out and goes home.* The ink came out blue and ordinary. She dotted nothing, crossed the *t*, and her sevens were not needed, and she was glad of that for no reason she could name.

The woman's hand was still moving.

It lay on the blotter, fingers curled around nothing, and it traveled along the next line with the same small, patient strokes. There was no pen in it. The nails scratched faintly on the paper.

Marta watched her own sentence. The *C* went soft at the edges. The blue spread into the fibers and thinned, the way a drop of water goes into a rag, and the carbon beneath it took it down. *Walks out* lost its shape. *Goes home* held a moment longer, then sank.

Under the woman's fingers the paper stayed dry and pink and blank. The keys ticked once against Marta's thumb.

Scene 8

She pinched the top edge of the form and pulled. It came away from the pad with a dry ripping sound, the glued strip peeling in a long white curl. Her own sentence was gone from it. The rest was still there, *Cleaner crosses floor, Stops behind chair, Reads*, and she folded it in thirds along the creases it already seemed to have and pushed it into her apron, under the roll of tape.

The lamp went out. There was no flicker. The dark simply arrived.

The chair was empty. She put her hand on the seat and felt nothing, not even the warmth. The pen was gone from her fingers, though she had not set it down.

She stood until her eyes found the room. Then she saw that it was not dark. Along every aisle, in every cubicle, a monitor had come on, each one pale pink at the center. She stepped to the nearest. A form filled the screen, the carbon kind, its boxes crowded with square print. *Reported by: M. Ilves.* The sevens had their bars. The 4 was open at the top. The date was in March.

The next screen held another. The date was in April.

She turned. The rows ran east past the window, where there should have been glass and the lights of the next tower. They ran north and south past the columns and the walls. Screen after screen glowed down the long aisles, each with its pink page, getting smaller until she could no longer read them.

C: Fixed

Scene 1

Ines had been vacuuming the tenth floor for a year, and for most of that year she had not thought about the desk by the east window. Tonight she thought about it. The chair was pulled out from the desk at an angle, as if someone had just stood up. Every other chair on the floor was pushed in and shrouded in a fine gray fur.

She took a paperclip from her apron pocket and bent it into a hook with a small kink in the tail. She set it in the middle of the blotter, the hook facing the window. Then she stood there feeling foolish, a grown woman arranging evidence for a crime that was only a chair.

She did the bins on nine, then the restrooms on nine, and rode the service elevator back up forty minutes later. The floor was as she'd left it. The ceiling panels hummed, and a copier standby light glowed red in the dark.

The blotter was bare.

She checked the floor beneath the desk and the drawer pulls. Nothing. Then she walked to the elevator lobby, where she always parked her cart, with the front left wheel against the seam between two carpet tiles, beside the pillar.

The paperclip lay on the seam, hook facing the window, its kinked tail an inch from where the wheel would sit.

Ines looked at it for a long time before she rolled the cart forward and stopped it just short.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She leaves a small marked object on the desk, such as a paperclip arranged in a particular shape, to test whether anything is truly touched. When she returns on her next pass, the paperclip has been moved to the exact spot where she herself usually leaves her cleaning cart, as if the desk's user is watching her routine.

She tells herself a security guard must be sneaking naps there, but the dust on every other surface is undisturbed, and she realizes she has been cleaning around this desk for weeks without questioning it.
  • 1.00 The cleaner checks the building's sign-in log and the elevator records at the security desk, hoping for a mundane explanation. The night guard shrugs and says nobody has gone up to ten in a year, and then, a little too casually, asks her not to mention the floor to anyone else, which makes her suspect he already knows.
  • 1.00 The cleaner sits at the desk for a moment to rest her feet, and finds the drawer slightly open with a name tag inside bearing the name of a former employee who left the company a year ago. When she looks up, the lights at the far end of the floor click off one row at a time, and she realizes she has stayed past the hour when she normally goes down.

Scene 2

Ines left the cart by the pillar and walked back to the east window. The paperclip stayed on the seam behind her.

The top drawer slid out easily. Pens, a stapler, a roll of stamps. The second held a cardigan folded in thirds, oatmeal-colored, with one leather button replaced by a plastic one that didn't match. She lifted it. It smelled faintly of the hand cream she kept in her apron, the cheap one with almond in it. She put it back exactly as it had lain.

The third drawer held a tin of mints, the flat kind with a hinged lid. Two were left. Under the tin was a newspaper folded to the crossword, a pen clipped to the corner.

It was half done. Seven across, *ESCAPADE*. Twelve down, *LANTERN*. She read the letters twice. The sevens had a bar through the stem, the way her mother had taught her, the way nobody here did. Ines didn't do crosswords at work. She did them at her kitchen table on Sundays, and she never finished them.

Fourteen down was blank. *Something kept, five letters.*

Her knees ached. She looked at the chair, still angled out from the desk, and sat, only to think, only to take the weight off. The vinyl gave under her with a small sigh.

It was warm. Not the warmth of a seat in sun. The warmth went all the way through, as if someone had just risen from it, and she could feel it settle against the backs of her legs.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ines opens the desk drawers and finds ordinary things: a cardigan, a tin of mints, a half-finished crossword with the clues answered in her own handwriting. She sits in the pulled-out chair to think, and the seat is warm.

Over the following nights each item is returned to a spot where she would have put it herself, and she sees that whoever uses the desk is learning her routines.

Scene 3

The pen was in her hand before she decided to take it. It was a cheap ballpoint, and the cap end was chewed flat.

Fourteen down. *Something kept.* She counted the squares with the pen tip and got six. She looked at the clue again. It said *(6)*. She had read five. She was nearly sure she had read five.

She wrote SECRET in small capitals, the way she did on Sundays, and the letters went down without any trouble. The E at the crossing matched the E already there.

The chair held its warmth against her legs. She stood, and the vinyl sighed again behind her.

Under the desk lamp the grid looked different. Not much. Seven across was still *ESCAPADE*. But thirty-one across, which she remembered as blank, now read MARTA, her sister's name, in the same slanting hand as the sevens. Below it, running down from the A, ALDER, her street, with the D squeezed into a square that was too small for it. Near the bottom corner, in letters pressed hard enough to dent the newsprint, CHUCHURRÍO. The accent was there. She said that word to the basil on her windowsill. She said it to no one else, and only when the kitchen door was shut.

She put the pen down exactly where it had been clipped. Then she picked it up again and looked at the chewed end, and held it a long moment before she set it back.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ines stays in the warm chair and fills in fourteen down with the pen, writing SECRET, then stands to find the crossword's other half-finished clues have changed. Several now hold words from her own life: her sister's name, her street, a word she only ever said aloud in her kitchen.

Scene 4

She did not decide until the end of her shift. At 4:40 she opened the second drawer, lifted the cardigan out, and pushed it into her tote bag under the thermos and the folded plastic raincoat. It took up less room than she expected.

On the bus she held the bag on her lap with both arms around it. At home she set it on the kitchen table, under the light, and looked at the plastic button, the cream-colored one with four holes that didn't match. She had the sewing scissors in her hand. She put them down again.

She hung the cardigan on the back of the kitchen door and shut the door's latch, which she never did. Then she lay on top of her bedspread in her work clothes and listened for the kitchen. The refrigerator cycled twice. Nothing else happened. At noon she went in and the cardigan was still on its hook, and she stood looking at it with her hand flat on her chest.

That night the elevator opened on ten at 1:55. She went straight to the east window.

The second drawer slid out on its own weight. The cardigan lay inside, oatmeal-colored, folded in thirds.

She turned it over. The plastic button was gone. In its place was a leather one, worn dark at the edge, sewn with the same brown thread as the others.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ines takes the cardigan from the second drawer and carries it home, hoping that moving it will break the pattern. The next night the cardigan is back in the drawer, and the plastic button has been replaced by a leather one that matches the rest.

Scene 5

She stopped wiping the desk. The vacuum went around its legs and the cart stayed by the pillar, and the paperclip stayed on the seam where she'd left it.

On Monday she set one mint on the blotter, still in its wrapper, from the bag in her apron. When she came back from nine, the mint was gone and the wrapper lay beside the lamp, smoothed flat and folded into a small square, the way she folded them herself.

On Tuesday she left a black hair tie, one she'd worn that morning, with two of her hairs still in it. Wednesday it was looped twice around the neck of the pen, snug, the pen standing upright in the cup.

On Thursday she wrote on the back of a receipt, in the pencil stub she kept for the supply log: *Fry the garlic until the oil gets shy.* It was her mother's phrase. Her mother had said it in the kitchen on Alder Street, with her back turned, and Ines had never seen it written anywhere. She propped the receipt against the lamp and went down to nine and scrubbed a sink that was already clean.

When she returned the receipt had been turned over. Beneath her line, in the slanting hand with the barred sevens, it said: *And then the tomatoes, and you stand there and wait. You never could wait.*

She stood a long time without touching it. Her mother had said that too.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

She stops cleaning the desk and begins leaving small things on it each night: a mint, a hair tie, a line from her mother's recipe. Each morning the objects have been moved or used, and one night a reply is waiting. The exchange is gentle and intimate, and it unsettles her more than any fright could.

Scene 6

At handover Tomasz was pouring coffee into the lid of his thermos. Ines waited until he had drunk some.

"Who had the tenth floor? Before it closed."

"Nobody. The lease ended a year ago." He screwed the cup back on. "It's not on your contract. Nobody told you to go up there."

"I know."

"Then why are you asking?"

"There's a desk by the east window."

He looked at the monitors instead of her. A long time passed. "A woman had it," he said. "She stayed late. The morning crew found her there, sitting up, like she was reading. Then the firm left." He rubbed his thumb along the counter's edge. "I don't know her name. Try the lease files, in the basement."

The basement smelled of wet cardboard. The files stood in gray cabinets with typed labels, and under *10 – Tenancy* she found a drawer of index cards, one per desk. She went through them with a wetted thumb. *10-E*, east window.

The card was typed except for the signature line. The slant was unmistakable, and the sevens in the date had bars through their stems.

*Inés*, with the accent she never bothered with on her timesheet. Her own surname after it, all of it.

The date at the top was three years before her first shift in the building. Across the bottom, in different ink, someone had written *vacated*, and a date a year gone.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ines searches the building's records, asking the day security guard and checking old lease files in the basement, and learns that the tenth floor's last occupant was a woman who died at that desk a year ago. The woman's name is Ines's own, in the same slanting hand, on a tenancy card that predates Ines's employment.

Scene 7

She carried the card up in her apron pocket, against the hip, and the elevator opened on ten at 2:05. She did not go to the pillar. She went to the east window and laid the card on the blotter beside the crossword, squared to the edge, the signature toward the lamp.

Then she did not leave. She stood with her hands in her apron, and the ceiling panels hummed. At nine, the sinks would be waiting for her. She pulled out the chair, which was already angled, and turned it a few degrees more toward herself, and sat.

The vinyl was warm before her weight settled.

She waited. A pipe ticked somewhere above the ceiling tiles. The copier's red light glowed. Her own breath sounded loud to her, and she made it quieter.

Slowly, with no sound but the swivel's faint dry creak, the chair began to turn. It carried her around until her knees pointed at the desk and then past it, until she faced the crossword square on. She had not pushed with her feet. She looked down at them to be sure.

The pen lay in its clip. It didn't lift. The ink simply arrived, a thin line drawn under SECRET, ruled straight. Beside it, in capitals pressed hard enough to dent the newsprint:

VIGIL

Five squares. The V crossed the V of *VERSE* already there.

It was what her mother had called sitting up with the dying, in two languages. Ines had never said it aloud about herself.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ines takes the index card upstairs and lays it on the blotter beside the crossword, then waits at the desk instead of going down to nine. The chair slowly angles toward her, and a line appears under the clue for fourteen down, correcting SECRET to a five-letter word that she realizes is her own name for what she has been keeping.

Scene 8

She stood, and the chair went on turning a quarter inch after she let go.

The second drawer slid out under her fingers. She lifted the cardigan, shook it once, and hung it over the back of the chair, the leather button between the shoulder blades. She smoothed the collar flat. The wool was neither warm nor cold under her hand. It was only wool.

The card lay on the blotter where she'd squared it. She read the slanted signature one last time and tore the card once across. The paper was old and gave easily. She laid the halves side by side, their edges not quite meeting.

The pen rolled out of its clip. It crossed the grid, over SECRET and over VIGIL, and stopped against the base of the lamp with a small click.

Behind the desk the chair swiveled, slowly, with its dry creak, until the cardigan faced the elevator lobby, the pillar, the cart with its wheel against the seam.

Ines took the service elevator down to nine. In the restroom every tap was running, all five, full and cold, the basins loud with it. She did not turn them off. She held her hands under the nearest one, then dried them on a paper towel, between the fingers, the way she always did. The water stopped behind her when she reached the door.

On ten the lamp was still lit. She pulled the chair out from under the cardigan, sat, and felt the warmth come up through the vinyl to meet her.
