family drama

A newly qualified nurse takes a post at a clinic on a tidal island, where the road floods twice a day and the only doctor has stopped coming back.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

The tide table was nailed to a post at the mainland end of the causeway, the times chalked over the printed ones. Ruth Adeyemi read it twice with the engine running. A man in a van pulled up beside her and wound down his window.

"You're the new nurse. You've got forty minutes, maybe thirty-five. Don't stop for the seals."

She didn't stop. The road was a grey strip with wet sand rippled on both sides, and marker poles stood in the mud with orange lifebelts on top. Halfway across, her phone buzzed on the passenger seat. *Mum.* She let it ring out.

The clinic was a single-storey building with a ramp and a hand-painted sign. The door was unlocked. Inside, a woman in a cardigan sat behind the desk with a mug in both hands.

"Mrs. Collick," she said. "Reception, cleaning, and whatever else."

"Is Dr. Hale in?"

"Dr. Hale went over for his prescriptions on the ninth." Mrs. Collick nodded at the wall calendar. The squares were crossed off up to yesterday. "Nine days now."

His waxed jacket hung on a hook behind the door. An appointment book lay open on the desk, with names written in a tight, slanting hand down to the bottom of the page.

Ruth took her lanyard from her bag and hung it on the hook beside the jacket. Outside, the first thin line of water slid across the sand.

Scene 2

Mrs. Collick showed her the treatment room: a couch, a sink, a glass-fronted cabinet with a padlock the size of a fist.

"Keys?" Ruth asked.

"Dr. Hale has those. Had those." Mrs. Collick opened the desk drawer, looked in it, and shut it again. "There's a spare set at his house. Up the lane, blue door. I'm not going in without him."

The appointment book had four names for today. The first was already in the waiting room, a man in his seventies with his trouser leg rolled to the knee and a dressing gone yellow at the edges. He introduced himself as Mr. Pascoe and kept his eyes on the window while she cut the bandage away.

"He does it with the green tape," he said. "Not the white."

"I'll find the green tape."

The ulcer was wet but clean, the skin around it pink and not hot. She photographed it, measured it, and wrote the numbers on a sheet. In the margin of his notes, in Hale's slanting hand, was a column of earlier measurements. They stopped on the eighth.

While she dressed the leg, her phone buzzed on the counter. She turned it face down. It buzzed again and a message slid up: *Ring me. It's about Sunday.*

"Your mother?" said Mr. Pascoe.

"Yes."

"Ring her," he said. "I'm not going anywhere. Tide's in."

Scene 3

Ruth took the phone out to the ramp. The causeway had gone. Where the road had been there was flat brown water with the marker poles standing up out of it, the lifebelts level with the surface.

Her mother answered on the first ring. "You're not working?"

"I'm on a step. I've got five minutes."

"Sunday's at one. Funmi booked the Italian place, the one with the garden. Your father thinks it's just us." A pause, and the sound of a tap running. "Funmi says you took this job so you'd have a reason."

"The road floods, Mum. Twice a day. I can't promise what time I'd get across."

"Then leave on Saturday night."

"The doctor's missing. I'm the only one here."

"Missing?" The tap stopped. "Ruth."

"He's gone to the mainland for prescriptions and hasn't come back. That's all. It's not a story."

Her mother said nothing for a while. A gull stood on the nearest pole and looked at her.

"Sixty," her mother said. "He won't say it, but he's counting."

"I'll ring you Friday."

"Ring me Thursday."

Ruth said she would. Behind her the door opened and Mrs. Collick held out the tin of tape, green side up.

"Found it in the dresser," she said. "Mr. Pascoe's asking if you want tea."

Up the lane, a blue door stood shut among the grey ones.

Scene 4

Ruth went up the lane after the last patient, while the sand was still shining wet below the sea wall. The blue door had a brass knocker shaped like a fish. She knocked twice.

The woman who opened it was about forty, barefoot, in a man's jumper with the cuffs pushed up. She held a tea towel and didn't look surprised.

"You're from the clinic."

"Ruth Adeyemi. I need the spare keys, for the drug cabinet. Mrs. Collick said they'd be here."

"Mrs. Collick wouldn't come up herself." The woman stepped back to let her in. "I'm Tamsin. His daughter."

The hallway smelled of woodsmoke and old coats. A waxed jacket hung on a peg, identical to the one at the clinic. Tamsin saw her looking.

"He has two. Had." She went into the kitchen and lifted a ring of keys from a nail by the window. There were six, one with a strip of green tape wound round it. "That one's the cabinet."

"Has he rung you?"

"He rings on Sundays. This Sunday he didn't." Tamsin dried her hands slowly, finger by finger. "Don't tell Mrs. Collick I said so. She'd start crossing off the calendar in red."

She put the keys in Ruth's palm and closed Ruth's fingers over them.

Scene 5

Back at the clinic, Mrs. Collick had her coat on and was winding a scarf twice round her neck. She looked at the keys in Ruth's hand and then at the window.

"She was in, then."

"She was." Ruth went through to the treatment room. The green-taped key turned the padlock on the second try.

Inside, the shelves were orderly: insulin in the small fridge, dressings by size, two boxes of diazepam, one of morphine ampoules. The controlled drugs register lay on the bottom shelf. She counted the ampoules twice, with the door of the cabinet propped against her hip. Eight. The register said eight. Hale's last entry was the seventh, a single ampoule, initialled *J.H.* The ink had a faint shine where he'd pressed hard.

Mrs. Collick appeared in the doorway. "Does it tally?"

"It tallies."

"He's careful."

Ruth wrote the date, the count, and her own initials under his, in a hand that looked round and young beside the slant. She locked the padlock and dropped the keys into her breast pocket, where they dragged the fabric down.

"Did she say anything?" Mrs. Collick asked.

"She said the green key was the cabinet."

Mrs. Collick nodded slowly and picked up her bag. "Tide's off at seven," she said. "I'll leave the lamp on."

Scene 6

The lamp was on, as promised. Ruth sat at the desk with the appointment book and turned to tomorrow. Five names, none she knew. She opened the drawer Mrs. Collick had shut that morning, looking for a pen.

Under a roll of stamps and a tin of drawing pins lay a bundle of envelopes with a hospital's franking on them, held by an elastic band gone soft with age. All were addressed to *Dr. J. Hale*. She slid the band off. Four were unopened. The fifth had been slit along the top with a knife, neatly, and refolded.

She read the first lines standing up. *Cardiology Outpatients. Appointment: 9th, 10:40. Please bring a list of current medications.*

Below it was a second sheet, in the same slanting hand she'd seen all day in the margins. It was a list of drugs with doses, none of them in the cabinet behind her. At the bottom he'd written *ask re: dizziness on stairs* and underlined it once.

Outside, the water was pulling off the sand with a hiss. Her phone lit up on the blotter. Funmi: *Dad asked what you'd like to eat Sunday. Just give me a dish.*

Ruth folded the letter along its creases and put it back in its envelope. She put the envelopes in the drawer, band and all, and then took them out again and slid them into her bag.

Scene 7

Ruth was at the blue door at ten to seven, with the envelopes in her coat pocket and the sand still glistening on both sides of the lane. Tamsin opened it before she knocked. She was dressed this time, boots on, a mug in her hand.

"You've not slept."

"Some." Ruth held out the bundle. "These were in the clinic desk. Mrs. Collick may not know. One's been opened."

Tamsin sat down at the kitchen table and took off the elastic band. She read the appointment letter first, then the second sheet, moving her lips slightly at the drug names. When she reached *dizziness on stairs* she put her thumb over the line.

"The ninth," she said. "He told me he was going for his tablets. Said it like he was popping to the chemist."

"I don't know that anything's happened to him. I only know he had an appointment."

"Cardiology doesn't phone you if you miss it. It sends another letter." Tamsin tapped the unopened ones. "Which he'd never see."

She drank the tea standing up, took a set of car keys from the nail where the clinic keys had hung, and lifted the waxed jacket off its peg. She looked at it, then put it back.

"Tide's off till one," she said. "Can you leave Mrs. Collick the book?"

"I can ring her from the car."

On the causeway the last water was draining off the tarmac, and the lifebelts stood clear of the mud.

Scene 8

The hospital car park was pay-on-exit. Tamsin drove round it twice before she found a space, then sat with her hands on the wheel until Ruth got out and shut her own door, and Tamsin followed.

At the cardiology desk a clerk typed the surname, frowned, and typed it again. "He didn't attend on the ninth. But there's an admission that evening, through Emergency. Ward 14."

The ward sister met them at the double doors. "Family?"

"Daughter," Tamsin said. Her voice came out smaller than it had in the kitchen.

"He's been asking us not to ring anybody. He said there was nobody on the mainland, and the island would manage." The sister looked at Ruth's lanyard. "You're from his clinic?"

"I'm covering it."

"Bay three. He's stable. He's been doing the crossword in biro, which I'm told is a sign."

Through the glass, Hale sat propped on two pillows in a hospital gown, reading glasses on a cord, a folded newspaper on his knee. He looked smaller than his jacket. He looked up and saw his daughter, and his pen stopped.

Tamsin went in. Ruth stayed at the door.

"Did she find the green tape?" Hale said, past Tamsin's shoulder. His voice was dry and unsteady.

"Mrs. Collick did," Ruth said.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. *Funmi: Dish?* She stood in the corridor and typed *Jollof. I'll be there by one,* and watched the word *Delivered* appear.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The water came across the causeway in thin sheets first, sliding over the tarmac from both sides, and Imogen kept driving until the Fiesta's wheels began to hiss. Then the engine coughed and died. She turned the key twice. Seawater was already at the sills, brown and busy with weed.

A horn sounded behind her. A tractor came down the slope with its wheels throwing up wakes, and a man leaned across and shoved the passenger door open before she'd reached for the handle.

"Leave it. Bag, now."

She climbed up with her holdall and her good shoes in her hand. The cab smelled of diesel and wet wool. He was sixty, perhaps, with salt-cracked knuckles, and he didn't look at her until the tractor had lurched forward again.

"You're the nurse."

"Imogen Hale."

"Tom Peverell. My brother's the doctor." He said it flatly, watching the road marker poles. "Was."

"Was?"

"Is. Whatever he is." The water slapped the undercarriage. "That agency told you it's a quiet post. Gentle. Sea air."

"They said it was well-supported."

Tom laughed once, without any pleasure. "Go back on the next low tide. Quarter to four in the morning. Don't unpack."

The island rose ahead, grey roofs and a squat white building with a blue lamp over its door. He stopped beside it and didn't switch off the engine.

"Why?" she said.

He stared at the clinic windows. "Mind the step," he said. "It's loose."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imogen is nearly caught by the rising water on the causeway and is pulled into a tractor cab by a local fisherman. He turns out to be the doctor's brother, and on the drive he warns her the clinic is not what the agency told her and that she should leave on the next low tide. She gets out at the clinic with his warning unresolved.

  • 1.00 Imogen arrives to find the doctor's family living in the flat above the clinic: his wife, who is polite and evasive, and a teenage daughter who watches her closely. They insist he is only 'on the mainland', and the wife hands Imogen his keys without being asked, as if to settle something between them.
  • 1.00 On her first evening Imogen opens the clinic's patient ledger and finds the doctor's handwriting ending mid-entry three weeks ago, beside a series of house calls to the same remote cottage. A call comes in from that cottage, and she has to decide whether to take it alone before the tide cuts her off.

Scene 2

The step shifted under her heel, and Imogen stepped over it. Behind her the tractor's engine idled a moment longer, then dragged away up the lane.

The door was unlocked. Inside, the clinic smelled of floor polish and damp coats. A row of plastic chairs stood empty under a noticeboard of vaccination posters, and a radiator ticked. Nobody sat at the reception hatch. She rang the brass bell and listened to it fade.

"Hello? Imogen Hale. The agency sent me."

Two treatment rooms, both tidy, the couch paper in each torn off and not replaced. At the end of the corridor a third door had a frosted glass panel and a brass plate: *Dr. A. Peverell*. She turned the handle. Locked.

She cupped her hands to the glass. The desk was a smear of shapes, but she could make out a plate with a fork lying across it, a mug, and a long printed sheet pinned flat under a stapler, its margins crowded with blue ink.

A key hung on a nail beside the fire extinguisher, tagged in the same blue ink: *Consulting*. She took it down. It turned stiffly.

The toast on the plate had gone green at the edges. The tide table was for the whole month, every crossing circled, and the figures were scribbled over with minutes and arrows and the same word, again and again: *Tom*.

In the top drawer lay a stack of envelopes, each addressed *Tom Peverell, Harbour Farm*. None had been stamped. The topmost was open.

*Tom,* it began. *I know you'll say*

She put it back and picked up the next.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Ignoring Tom's warning, Imogen walks through the clinic and finds Dr. Peverell's consulting room locked, with a half-eaten meal and a tide table covered in his handwriting on the desk. When she picks the lock with a key hanging by the door, she finds a stack of unsent letters addressed to Tom, and that suggests the brothers' estrangement is the real reason he has stopped coming back.

Scene 3

The phone on the desk was black, with a curled cord, and it rang so suddenly that the envelope jumped in her hand. It rang four times. She put the letter down on the tide table and lifted the receiver.

"Island clinic."

Breathing, then a hoarse voice, pitched low as if someone might be standing near him. Behind it she could hear a hollow echo and a distant tannoy.

"Has Tom sent you?"

"I'm Imogen Hale. The agency—"

"Thank God." He coughed. "Thank God. Listen, I haven't long. The controlled drugs key is taped under the second drawer of that desk. Not the top. The cupboard's in Room Two, behind the sharps bin. Count everything before you sign anything."

She was already crouching. Her fingers found tape, then a small cold key. "Dr. Peverell?"

"The notes for the housebound are in the green folders, bottom of the grey cabinet. Mrs. Quill's on top. She'll tell you she's fine."

"Where are you?"

"Please don't tell Tom I rang. Whatever he says to you. Promise me that."

The radiator ticked. On the desk the blue ink ran in arrows across the month of crossings.

"When are you coming back?" she said.

The line clicked, and then there was only the tone, long and level, in her ear.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

A phone on the doctor's desk rings, and when Imogen answers, Dr. Peverell's voice comes from the mainland, hoarse and relieved, asking whether Tom has sent her. He tells her where the controlled drugs key and patient notes are, begs her not to tell Tom he called, and hangs up when she asks when he's coming back.

Scene 4

Mrs. Quill's cottage was the last before the dunes, with a lobster pot for a doorstop and a bell pull instead of a bell. Imogen had the green folder under her arm and sand in her good shoes.

"I'm fine," said Mrs. Quill, before the door was fully open. She was tiny, upright, in a cardigan buttoned wrongly by one hole. "You can write that down."

"I'd still like to check your blood pressure."

"Then you'll do it in the kitchen. I'm not having it done in the front room like a sickbed."

The cuff hissed. Imogen watched the dial and the dresser behind it. Among the Toby jugs stood a plastic pill organiser, seven days, the lids labelled in small blue capitals. THURS. FRI. SAT. The ink was the same as on the tide table. The Thursday compartment was empty. Friday's was full.

"Someone's been busy," Imogen said.

"My niece."

"Your niece writes like a doctor?"

Mrs. Quill took her arm back and rolled the sleeve down, slowly, one fold at a time. "Don't tell Tom."

"I haven't told anyone anything."

"He's not missing, you know. Everyone says missing. He's ashamed." She looked at the kettle, not at Imogen. "He got something wrong in the winter, and he thinks the whole island's holding it up to the light. Tom will tell you something harder. Tom's had longer to practise."

"Wrong how?"

"A hundred and thirty over eighty," said Mrs. Quill. "Is that good?"

Imogen takes the green folders to Mrs. Quill's cottage, and the old woman insists she's fine while a half-hidden detail, such as a hospital discharge bracelet or a pill organiser in Dr. Peverell's handwriting, shows he has been visiting in secret. Mrs. Quill tells her the doctor is not missing but ashamed, and she gives Imogen a first, partial explanation that does not match Tom's.

Scene 5

The knocking came in threes, flat-handed, rattling the glass in the door. Imogen opened it on a boy of about twelve, soaked to the thighs.

"Grandad's on the kitchen floor. He won't answer me."

"Where?"

"Salt Lane. The water's over it."

She was already pulling the emergency bag from under the hatch. Outside, the lane at the bottom of the hill had become a brown channel with a gatepost standing in it. No car would manage it. The only lights on the island that moved belonged to a tractor, parked in the yard of Harbour Farm.

Tom was under its bonnet with a torch in his teeth. He took it out when he saw the boy.

"Joss Pritchard," the boy said. "Not breathing right."

Tom looked at Imogen. She waited for the speech about the 3:45 tide. He wiped his hands on his trousers and climbed into the cab.

The water came over the step plates. In the cottage an old man lay by the range, grey, a hand fisted against his breastbone. Tom was on his knees before she'd set the bag down, two fingers at the neck, his ear to the open mouth.

"Breathing. Pulse is thready." He said it quickly and quietly, like something recited. "Aspirin, three hundred. Chew, don't swallow whole."

"I know," she said.

"I know you know." His hand, holding the torch to the old man's pupils, was not steady. "He'd have said it just like that."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

That evening a boy from the village bangs on the clinic door because his grandfather has collapsed. Tom's tractor is the only thing that can cross the flooded lane to the house. Imogen must ask Tom for help, and in the emergency she works beside him and sees the competence and fear that connect the two brothers.

Scene 6

Imogen crushed the aspirin between her fingers and tipped it onto Joss Pritchard's tongue. His jaw worked slowly. She tried her mobile: no bars. The landline on the dresser gave her nothing at all, not even a tone.

"Line's down," she said.

"It goes with the tide." Tom didn't look up. "No one's crossing till four."

"Then we keep him here."

Footsteps splashed in the passage. A woman in a man's waxed coat stood in the doorway with the water running off her hems, and the boy went to her without a word. She looked at the old man, then at Tom, and her face changed.

"You."

"Carys," Tom said.

"You come in here with your bag and your torch." Her voice was very quiet. "Danny's been in the ground since February. Did you think we'd stopped counting?"

"Not now."

"He rang that surgery three times. Three. And your brother wrote a number on a piece of paper and nobody on this island could get across to say it was wrong." She turned to Imogen. "Did they tell you? Did anyone tell you who you're working for?"

Behind her on the dresser stood a pill organiser, lids marked in blue capitals. Friday's was still full.

Tom stood up. His knees cracked. He put the torch on the table, carefully, as if it might wake someone, and went out through the door. Through the window Imogen watched him walk down the lane and into the flood, past the gatepost, until it reached his belt.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

While they stabilise Joss Pritchard, the old man's daughter-in-law arrives and recognises Tom, then accuses him of what happened in the winter, naming a death that Tom has never mentioned. Imogen realises the doctor's shame and Tom's harshness both come from the same event, and Tom walks out into the water.

Scene 7

Imogen took the torch from the table. Carys didn't look up from the old man.

"Keep his head turned to the side," Imogen said. "Shout if his colour changes."

The lane took her at the shins, then the thighs, cold enough to feel like a burn. The beam found Tom's back thirty yards ahead. He had stopped where the water reached his belt and was standing with his hands open on its surface. She waded to him and caught a fistful of his coat.

"Tell me," she said.

He didn't pretend not to understand. "Danny's bloods came back in January. Potassium. Alasdair read the line above, the normal one. Doubled the dose and sent him home." The water slapped between them. "Danny rang three times. The road was shut two days. By the time anyone could get across."

"And the letters."

"He writes to them all. Leaves them in the outgoing tray." His jaw worked. "I collect on Fridays and burn them in the range. Carys has enough to carry without his handwriting on top."

"Nobody asked you to."

"No."

Her teeth were chattering. She pushed the torch into his chest until his hand closed around it.

"There's a pantry door on Salt Lane that comes off its hinges. Mr. Pritchard needs it as a stretcher, and I need somebody who can lift. Carry that."

The beam wavered over the water, then swung round toward the cottage window and its yellow square of light. He turned and began to wade back, and she followed in his wake.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Imogen follows Tom into the flood, leaving Carys to watch Joss, and catches him at the waist-deep point of the lane. He finally tells her what happened in winter: Dr. Peverell misread Danny's bloods, and Tom has been intercepting the doctor's unsent apologies so no one else would have to read them. She hands him the torch and tells him to carry the old man's stretcher, not his guilt, and he turns back with her.

Scene 8

The causeway at 3:45 was a black strip with the sea drawn back off it, and the marker poles stood up out of the wet sand like stitches. Imogen drove the tractor because Tom's hands wouldn't close on the wheel. Carys sat beside her in the cab, saying nothing. Tom rode in the trailer with his father-in-law's head on his knee, and when they reached the mainland end, Imogen saw him look back once at the road they had come by.

The ambulance crew took Joss Pritchard at the barrier. Carys went with him.

Imogen found the other man in the corridor outside Cardiac. He lay across three chairs with a hospital blanket pulled over his anorak, and his shoes were set side by side on the floor. Three weeks of grey stubble. A paper cup of cold tea by his head.

"Dr. Peverell."

He sat up too fast and held the chair arm. "The tide," he said. "It was in every time I got to the road."

"It's out now." She put the green folders on his lap, then the small cold key on top of them. "Mrs. Quill's first. She says she's fine."

He looked at the key. "You're staying."

"Yes. And the door stays unlocked. You can come back and work, but you won't sit in that room with the door shut."

His thumb moved over the blue ink on the folder tab.

"Your brother's in the car park," she said.

She hands him the green folders and the controlled drugs key and says she is staying on, but the clinic will no longer be his to hide in.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

Priya found the key where the agent's email said it would be, under a chipped saucer of cat food by the back step. The cat itself sat on the wall and watched her turn the lock.

The kitchen smelled of cold toast. A plate sat at the head of the table with two slices gone hard as slate, a knife laid across the butter dish, a mug with a brown ring dried inside it. A chair had been pushed back at an angle, as if someone had stood up to answer the door.

She set her suitcase down. In the hall, a hook by the door held a waxed coat. Beneath it was a clean rectangle in the dust on the side table, the size and shape of a medical bag.

"Dr. Hale?" she said, feeling foolish. Her voice went into the rooms and nothing came back.

The letters were in the dresser drawer she opened looking for a tea towel. Twenty or more, bound with a rubber band gone soft, all addressed in the same slanting hand. *Dr. E. Hale, Clinic Cottage, Saltreach.* Every one was sealed. The postmarks ran back eleven months.

She sat down at the table without deciding to. She slid the band off and opened the oldest with her thumb.

*Dad, I rang the clinic and a woman said you were out on a call. You're always out on a call.*

Outside, the light was going copper over the flats. Priya read the second letter, then the third. Nobody at the pub, the shop, or the ferry shed had said his name when she asked, only *Ah*, and looked at their hands.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

On her first evening, Priya lets herself into the doctor's cottage next to the clinic, which she was told would be her lodging. She finds his breakfast still laid out, his medical bag gone, and a stack of unopened letters from a daughter on the mainland. She begins reading them, and the island's silence about him starts to make sense.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 Nurse Priya Anand crosses the causeway on her first morning, misjudges the tide table, and has to be rescued by Tomas, a local oyster farmer, as water covers the road. He is the doctor's estranged son, and he tells her nothing about it. She reaches the clinic late to find the waiting room already full and the doctor's chair empty.
  • 1.00 Priya arrives to find the clinic unlocked and running on habit. The receptionist, Marguerite, has been quietly seeing patients and writing prescriptions on the missing doctor's old pads. Priya has to decide whether to report this or cover for it, and Marguerite makes clear that she is the doctor's sister and the island depends on the arrangement.
  • 1.00 A boy with a badly infected hand is brought in just as the tide cuts the island off, and Priya is alone with no doctor and no way to evacuate him. His grandmother, who knows exactly why the doctor left, offers to help by guiding Priya through the old procedures he used to follow. Priya gets a first test of her competence and a first glimpse of the island's tangled loyalties.

Scene 2

Priya drove back across the causeway with the water already in the ruts. She had spent an hour at the lay-by on the mainland side, where one bar of signal came and went, and she had listened to the health board's voicemail menu through to the end and hung up before the tone. Now the sea lay on both sides of the road, flat and pewter, and the marker posts stood in it to their knees. A wave of brown weed slid over the tarmac ahead of her wheels.

The clinic was a low grey building behind the church. The door was unlocked. Inside, every chair was taken. Eleven people sat in coats with their hands in their laps: a man with a bandaged wrist, two women sharing a flask, a child asleep across his mother's knees. Nobody was reading. They all looked up at her uniform.

"You're the nurse," said the woman behind the desk. She was sixty or so, with a cardigan buttoned wrong by one hole. "Morwenna. The kettle's in the back."

"Where's Dr. Hale?"

"Away on a long call." Morwenna said it smoothly, the way she might say *closed Sundays*. She slid a sheet of lined paper across the desk. Six addresses, in pencil, with a complaint beside each. *Leg dressing. Insulin. Mrs. Pascoe's chest.* "The tide turns at four. You'll want to be back before it."

The man with the wrist stood up. "I'll go first, if you're ready."

Priya looked at the paper. Then she took off her coat.

Scene 3

Mr. Treloar's leg took longer than the pencilled note allowed. The ulcer had to be soaked loose from the old dressing, and he wanted to tell her about the winter of '79 while she did it. By the time she had taped the last edge, the kitchen clock said ten to four.

The track from Penhallow dipped through a creek before it met the road. When Priya reached it, the water was brown and quick and already over the stones. She stopped the car with the bonnet a yard from it and sat with the engine running.

A man came down from the yard behind her, in waders, one hand still wet from the fish he'd been gutting. He looked at the creek, then at her.

"Not in that," he said. "That's my father you've just been seeing."

"I know. Is there another way round?"

"There's the boat."

The dinghy was drawn up on the slip below the farm. He handed her in without ceremony and pushed off, and the outboard coughed twice before it caught. She sat with her bag on her knees. The mudflats were going under in long silver tongues, and out in the channel a pale hump of sand still stood clear.

"Bank'll be gone in an hour," he said. "Never stops him. Out there every low water, sits till it's near his boots."

"Who does?"

He looked at the throttle. Then he turned the bow toward the church tower and said nothing else.

Priya cuts it too fine on the last visit, and the tide closes the causeway while she is at a remote farmhouse. A gruff fisherman, the patient's son, offers to take her back by boat, and on the crossing he lets slip that Hale takes the boat out to the sandbank every low tide and sits there.

Scene 4

The slip below the church was green to the waterline. He brought the dinghy in sideways and held it against the stone with one boot while she got her bag onto the step, then herself after it. Weed slid under her shoe. He put a hand flat against her back until she was steady, then took it away.

"Thank you," she said. "I don't know your name."

"Jago." He was looking past her, out over the flats. "I'm next door to the cottage. The one you're in. I've got his spare key on a nail, and I watched you find the saucer."

"His."

"Dr. Hale." He nodded at the channel. "That's him on the bank. Has been every low water since last spring. Goes out after the morning clinic, and somebody walks down to the shore around the turn and waves a torch, or a tea towel if it's light. He comes in when he's ready."

Priya turned. The hump of sand was an island now, no bigger than a table from here. A dark upright shape sat on it, not moving, with the water gathering round on three sides.

She thought of Morwenna's smooth voice. *Away on a long call.* Eleven people in coats who had looked at her uniform and not at the door.

"Does everyone know?"

Jago pulled the cord. The outboard caught first time.

"Mind the third step," he said. "It's loose."

Scene 5

The rota was pinned inside the shop door, a column of names in biro, and Thursday's said *Nurse* in Morwenna's hand. Nobody had asked her. Jago brought the torch to the cottage at half past five and set it on the table beside the letters, saying nothing about either.

She stood on the slip with it in her fist. The light was going from the flats in long brown stripes. Out on the bank the dark shape had not moved, and the water was around it on every side. She switched the torch on and off, on and off, her arm aching by the tenth minute. It seemed a ridiculous thing to do for a grown man.

Then the shape stood. It came toward her along the ridge, stooped, in no hurry, wading to the knee and then the shin. She kept the beam low on the sand. He was thin, hatless, in a wet shirt with the sleeves rolled. He came up the slip past her close enough to touch and did not turn his head.

She followed him to the cottage. In the hall he lifted the waxed coat from its hook and shook it once.

"Church," he said. His voice was rusty. "Vestry, under the surplices. I'd not leave it where anyone could count the furniture."

He put one arm into the coat.

"The Pascoe woman's due at nine."

Scene 6

She had cleared the toast away while he was at the church. The ring in the mug she had left, because it seemed not hers to scrub.

He came in at eight with the bag under his arm, still damp to the thigh, and stopped in the kitchen doorway. The cat was on his chair. He lifted it off and set it on the floor, and it went and sat by the stove with its back to him.

Priya had the letters squared on the table in front of the empty place. The rubber band lay beside them. She had put the oldest on top, flap torn open along its edge. When he looked at her she moved to the sink and ran the tap over nothing.

He sat. For some time he only looked at the envelope. Then he drew out the sheet with two fingers, as if it might be hot, and unfolded it. His lips moved at the first line. *Dad, I rang the clinic.* She saw his eyes stay on it well after they should have moved down.

He folded it along its creases and laid his palm on top.

"Her number," he said. The word cracked. He cleared his throat and tried again. "It'll have changed. They do. Find out if it's still the same."

"Should I?"

"Yes." He did not look up. "Please."

The kettle ticked on the hob. Priya turned off the tap.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

That night Priya sets the rubber-banded letters on the kitchen table in front of Dr. Hale and says nothing. He reads only the first line of the oldest, then asks her, hoarsely, to find out if his daughter's number is still the same, which commits her to making a call she isn't sure she should make.

Scene 7

The number was under the signature on the oldest letter, in the same slanting hand, with a line drawn beneath it twice. Priya drove to the lay-by on the mainland side and stood at the fence with her arm raised toward the pylon. The bar came, went, came. She dialled before it could leave again.

It rang six times. Behind her the causeway lay bare and shining, a gull walking the white line.

"Hello?" A young woman, breathless, with a hard sound behind her like wind across an open window.

"Hello. My name's Priya Anand. I'm the nurse at Saltreach clinic."

Nothing. The hard sound went on. She checked the screen; the call was still there, the bar a single sliver.

"I have your letters," Priya said. "He's read the first one. He asked me to find out whether this was still your number."

An indicator ticked on the line, ten, twelve beats. Then a long breath out.

"I'm in the car," the woman said. "I'm past Truro. I was going to turn up and shout at him." Her voice wobbled and she flattened it. "Is he all right?"

"He's standing up. He's eating."

"When's the road open?"

Priya pulled the tide table from her pocket. Her thumb had worn the fold soft. "Low water's nine thirty tonight. You'd have about two hours either side, but it'll be dark."

"Then I'll be there for nine thirty."

The line cut. The bar was gone.

Scene 8

The headlights came down the mainland slope at ten to eight, an hour and a half before they were wanted. Priya saw them from the shore end of the causeway, where she had been standing since seven with the torch off to save the battery. The tide was still making. Water ran across the tarmac in a brown sheet, and the marker posts stood in it like men wading.

The car came on slowly, then stopped at the third post. Its beams lay flat on the water. Wipers went once across the glass and quit.

"She'll not try it," Jago said behind her. He had come down without a word, as he did. "Not if she's got sense."

"She's got her father's," Priya said.

The door behind them opened and shut. Dr. Hale came down the shingle in the waxed coat with the bag in his right hand, and for a moment she thought he was going to the bank, that the bank was simply the other direction. He passed her. He passed the torch, held out and ignored. His boots went into the water and kept going, to the shin, to the knee, the bag lifted clear against his chest.

Priya switched on the beam and laid it along the white line ahead of him. He stayed on it. Halfway out, the car's door swung open, and a figure in a pale jacket stood up into the light.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The daughter arrives early, before the road is safe, and finds the water already running over the tarmac. Priya, watching from the shore, sees the headlights stop at the marker posts, and Dr. Hale wades out along the flooded causeway toward the car with his bag. It is the first time in a year he has walked toward someone rather than away.

historical fiction

A surveyor is hired to map a mountain valley before it is flooded for a dam, and the villagers keep moving the boundary stones at night.

A: Plain

Scene by scene, with no memory of other options.

Scene 1

Aldous set the first stone on the Tuesday, at the corner of the chapel field, a squared block of Pennant sandstone with a cross chiseled on top and the number 14 cut beneath. He took the bearing twice, wrote it in the field book, and wedged slate chips around the base with the heel of his boot.

On Wednesday morning he came up the lane with the chain over his shoulder and his assistant, a Cardiff boy named Pugh, trailing behind with the staff. The stone was not at the corner of the chapel field. It sat eleven yards down the slope, beside the hawthorn hedge, upright and tidy, its slate chips packed around it.

"Perhaps you set it there," Pugh said.

"I did not."

Aldous crouched. The grass at the base had been cut away and laid back like a lid. Under it the soil was black and damp. At the original corner there was a patch of turf that did not match the turf around it, pressed down, still faintly square.

He stood and looked across the valley. Smoke rose from six chimneys. A woman was hanging washing on a gorse bush by the ford, and she did not look up. A dog barked once and stopped.

Aldous opened the field book and wrote the date, the number of the stone, and *displaced, 11 yds SSW*. Then he told Pugh to bring the spade.

Scene 2

Aldous had Pugh dig the stone out and carry it back up the slope on a hurdle. It took them most of an hour. He reset it at the corner, over the square of mismatched turf, and this time he poured a bucket of lime slurry around the base from the ford.

"That'll show whoever lifts it," he said.

Pugh wiped his hands on his trousers and said nothing.

At noon Aldous walked to the nearest farm, Tŷ Isaf, where a man in shirtsleeves was splitting kindling on a block. The man was perhaps sixty, with forearms like fence rails. Aldous gave his name and the name of the Corporation, and said that a survey stone had been moved.

The man set down the hatchet. He answered in Welsh, slowly, looking at the chain over Aldous's shoulder rather than at his face. Aldous caught only *nos*, night, and something that might have been *glaw*, rain.

"English?" Aldous said.

The man shrugged and went inside. A girl of about nine came to the door with a tin cup of buttermilk and held it out. Aldous drank it because it seemed rude not to. It was sour and cold.

When he handed back the cup, he saw the hatchet blade on the block. Fresh lime was dried white along its edge, though he had only mixed the slurry that morning.

Scene 3

Aldous and Pugh took the chapel porch for the night, with a blanket, a flask of tea, and the lantern shuttered to a slit. Stone 14 stood white-ringed in the field, a pale shape against the dark hedge.

Pugh lasted until eleven. He slept sitting up, his chin on the staff. Aldous kept his watch hand on his knee and counted the chapel clock's quarters through the wall behind him. An owl worked the hedge. Once a sheep coughed like an old man. Nothing crossed the field.

At first light the stone was still at the corner, the lime ring unbroken. Aldous let out a breath and felt foolish for it. He woke Pugh with a boot against his shoe.

"Nobody," Pugh said, rubbing his face. "Well. There."

"Get the chain."

They walked the ridge line to check the others. Stone 13 should have stood by the sheepfold wall. It was in the bracken thirty yards off, on its side, the cross facing the ground. Stone 15 was in the stream. Stone 16 was gone altogether, and in the mud where it had stood someone had pressed a flat river cobble, neatly, like a lid on a jar.

Aldous turned the cobble over with his toe. Pugh was looking down the valley, where a thread of smoke had already started from Tŷ Isaf.

Scene 4

The minister's house stood behind the chapel, with a slate path and a rain barrel under the gutter. Mr. Rees opened the door with a pen still in his hand. He was a narrow man in a waistcoat gone shiny at the buttons.

Aldous held out the river cobble. "This was in the place of stone sixteen."

Rees took it, weighed it in his palm, and gave it back. "It's a good stone. From the ford, I should think."

"I need to know who is moving them. I'd like you to put a question to Tŷ Isaf for me."

"I can put it." Rees set the pen on the doorframe. "I can't promise what comes back."

They walked down together. Pugh stayed behind at the sheepfold, sitting on stone 13 with the staff across his knees. At the farm the same man was at the same block, though no wood lay on it now. Rees spoke. The man answered at some length, and the girl watched from the doorway with the tin cup in both hands.

"He says the ground is soft this month," Rees said. "He says stones sink and slide. He says you should not trust it."

"Is that all he said?"

Rees looked at the man, who looked at the chain on Aldous's shoulder.

"He said a good deal more," Rees said. "That was the part about the ground."

Scene 5

Aldous sent Pugh to the village for bread and went back to the chapel field alone. He lifted stone 14 with the crowbar, rolled it onto its side, and knelt at the square of mismatched turf. The ground gave under his knee.

He pushed the probing rod in. At a foot and a half it stopped against something flat.

He cut the turf back with the spade and then dug with his hands, because the spade rang. The slab was slate, no bigger than a bread board, lying face up. Someone had scratched letters into it with a nail: *GWEN, 1847*. Beside it his fingers found a second edge, then a third. Small slabs, laid in a row along the hedge side, each a hand's width from the next.

He counted seven before the light started to go. The last had no letters, only a cross.

He sat back on his heels. The stone he had set stood tilted on its side, the number 14 facing the sky. The lime ring had cracked where he rolled it.

At the ford a woman was filling a pail. She straightened and looked up the slope at him, at the open ground, and stood holding the pail with water running over her wrist. Then she turned and walked toward Tŷ Isaf without spilling any.

Aldous took out the field book. He held the pencil over the page for some time.

Scene 6

Pugh came back along the lane with a loaf under his arm and stopped at the gate. He looked at the open ground, the slabs in their row, and the crowbar lying in the grass.

"Is that what I think?" he said.

"Hold the lantern."

They worked without speaking. Aldous set each slate back where it had lain, face up, a hand's width from the next, and pressed the soil around it with his palms. Pugh held the light low and read the letters aloud when Aldous asked him to, because Aldous could not make out the scratches in the dusk. *GWEN, 1847.* Another name he could not pronounce. Another. The last, the cross.

When the turf was down he stamped it flat along the edges, then stopped and did it again more gently.

Boots sounded on the slate path. The man from Tŷ Isaf stood at the gate with his hat in his hand. The girl was at his hip, holding something against her chest. He did not come in.

Aldous wiped his hands on his coat. He picked up stone 14 and carried it, bent under the weight, to the far side of the field. He set it down against the wall, forty paces from the hedge, and kicked the slate chips in around it.

The man watched him do it. The girl stepped forward and laid a river cobble on the new turf, at the end of the row.

Scene 7

Mr. Hallam of the Corporation came up the valley on Thursday in a hired trap, with a roll of the engineer's plan across his knees. He climbed down at the chapel gate and looked at the field.

"Fourteen is the top corner of the compensation line," he said. "Your last return had it by the hedge."

"The ground is soft this month," Aldous said. "It slid. I've reset it where it's firm."

Hallam walked to the wall and stood over the stone. He pressed his boot against its side. It did not move. He walked back along the hedge, and Aldous watched his shoes cross the turf a hand's width from the row and then past it.

"Forty paces off the plan."

"Yes."

"That's a quarter acre the Corporation won't have to pay for, then, or one it will." Hallam unrolled the plan on the trap's seat and weighed the corners with the chain, a flask, and his gloves. "Show me the book."

Aldous gave it to him. Hallam turned pages. At the entry for Tuesday he stopped, read, and turned on. The last page held only the date and *14, reset, 40 yds NE.* Nothing else.

"Pugh, is that how you remember it?"

"Yes, sir," Pugh said. "Soft ground."

A cart went by on the lane. The driver kept his eyes on the horse's ears.

Hallam took a pencil from his pocket and marked the plan.

Scene 8

Aldous walked the line a last time on Saturday, with Pugh behind him carrying the staff and the folded chain. Stone 13 stood by the sheepfold wall, cross up. Stone 15 stood dry on the bank above the stream. At the place where sixteen had been, a new block sat in the mud, cut by Pugh the evening before from the spare sandstone, its number still sharp.

They reached the chapel field at noon. Stone 14 stood against the far wall with the lime gone grey around its base. He did not go to the hedge. From the gate he could see the turf there, the green a little darker in a strip, and at the end of it the river cobble, dry now, with a sparrow sitting on it.

At Tŷ Isaf the man was not at the block. The girl came out with the tin cup and held it up to him in both hands. Buttermilk again. Aldous drank all of it this time, to the grit at the bottom, and gave her the cup back.

"Diolch," he said. He had practised it with Pugh on the road.

She looked at him, then at the chain, then said something quietly in Welsh and went in.

The trap was waiting in the lane. Aldous put the field book in his coat, climbed up beside Pugh, and took the reins.

B: Decay

Rejected moves stay in play and fade over the scenes.

Scene 1

The innkeeper read the commission's letters slowly, holding each one at arm's length, and then folded them along their creases and handed them back.

"They are very fine letters," he said. "Good paper."

"Then I can have a room."

"You can have a room when Aldric says you can. He is the headman. He's at the upper pasture until tomorrow, or the day after." The old man smiled apologetically, as if the delay were a small illness in the family. Behind him a woman stopped wiping a table and did not start again.

Hendry set down his case. The theodolite's box had left a red groove across his palm. "And tonight?"

"The storehouse is dry."

It was not very dry. The wind came through the slats in thin, cold strips, and the hay in the corner smelled of last summer. The innkeeper left him a lamp and a blanket that smelled of goat. Hendry had just unbuckled the tripod straps when he noticed the girl in the doorway, perhaps eight, barefoot on the frozen dirt.

She said nothing. She crossed to the hay, knelt, and pulled back an armful with both hands.

Under it lay stones, twenty or more, flat-sided and squared at the top. Each had a cross chiseled into its face, the commission's mark, and the earth still clung to their bases.

She looked at him. Then she covered them again, patting the hay flat.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

The surveyor arrives at the village inn with his letters from the dam commission, and the elderly innkeeper politely refuses him a room until the headman has consented to his presence. He is led to a drafty storehouse instead, where a child quietly shows him a pile of stones hidden beneath the hay.

Buffer (3 moves)
  • 1.00 On his first morning in the valley, the surveyor sets his theodolite on the ridge and records the first line of boundary stones, then returns the next dawn to find every stone shifted several paces uphill. He says nothing to the villagers who watch him from their doorways, and quietly decides to re-measure rather than report it.
  • 1.00 Before he even starts work, the surveyor is walked by the headman to the old churchyard, where the headman insists the graves lie beyond any line the commission has drawn. The surveyor, moved despite himself, pencils a secret mark in his notebook that deviates from his official instructions.
  • 1.00 The surveyor's young assistant, a local boy hired as chainman, leads him up the valley at dawn and proudly sets the first stake. That night the surveyor wakes to the sound of voices and sees lantern light moving across the slopes, and realizes his assistant's own father is among those carrying the stones.

Scene 2

Frost lay on the ridge grass so thickly that Hendry's boots left dark prints. He set the tripod over the old survey's brass pin, a cairn at its shoulder, and spent a quarter hour on the legs until the bubble sat dead center. Below him the village was nine roofs and a thread of smoke. Nobody was in the lane.

The previous survey's field book gave the baseline bearing in a cramped, confident hand. He swung the telescope to it and clamped the plate. Along that line the first stones should have stood at four hundred and eight hundred yards, each with its cross facing the ridge.

He found the first one easily. The cross was on it. But the vertical hair fell a thumb's width to the right of it, and when he looked up from the eyepiece and back again, the stone had not moved.

He read the vernier twice. He unclamped, swung away, and sighted again from the beginning.

Then he carried the chain down. The turf around the base of the stone had been cut in squares and laid back like a lid, the seams still black and loose. From the baseline he paced it: four and a half paces uphill. The second stone was the same, and the third was nearly so.

Hendry stood among them with the chain slack in his hand. He thought of the hay, and of the girl's palms flattening it. Across the valley a door opened, and a man stood in it without coming out.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

At first light Hendry sets up the theodolite on the ridge above the village and sights the nearest surviving boundary markers, only to find they are a few paces off the commission's own baseline from the old survey. He realizes the stones in the storehouse were not stolen but pulled up by the villagers, and the ones still standing are the ones they have already moved.

Scene 3

Aldric came down from the pasture at noon, a tall man leaning on a crook he did not seem to need. Hendry was waiting in the inn yard with a stone at his feet, still caked with earth from the storehouse hay.

"Four and a half paces uphill," Hendry said. "The first three, at least. The turf was cut and laid back. There are twenty more under the hay in the storehouse."

Aldric looked at the stone, then at the cross cut into its face. He did not look toward the storehouse. "Five on the third," he said. "The ground is steeper there."

"You knew that."

"I know the ground."

Behind the shutters of the nearest house, something shifted. Hendry kept his eyes on the headman. "I'm obliged to report interference with the line."

"Yes." Aldric rested both hands on the crook. His knuckles were split from cold. "The church stands below your line, and so does the yard behind it. When the water comes it will stand forty feet over the roof. Your drawing shows a contour. It does not show my mother."

"I don't draw the contour."

"No. You only put the stones in it." He turned his head toward the lane. "Walk the yard with me before you drive another stake. An hour. Then write what you like."

Hendry looked down. The cross faced up at him, sharp and new. He picked up the blanket.

Scene 4

The churchyard wall was knee-high, and the gate hung from one hinge. Aldric walked the rows without speaking. Hendry carried the stone in the blanket and set it down by the gatepost. He read the slates as he passed: names worn to shadows, a run of dates from one bad winter, and at the end a mound no longer than his arm, the earth still pale. The date cut into its small board was eleven months old.

"Whose?"

"Tomas's girl." Aldric did not stop walking.

Through the gate Hendry saw a child cross the lane toward the storehouse, barefoot, in no hurry. He watched her go in. Aldric was pointing out the wall where the water would stand, and Hendry looked at the wall.

When the hour was done he went back with the stone in his arms. The storehouse door stood open. The hay was flung across the floor and the straps of his tripod case had been kicked aside. In the corner the dirt was bare, and two shallow grooves ran out over the threshold and down toward the stream, where the frost had been scraped to black.

A bay horse stood steaming at the inn door. A young man in a commission greatcoat was beating dust from his hat against his knee.

"Mr. Hendry? Pruett. Mr. Calloway wants to know how the line stands." He glanced past Hendry at the scattered hay. "And your stones?"

Hendry shifted the weight against his chest. Aldric was somewhere behind him in the lane.

"Set," he said. "Every one."

Hendry has to decide on the spot whether to lie about the missing stones, and the rider's presence leaves him no time to ask Aldric what he should say.

Scene 5

Pruett ate two helpings of the innkeeper's barley and asked nothing about the valley. Afterward he stood in the storehouse door with his hat in his hand, looking at the bare dirt in the corner.

"I'll sleep here," he said.

"The inn has a bed," Hendry said.

"Mr. Calloway had a survey in the north lose a month to this sort of thing. Stones walk off." He spread his greatcoat over the hay. "Tomorrow we go up together and I'll see them."

Hendry waited until the lamp in the storehouse went out. Then he went up the lane to the headman's house and knocked with two fingers.

Aldric opened it with a spoon in his hand. Behind him a woman moved out of the firelight.

"The ridge stones," Hendry said. "And the ones in the stream. All of them in their places before light, to the pace. Pruett will check the field book."

"You told him they were set."

"I did." He held the doorframe. "Give me the stones, and I'll give you a case. The church lies close to the line. If the old figures are wrong, someone has to carry that to Calloway, and he won't believe me alone. I need the parish book and every man who'll swear to the ground."

Aldric looked at the spoon. "You can promise nothing."

"No."

The headman set the spoon on the sill, took his crook from the wall, and went past Hendry into the dark.

Hendry has to get the villagers to put the stones back before dawn, so he goes to Aldric and offers a bargain: the stones return to their true places, and in exchange Aldric helps him build a case for moving the dam's edge.

Scene 6

Pruett was already on the ridge when Hendry came up, stamping his boots in the frost. The first stone stood at its place with the cross turned to the ridge. The turf around its base had been laid back so neatly that only the frost gave it away, a pale square with a dark seam. Mud had dried on the stone's face in the shape of a small hand.

Pruett crouched, looked at it, and stood up again without saying anything.

"The book," he said.

Hendry gave him the old field book. Pruett read standing, his lips moving, a finger running down the columns of chainage. At the foot of the second page it stopped.

"He tallied forty-one chains here. Then he's written *chain stretched, allow* and left it blank." Pruett turned the page toward the light. "He never allowed it. Carry a short chain forty-one times and you've a quarter-pace by the church wall."

"Which way?"

Pruett paced it off, counting under his breath, then paced it again. "The wall comes out above the line. Barely. The old figures drown it, and the true ones don't."

Hendry looked down the slope at the nine roofs, at the roof of the church with its crooked cross. Four and a half paces uphill, and all of it for nothing.

Pruett held out the book and the pencil. "You'll want to initial the correction," he said. "Since you set the stones."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Pruett's reading of the field book on the ridge shows the old survey's baseline was itself mis-chained, a quarter-pace error that happens to favor the church. Hendry realizes the villagers' tampering was unnecessary, but the discovery only helps if he exposes his own lie and the stones he swore were set.

Scene 7

Hendry took the pencil. The lead was worn to a blunt slope, and he turned it in his fingers, looking for the line on the page where his initials would go.

"You can set it down," Pruett said. "I'm not going to snatch it."

"You said stones walk off."

"They do." Pruett shut his mouth on the rest of it, then opened it again. "I heard the sledge last night. Around two. I lay with my eyes closed and my coat over my head, and I thought, a man asleep in the doorway hears nothing he has to put in a letter." He rubbed his thumb across the dried mud on the stone's face, not quite touching the print. "I saw the bare corner when I came in. I knew before I ate your barley."

Hendry's grip tightened. "Then why ask me for the book?"

"Because Calloway's engineers don't trust the old survey. They've said so twice, in the room, and he's said nothing back. A paper from the commission's own man on the ground, over his own initials, is the only thing that makes them stop the work and measure again." He looked down the slope. "And they'll remember whose initials. Not the dead man's. Yours."

The frost was going from the grass in patches. Hendry held the pencil over the foot of the second page, over the blank where *allow* had been written and never filled in.

Scene 8

Hendry wrote *H.* and *W.* under the blank where *allow* had never been filled in, and the pencil skipped on the grain of the page. Pruett blew on the graphite, closed the book, and buttoned it inside his greatcoat. He did not say thank you. He mounted at the inn door and rode down the valley road at a walk, the bay's breath showing in the cold.

In April the road was a stream. Hendry came over the last rise on foot, the carter having refused to go farther, and saw the lower meadows gone to brown water with fence tops standing out of it in rows. The storehouse roof was dry. The lane was not.

The commission's engineers had re-chained the baseline in February. He had read the result in a Calloway letter, two lines long: the old datum was corrected, the contour was corrected, and the corrected contour passed two yards above the church wall.

Aldric stood at the wall in rubber-soled boots too big for him, his crook planted in the mud. Water lapped the third row of slates. Above them four men on a ladder were easing the bell from its frame with ropes, and the clapper knocked once against the bronze as it swung free.

"You came," Aldric said.

"I came."

The bell went down into the arms of the men below. The girl stood at the gate, holding the rope's slack end in both hands.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hendry initials the correction and Pruett departs. Months later, in spring, Hendry returns to find the engineers' re-measure has gone against the village after all, and the water is rising. He stands with Aldric at the church wall as the first bell is taken down, having bought the village only a season.

C: Fixed

Rejected moves stay in play and never fade.

Scene 1

The engineer's office smelled of wet wool and lamp oil. Mr. Pruett unrolled three sheets across his desk and weighted the corners with a stapler, an inkwell, and a chunk of grey concrete.

"Ordnance sheets, 1894. Useless above the tree line, but they'll give you the river." He tapped a pencilled line. "Waterline at four hundred and ten meters. Everything under it gets a stone by the first of October. Roads, walls, houses, the lot."

"That's eleven weeks," Hale said.

"It's what the Board gave me."

Hale rolled the maps and slid them into the leather tube. Pruett came around the desk and shut the door, though no one else was in the room.

"Mr. Fenn had the job before you. He went up in April." Pruett straightened the inkwell. "In June he came down without his instruments, and he didn't stop at this office. I had his bill from a hotel in Carlisle."

"Did he say why?"

"He wrote that the work could not be completed. That was all." Pruett offered his hand. "I'd just like you to finish."

The road beyond the last farm was a cart track, and then a mule track. Hale walked beside the animal where the slope steepened. Near noon he came upon a woman bent nearly double, a flat grey stone the size of a bread board lashed to her back with rope. Her lips were pale with effort.

"Good day," he said. "That's a heavy load. Where are you taking it?"

She looked at him, then at the mule, and went on up the track.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

At the company office in the lowland town, the dam engineer hands the surveyor his maps and a deadline, and privately warns him that the last surveyor left the valley without finishing. On the road up, the surveyor passes a woman carrying a stone on her back, and she refuses to say where she is taking it.

  • 1.00 Surveyor Edmund Hale arrives by mule in the valley village of Karrow in 1927 and sets his first boundary stones along the river. At dawn he finds every stone shifted several yards uphill, and the headman politely claims to know nothing about it.
  • 1.00 On his first evening in the valley, the surveyor is hosted by an old widow whose house sits exactly where the dam's waterline will fall. She tells him the stones mark graves rather than property, and he must decide whether to record what she says or keep it out of his report.
  • 1.00 The surveyor spends his first day carefully triangulating and stakes the first stones with the village boys watching. That night he stays awake in his tent and sees lantern-bearing figures dismantle his work, and he recognizes his own guide among them.

Scene 2

The lower road ran along the river on a shelf of packed gravel, and Hale chose a place where it crossed a dry stream bed. He set the theodolite on its tripod, sighted back to the bridge pier, then across to a lightning-split ash on the far bank. Twice he read the vernier. He drove an iron pin at the station and dug a hole knee-deep a few feet off.

The post was squared granite, a little longer than his arm, with 410 chiselled into the top and the Board's broad arrow on one face. He lowered it in, packed the hole with fieldstone and earth, and stamped it down with his heel. The sun slanted yellow down the valley. Three boys sat on the wall above the road and said nothing. When he looked up, one raised a hand as if to a passing train. Hale wrote in his field book: *Station 1, bearing, distance, 4.20 p.m.*

He slept in the tent beside the road and heard only the river.

At first light he walked down to the station. The iron pin was there. The hole beside it was a patch of loose dirt. He climbed the road, counting paces, and stopped at a hundred.

The post stood upright in a new hole, the earth still dark and damp, tamped harder than he had tamped it. At its foot lay harebells and yellow pansies tied with red wool, and a heel of bread. The spade marks were clean. Nothing had been scuffed or kicked.

He crouched. The number 410 faced the river, as he had left it.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hale sets his first stone on the lower road, driving a marked granite post into the ground in the afternoon light. At dawn he finds it a hundred paces uphill, standing in a freshly dug hole with flowers laid at its base, and he realizes the villagers are moving the stones with ceremony rather than spite.

Scene 3

The hamlet was eleven houses and a chapel, strung along a terrace above the river. Hale came up with the mule's rope wound around his fist. Two men at a water trough straightened when they saw him and went on staring while he spoke.

"Someone has been at my survey post. It's Board property." He pointed back down the slope. "Who here speaks English?"

One of them looked at the other. A child ran off between the houses.

The woman who came out of the schoolhouse was perhaps forty, with chalk dust on her cuffs and a grey braid pinned flat. She heard him out with her hands folded.

"The post is not damaged," she said. "You said so yourself."

"It's been moved a hundred paces."

"To where it belongs." She said it plainly, as if correcting a sum. "Your maps show a river, a road, and the houses. They don't show who is buried along the river. Or where the Pryor field ended, or the Alder field. The stones go to those places."

"Graves?"

"Some. Walls that fell before your Ordnance men came." She looked past him at the mule. "I'll show you the churchyard, Mr. Hale. But you'll walk the valley with me first, and set no post until we've done it."

"How long would that take?"

"Longer than you'd like."

He took out his field book, looked at the blank page, and put it away. "Show me the churchyard."

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hale climbs to the nearest hamlet to confront the villagers, and the schoolmistress, the one person who speaks English, tells him the stones are being moved to stand over the graves and old field-edges that the Board's survey never recorded. She offers to show him the churchyard if he will agree to walk the valley with her before setting another post.

He leaves the lower road and follows them, finding Fenn's abandoned theodolite case wedged in a drystone wall, with a field book inside that stops mid-sentence.

A telegram from Pruett waits on the counter, moving the deadline up to mid-September, and Hale has to choose between obeying the Board and trusting the villagers' silence.

Scene 4

The cart came up the terrace road a little after seven, the mule blowing hard, two men in Board oilskins walking at its tail. Pruett sat on the box in a town coat, mud to the knee. Hale was at the chapel gate with the schoolmistress, who had just lifted the latch.

"The farmer at Low Garth sent a boy down," Pruett said, climbing off. He did not look at her. "Eleven days I've paid you, Hale, and I have one post."

"It's been moved, sir. I was about to explain why."

"I don't need it explained." Pruett nodded at the cart bed. Granite posts lay in straw, each with its arrow. Spades, a coil of rope, a pair of lanterns. "Mr. Dacre and Mr. Wing will stand with you every night until the first. Every stone you set, you set again if it walks. They'll sit on it."

One of the men had already lifted a spade onto his shoulder. Along the terrace, doors had opened a hand's width. No one came out.

"There are graves under some of these," Hale said.

"Then the Board will compensate the parish." Pruett lowered his voice. "I'll fetch the constable from Brough by Thursday if I must. He'll find a good many people here obstructing a public works order. Include yourself or don't."

The schoolmistress's hands were folded at her waist. She looked at Hale, only that.

He picked up the tripod from the wall and carried it to the cart. Behind him the chapel latch clicked shut.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Pruett arrives unannounced at the hamlet with two Board men and a cart, having heard of the trouble. He orders Hale to reset every stone under guard and threatens to bring in the constable, which forces Hale to choose between his contract and the promise he made to the schoolmistress.

Scene 5

By Tuesday night Hale had set nine posts where the Board's sheet put the line, reading each vernier twice. Dacre held the lantern. Wing dug. In Hale's breast pocket the field book carried two sets of figures. The Board's were on the right-hand pages. On the left, in pencil, were the places the schoolmistress had stopped and said *here*, with what lay under each.

The tenth post went into the Alder field. Under the lantern the turf showed long low swells in rows, with no stone at any head. Hale drove the pin, set the post at the line, and wrote nothing about the swells on the right-hand page.

Dacre had drifted off a few yards. He stood with the lantern held low, then came back.

"Those are graves, Mr. Hale."

"It's pasture."

"Wing's people are chapel. He knows a grave when he walks on one."

Pruett came up the track at first light with mud to his thighs. Dacre spoke to him beside the cart. Pruett crossed the field, kicked the base of the post, and held out his hand. Hale gave him the book. He turned the left-hand pages slowly, lips moving over the pencil, then handed it back.

"Wing," he said. "Take the mule to Brough. Tell Sergeant Atkin today, not Thursday."

By noon Hale stood at the chapel gate. A trap was coming up the lower road, a black hat in it. Behind him doors were opening along the terrace, and the schoolmistress stood in hers with her hands folded, waiting to see where he would put his feet.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hale refuses to set the posts at the villagers' graves. He marks the waterline on the Board's chosen spots and plans to record the true places in a second private set of notes. Pruett finds out when Dacre reports a post set in a field of unmarked graves. The constable is sent for early, and Hale has to decide whether to stand beside the villagers when he arrives.

Scene 6

Hale crossed the terrace to the schoolhouse door. She had not moved from it.

"The sergeant is an hour out," he said. "Bring everyone to the Alder field. Spades, barrows, whatever you have. The posts go to the graves, and they go in daylight."

"Mr. Pruett's men are in the field."

"Mr. Dacre will watch. He won't stop you." Hale heard how little certainty was in it. "If Atkin finds one man at a post, he takes that man. I'd rather he find all of you."

She looked at him a moment. Then she took the bell rope from its hook inside the door and rang it, twice, and let it swing.

They came with mattocks and a handbarrow, two boys with a door off its hinges. Dacre stood at the field gate with his lantern unlit in his fist. Hale pulled the tenth post himself, rocking it free of the damp earth. Old Pryor took the other end. They carried it across the turf between the swells, and the schoolmistress knelt and pressed her palm to the ground at three places before she nodded. The spades went in.

By the time the trap came up the lower road, nine posts stood in the chapel yard and Alder field at heads and corners, the broad arrows facing the river. Forty-odd people were tamping earth. A girl carried a bucket of water for the dust.

Atkin stepped down. He counted the spades, then the faces, and took off his hat.

"Which of you is in charge here?"

Nobody straightened up.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Before the sergeant arrives, Hale goes to the schoolmistress and asks her to bring the villagers to the Alder field. Together they dig up the posts and carry them to the true graves in daylight, so that Atkin finds the whole valley openly defying the order and cannot name one culprit.

Scene 7

Hale set down the post he was holding. "I am."

Atkin looked at him, then at the forty people with dirt on their hands. "You."

"The posts were moved on my orders. I'm the Board's surveyor." He took the field book from his breast pocket. "Everything in it is mine. Nobody here touched a stone I didn't tell them to."

Behind him a spade was set down very quietly. The schoolmistress did not speak.

Atkin turned the pages as Pruett had, slowly, without reading aloud. At the Alder field he stopped and held the page flat with his thumb. Then he shut the book and put it inside his coat.

"You'll ride down with me, Mr. Hale. Now, while the light's good."

Nobody followed to the trap. They stood among the new posts and watched him climb up. Atkin clicked to the horse, and the wheels ground over the terrace gravel.

Fifty yards on, someone was running. The schoolmistress came alongside, skirt in one fist, and Atkin slowed without being asked. She held up a leather case, black with damp, the brass corners gone green.

"It was under the chapel floor," she said. "He left it with me."

Hale took it. The catch was stiff. Inside, the theodolite lay in its velvet, its lens clean, and beneath it a roll of paper tied with red wool. He unrolled one turn. Pencilled crosses in rows. The Alder field.

The horse walked on. She stopped in the road.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

Hale tells Atkin he is in charge, taking the blame to shield the villagers, and Atkin takes him down to Brough in the trap that afternoon. As the trap pulls away, the schoolmistress hands up Fenn's lost instrument case, which she has kept hidden, and Hale realizes why his predecessor really left.

Scene 8

The cell at Brough had a plank bed, a bucket, and a window the width of a hand. Atkin brought a stool in himself, sat, and untied the red wool.

"Your Mr. Fenn wrote small," he said. He tilted the paper to the window. "'Alder field, forty-one. Pryor boundary, nineteen, one a child. Chapel yard, east wall, unmarked, count uncertain.'" He turned the roll a length. "Here he's written, 'Cannot set a line through them. Told P. so. P. says set it.'"

Hale sat with his hands between his knees. "Pruett said Fenn walked off."

"Pruett says a good deal." Atkin laid the roll across his thigh. "I had a letter in July from the superintendent of the Cumberland asylum at Carlisle. Fenn was brought in by a hotel keeper, not speaking. He's speaking now. He asked that his map go back to the village, and not to the Board. The letter went to Pruett first. Pruett wrote that it was a private matter."

"He's alive."

"He's in a ward with a garden." Atkin said it flatly. "I can't send a constable to Carlisle on a surveyor's say-so, and I can't open the Board's files. You can do either one. You can go to Pruett's office with this, or you can go up the hill and read it out to them."

The latch was already lifted. Hale took the roll, found the red wool, and tied it in the same knot.

Chosen move and bufferChosen move

At Brough, Atkin sits Hale in a cell and reads aloud from Fenn's roll, then reveals that Fenn is not lost: he is a patient in a Carlisle asylum who sent word asking that his map be returned to the village. Hale must decide whether to take the case to Pruett, who has been hiding this, or to carry Fenn's testimony back up the mountain.
