He recognizes one of the two men from the trough and follows him, and is caught by the schoolmistress's brother, who says Fenn did the same thing before he left.
  • 1.00 Hale sets the posts at night as ordered, with Dacre and Wing sitting guard on the first one. Near midnight the villagers come up the road in silence with lanterns, carrying bread and flowers, and simply stand around the post. The guards have no order that covers this, and Wing slips away without a word.
  • 1.00 Hale returns to the churchyard alone before dawn and finds the schoolmistress's ledger of every burial, field, and wall in the valley. He sees that he could redraw the survey from it, and that a true map of what will be drowned is a different job from the one he was hired for. He copies the first pages into his field book.
  • 1.00 Hale walks the valley with the schoolmistress while Dacre and Wing trail behind. She leads him to the Alder field, where Fenn's abandoned theodolite stands on its tripod, rusted and half buried in bracken. A stone cairn beside it carries Fenn's initials. She tells him that Fenn did what she asked, and that it broke him.
  • 1.00 Hale walks out to meet the trap and tells Sergeant Atkin that the left-hand pages are his own work, and that he alone has been moving the posts. Atkin arrests him, and the villagers, who understand what he has done, stay silent as he is led down the road.
  • 1.00 Hale sits Atkin down in the schoolhouse with the left-hand pages and the parish registers and asks him to read the ground before he acts. The sergeant, whose own mother is buried in a drowned valley, tells Hale quietly that he will log the matter as a boundary dispute needing a magistrate, which buys the village three weeks but costs Hale his post.
  • 1.00 That night Hale slips away from Dacre's lantern and finds Mr. Fenn's abandoned theodolite case hidden in the chapel loft. Inside are Fenn's own pencilled maps of the graves, and he realizes the earlier surveyor did not flee the work but was driven out for refusing to finish it.
  • 1.00 Hale steps forward and says he is in charge, producing the field book with its left-hand pages as evidence that the Board's line runs over graves. Atkin, who has a mother buried in the next parish, takes the book and says he will carry it to the magistrate rather than arrest anyone, but Pruett is now left with a signed public record he cannot bury.
  • 1.00 Pruett arrives on the heels of the trap and demands Atkin arrest Hale and the schoolmistress for obstruction. Atkin, outnumbered and watching the whole valley kneel in the dirt, sends Pruett's men back to the cart and orders Hale to produce a full register of the burial places by the end of the week, which gives the villagers a fragile reprieve.
  • 1.00 The schoolmistress answers Atkin before Hale can, stating that no one is in charge because the valley has no single owner and the dead have been here longest. She then leads the sergeant and Hale through the chapel yard reading names aloud from memory, and Atkin, silenced, takes off his coat to help carry the next post.
  • 1.00 In the Brough police station, Hale lays Fenn's roll of pencilled crosses beside the Board's sheet and tells Atkin that Fenn mapped the graves too. Atkin, whose own parents lie in a drowned valley churchyard, files the charge as 'trespass, withdrawn' and sends the roll to the county coroner's office, which forces the Board to halt the work pending exhumation.
  • 1.00 Hale is released the same evening but goes to Pruett's office, not back to the valley. He offers to finish the survey with every grave marked and the dam line adjusted by eleven meters, and Pruett, afraid of a public inquiry into Fenn's disappearance, agrees to forward the revised sheet to the Board over his own signature.
  • 1.00 Months later, after the October deadline, Hale stands on the new dam wall as the water rises over the terrace. The villagers have already carried the posts, the chapel stones and the bones up to a new burying ground above the 410 line, and the schoolmistress hands him a single post from the Alder field as the last thing they will move.
